items.title: Quickstart
items.text:
openarena compares language models, and agents, on datasets. It runs every model you name on every dataset you name, scores each answer with a reward, and ranks the models on leaderboards. Everything is declared in YAML files and run from one command, openarena, on your own machine. No server and no web app: files in, files out.

This page takes you from nothing to a first ranking. You will:

  1. install the openarena command,
  2. create a workspace, a folder that already holds a working setup,
  3. give it a model it can reach (a local one, or a hosted one and its key),
  4. check the configs, run an evaluation, and rank the result.

Each step says what it does and why, so that when something differs on your machine you know where to look. The guides go deeper on every file.

flowchart LR
    A[openarena init] --> B[.env: keys]
    B --> C[openarena check configs]
    C --> D[openarena evaluations run smoke]
    D --> E[".open-arena/smoke/result.json"]
    E --> F[openarena leaderboards run overall]

Working with a coding agent?

openarena init also writes an AGENTS.md guide and one Agent Skill per task into the workspace. Start Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or another coding agent in the folder and ask in plain words ("add Mistral Small and compare it on GSM8K"). See With a coding agent. Reading this page first still helps you check what it does.

items.title: 1. Install
items.text:
openarena is a Python package (Python 3.12 or newer), developed in open-arena. It installs one command, openarena. The simplest way to get it is uv.

As a toolFrom a clone 
uv tool install "git+https://github.com/Atena-IT/open-arena"
openarena --help

openarena is then on your PATH in any folder. Pick this when you want to use openarena and keep your workspace wherever you like.

git clone https://github.com/Atena-IT/open-arena
cd open-arena
uv sync
uv run openarena --help

Pick this when you want to change openarena, or follow its main branch closely. The command lives in the clone's .venv: prefix every command on this site with uv run --project <path-to-open-arena> (which keeps the folder you are in), or activate the environment once with source .venv/bin/activate and type openarena anywhere.

Datasets kept on a platform

Reading rows from Hugging Face or from local files needs nothing more. Reading them from an observability platform (Langfuse, LangSmith, Opik, Phoenix, Braintrust, Unity Catalog) needs that platform's SDK, shipped as an extra of the package: openarena[langfuse], ..., or openarena[all] for every one. The clone's uv sync installs them all. You need none of them for this page. See Datasets.

items.title: 2. Create a workspace
items.text:
openarena init my-arena
cd my-arena

A workspace is a plain folder. init fills it with a setup that runs as it is, so your first run tests your machine, not your YAML:

What What it is for configs/ The registries, one YAML file each: models, rewards, datasets, mcp_servers, a2a_agents, environments, evaluations, leaderboards. Every file explains its own fields in comments. tasks/hello-world/ A Harbor task folder, for evaluating agents in a sandbox (not used on this page). environments/python/ The build context of the python sandbox environment (not used on this page). .env.template Every key and endpoint a run can read, commented out, each with a line on when you need it. .gitignore Keeps .env (your keys) and .open-arena/ (your runs) out of git. AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .agents/skills/ The guide and skills a coding agent reads. README.md A short version of this page.

The output ends with the next steps it expects you to take; they are the rest of this page.

init writes into the current folder when you give no name (openarena init). It refuses to overwrite any file already there, and then writes nothing at all; --force overwrites. See The workspace for every file and how registries refer to each other.

Run every command from the workspace root

openarena looks for ./configs, reads the .env beside it, and keeps runs in ./.open-arena, all relative to where you stand. Run it from somewhere else and it stops with no configs folder at configs; write one with openarena init. The commands take --configs DIR (and the run commands --state-dir DIR) when you need another layout; see the CLI reference.

items.title: 3. Give it a model
items.text:
The example evaluation, smoke, is a deliberately small sweep: one model answers 20 grade-school math questions from GSM8K, and an exact-match reward checks each answer. Before it can run, the model it names must be reachable.

Models are declared in configs/models.yaml. Each entry has a name, which everything else in the workspace uses, and the id it calls, in litellm's <provider>/<model> form. The prefix picks the provider, and the provider decides what you need: a local server, or an API key.

models:
  qwen38:
    model: ollama/qwen3.8:27b-mlx     # a local Ollama, no API key needed
    type: llm
    description: Qwen 3.8 27B (MLX) served by a local Ollama, no API key needed.
    params:
      temperature: 0
    tags: [local]
  gpt-4o-mini:
    model: openai/gpt-4o-mini          # needs OPENAI_API_KEY
    description: OpenAI's small model, the hosted baseline.
    params:
      temperature: 0
    tags: [openai, hosted]

params is passed with every call. temperature: 0 makes answers as repeatable as the provider allows, which is what you want when comparing models. Models covers every field.

Choose one of these setups.

Local model (Ollama)Hosted model (OpenAI)Both, side by sideAnother provider

smoke uses qwen38 out of the box. Install Ollama, then pull the model:

ollama pull qwen3.8:27b-mlx

No key is needed. ollama/... ids reach Ollama at its default address; if yours runs elsewhere, set OLLAMA_API_BASE in .env (step 4).

When to pick it: you want a first run that costs nothing and sends no data off your machine. Trade-off: a 27B model is slow without a strong GPU. Any model you have already pulled works: change the model: id of qwen38 to it (for example ollama/llama3.2), or add your own entry and name it in smoke.

gpt-4o-mini is already declared. Put your key in .env (step 4), then point smoke at it in configs/evaluations.yaml:

evaluations:
  smoke:
    description: A first run on the hosted baseline.
    language_models: [gpt-4o-mini]
    datasets: [gsm8k-20]
    batch_size: 4

When to pick it: you have no GPU, or you want the fastest first run. Trade-off: each run costs a little, and the questions go to the provider.

A comparison needs at least two models. With Ollama running and OPENAI_API_KEY set, list both:

evaluations:
  smoke:
    language_models: [qwen38, gpt-4o-mini]
    datasets: [gsm8k-20]
    batch_size: 4

Each model × dataset pair runs as its own cell, so one model failing does not stop the other.

Add an entry with that provider's prefix, then name it in smoke:

models:
  my-claude:
    model: anthropic/<model-id>    # the provider's own id; needs ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
    params:
      temperature: 0

.env.template lists the keys of the common providers (OPENAI_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, GEMINI_API_KEY, MISTRAL_API_KEY, GROQ_API_KEY, OPENROUTER_API_KEY) and the endpoint of a vLLM server (HOSTED_VLLM_API_BASE, with its /v1 suffix). See Models for providers and their settings.

Names, not ids

An evaluation lists models by their name in models.yaml (gpt-4o-mini, qwen38), never by the id they call. Two entries calling the same id with different params are two models, and rank separately.

items.title: 4. Set your keys
items.text:
cp .env.template .env

Then uncomment and fill in only what your models need, for example OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-.... Nothing else is needed for this page.

openarena evaluations run loads .env from the workspace before anything reads the environment. It never overrides a variable already set in your shell: if you exported an old OPENAI_API_KEY earlier, that one wins. Unset it, or fix it, rather than editing .env again.

.env stays out of git (.gitignore lists it). Keep keys there, never in the YAML files, which you will want to commit and share. A field that must carry a secret (an agent's headers, say) names the variable as ${NAME} and the run fills it in from the environment; see Secrets in configs.

items.title: 5. Check the configs
items.text:
openarena check configs

check reads every registry file with the same strict schema the run uses, then resolves the references between them: a dataset's reward, an evaluation's models and datasets. It runs nothing and calls no model, so it is instant. On the fresh workspace every file is clean:

✓ configs/models.yaml: 2 models, no problems
✓ configs/rewards.yaml: 2 rewards, no problems
✓ configs/datasets.yaml: 3 datasets, no problems
...
✓ configs/evaluations.yaml: 2 evaluations, no problems
✓ configs/leaderboards.yaml: 2 leaderboards, no problems

Run it after every edit. A typo in a name is the most common mistake, and check points at the line and suggests the fix:

✗ configs/evaluations.yaml: 2 evaluations, 1 error

  error    line 15  evaluations.smoke.language_models[0]
           'gpt4o-mini' is not in `models`
     fix   change 'gpt4o-mini' to 'gpt-4o-mini'

It exits with status 1 on an error, so it also fits a CI step or a pre-commit hook. Because it calls nothing, it cannot tell you that a key is missing or a model is not pulled; the run shows that (step 6). See Checking configs for every kind of problem it reports.

items.title: 6. Run the evaluation
items.text:
openarena evaluations run smoke

What happens:

  1. .env is loaded, as in step 4.
  2. The evaluation smoke and the entries it names are gathered into one config and validated. A copy is written to .open-arena/smoke/config.yaml, so you can always see exactly what ran.
  3. Every model in language_models runs on every dataset in datasets. Each model × dataset pair is a cell: the dataset's rows are rendered into questions, the model answers them batch_size rows at a time, and the dataset's reward scores each answer. A cell's reward is the mean over its rows.
  4. A table is printed per dataset, a row per model and a column per metric, reward first. The result is saved to .open-arena/smoke/result.json.
  qwen38 running…
  qwen38 done reward 0.8500
     gsm8k-20
┏━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━┓
┃ model  ┃ reward ┃
┡━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━┩
│ qwen38 │ 0.8500 │
└────────┴────────┘

Your numbers will differ. With the exact-match reward, 0.8500 means 17 of the 20 answers were exactly the reference. The run also prints the engine's own progress lines between these; -v adds a progress bar, -vv a line per batch.

items.title: What smoke is made of
items.text:
You need not edit anything to run it, but knowing the three entries behind it is what lets you change it. smoke in evaluations.yaml names the models and the datasets:

evaluations:
  smoke:
    description: A first run on the local model.
    language_models: [qwen38]          # `models` keys
    datasets: [gsm8k-20]               # `datasets` keys
    batch_size: 4
Field Value Default What it does language_models list of models names required The models compared. Each one runs on every dataset. datasets list of datasets names required, at least one The datasets every model runs on. batch_size integer, 1 or more each dataset's own Rows sent at once, for every dataset of the evaluation. Higher is faster, until the provider rate-limits you. --batch-size N overrides it for one run. description text none Shown by openarena evaluations list.

The dataset gsm8k-20 in datasets.yaml says where the rows come from, how each row becomes a question and a reference answer, what answers it, and which reward scores it:

datasets:
  gsm8k-20:
    type: huggingface
    description: Grade-school math word problems, GSM8K test split, 20 rows.
    config:
      path: openai/gsm8k                # the Hugging Face dataset
      name: main
      split: test
      limit: 20                         # only the first 20 rows
      batch_size: 4
      # Jinja2 over the row's columns: what the model is asked
      input_template: '{"question": {{ question | tojson }}}'
      # the reference: the text after `####`, commas removed
      output_template: '{"answer": {{ answer.split(''####'')[-1] | replace('','', '''') | trim | tojson }}}'
      input_schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          question: {type: string, description: The question to answer}
        required: [question]
        additionalProperties: false
      output_schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          answer: {type: string, description: "The final numeric answer only, no units or commas"}
        required: [answer]
        additionalProperties: false
    generator:                          # one model call per row
      chain_of_thought: true
      instructions: Solve the problem. Reply with the final number only, no units, no commas.
    reward: exact-match                 # a `rewards` key

The parts that matter most:

  • type and the provider settings (path, name, split, limit) say where the rows come from. limit keeps a first run short; remove it to run the whole split.
  • input_template / output_template turn each raw row into the JSON the model receives and the JSON the reward compares against. Here the reference is cleaned so that exact match is fair: GSM8K stores the worked solution followed by #### 72, and only 72 is kept.
  • input_schema / output_schema describe that JSON. The output schema is also what the model is asked to produce, so its description reads as an instruction: "the final numeric answer only".
  • generator says a model answers each row in one call. chain_of_thought: true lets it reason before answering, which usually helps on math; instructions is said to it before every row.
  • reward names the scorer, a key of rewards.yaml.

And the reward exact-match in rewards.yaml:

rewards:
  exact-match:
    type: exact_match
    direction: max
    description: One when the answer is exactly the reference, zero otherwise.

exact_match is strict and free: no grader model, no cost, but "72" and "72 apples" differ. It is the right choice for answers with one canonical form (numbers, labels, ids). For free text, use a judge reward such as lm_as_judge, which rewards.yaml shows commented out. See Rewards for the catalog and how to choose, and Datasets for every provider, template and answering block.

items.title: Running again
items.text:
Runs resume. Each finished cell is kept under .open-arena/smoke/, and running smoke again only runs the cells that are not scored yet, so an interrupted run picks up where it stopped. Add a model to smoke and only that model runs. --no-cache starts the evaluation over.

A model that cannot be reached fails its cell

A model that cannot be reached does not stop the run, but its cell gives no score. With a missing key (Missing credentials ... OPENAI_API_KEY) or a model Ollama has not pulled, every call fails, and the cell ends with qwen38 failed: no row got an answer: all N row(s) failed; the first error: <error> and — in the table. The other cells still run, and at the end the command prints 1 cell(s) failed: qwen38 × gsm8k-20 and exits 1.

Fix the cause and run the same command again: a failed cell is not kept, so the plain rerun runs it, with no --no-cache. A cell where only some rows failed (a rate limit, say) is different: it finishes, those rows score 0, and that score is kept.

Other mistakes and what you see:

Symptom Cause Fix no configs folder at configs Run from outside the workspace cd into the folder holding configs/, or pass --configs no evaluation 'smok' in configs; choose one of: harbor, smoke Wrong evaluation name Use a listed name; openarena evaluations list shows them failed: no row got an answer ... naming Missing credentials Key not in .env, or a stale one exported in the shell Set the key, then rerun failed: no row got an answer ... with a connection or "not found" error Ollama not running, or the model not pulled Start Ollama, ollama pull the model, rerun failed: ... under a model The cell raised an error; the message says why Fix what it names, and rerun not set in the environment: NAME (at ...) A config uses ${NAME} and the variable is set nowhere Add it to .env, or export it

--json FILE also writes the result to a file of your choice. See Running evaluations for every option, metrics beyond the reward and the trial state, and Reading results for what result.json holds.

items.title: 7. Rank the models
items.text:
openarena leaderboards run overall

A leaderboard runs nothing. It reads every result.json under .open-arena/, takes the newest score of each model × dataset cell across all your runs, and ranks the models in its scope. So you can rank as often as you like, and a model scored in one evaluation is ranked against a model scored in another. With no finished run yet, it stops with no finished runs under .open-arena.

With two models scored on gsm8k-20:

Overall — Every model on every dataset, reward first.
Datasets: gsm8k-20
Shares: reward 100%
┏━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━┓
┃ # ┃ model       ┃  score ┃ reward ↑ ┃ frontier ┃
┡━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━┩
│ 1 │ gpt-4o-mini │ 1.0000 │   0.9000 │    ★     │
│ 2 │ qwen38      │ 0.0500 │   0.8500 │          │
└───┴─────────────┴────────┴──────────┴──────────┘

How to read it:

  • reward ↑ is the raw mean reward; the arrow says higher is better.
  • score is relative, not absolute. Each metric is rescaled per dataset across the models in scope, the best to 1 and the worst to a floor of 0.05, then weighted by its share and averaged over the datasets. That is why 0.90 against 0.85 reads as 1.0000 against 0.0500: the score says who is ahead, the reward column says by how much. With a single model the score is always 1.0000.
  • frontier marks the models no other model beats on every weighted metric at once.
  • A model in scope that was not scored on every dataset in scope is listed under the table as Not ranked, with what it is missing.

The workspace has two leaderboards in leaderboards.yaml:

leaderboards:
  overall:
    title: Overall
    description: Every model on every dataset, reward first.
    datasets: []                       # empty: every dataset scored
    models: []                         # empty: every model scored
    shares: {}                         # empty: the default, reward first
  math:
    title: Math, quality only
    description: Grade-school math, the reward alone decides.
    tags: [math]
    datasets: [gsm8k-20]
    shares:
      reward: 100

overall is the one to start with: it ranks everything you have run. A scoped board like math is what you want once you run several kinds of datasets and need one ranking per question you care about. shares is how you trade quality against cost or latency, once your evaluations record those metrics; budgets leaves out models over a hard limit.

The leaderboard also looks up each model's end-of-life date online. Pass --no-eol to skip that, for example offline. --json FILE writes the ranking to a file. See Leaderboards for scopes, shares and budgets.

items.title: Where to go next
items.text:
You now have the whole loop: declare, check, run, rank. Everything else is more entries in the same files.

You want to Read Understand how a sweep turns rows into a ranking Introduction Know every file of the workspace and how they refer to each other The workspace Add or tune models, local or hosted Models Bring your own benchmark (files, Hugging Face, an observability platform) Datasets Score free text, with a judge or rubrics Rewards Evaluate a model that calls tools MCP tools Compare remote agents A2A agents Evaluate agents on tasks in a sandbox (the workspace's harbor evaluation; needs OPENAI_API_KEY, and Docker or E2B_API_KEY) Harbor tasks, Environments Rank by quality, cost and latency together Leaderboards Let a coding agent do the editing With a coding agent Look up a command or option CLI reference

items.title: CLI reference
items.text:
Everything openarena does from a terminal: start a workspace, check it, list what it holds, run an evaluation, rank the results. This page lists every command, every option and every exit code. The guides explain what goes in the YAML; this page explains how to drive it.

openarena --help                      # the command groups
openarena evaluations run --help      # one command's options

The command is installed with the package (openarena is its entry point). From a checkout of the library, prefix it with uv run: uv run openarena check configs.

items.title: At a glance
items.text:
command what it does reads writes openarena init writes a new workspace the packaged template DEST/ openarena check validates registry files configs/ nothing openarena <registry> list prints one registry as a table configs/ nothing openarena evaluations run runs a saved evaluation configs/, .env, tasks/, environments/ .open-arena/<name>/ openarena leaderboards run ranks models from finished runs configs/, .open-arena/*/result.json nothing, unless --json

A typical session:

openarena init my-arena && cd my-arena
cp .env.template .env                 # the keys your models need
openarena check configs               # fix what it reports
openarena evaluations run smoke -v    # a first, small run
openarena leaderboards run overall    # rank what ran

items.title: Paths, global options and exit codes
Run it from the workspace folder
items.text:
Every command resolves its paths against the folder you run it from. Two defaults matter:

option default used by what it points at --configs DIR configs every list, evaluations run, leaderboards run the folder holding models.yaml, datasets.yaml, ... (The workspace) --state-dir DIR .open-arena evaluations run, leaderboards run where runs are kept, one folder per evaluation

From the workspace folder neither is needed. From anywhere else, pass both, and pass the same --state-dir to every command that should see the same runs.

The two paths resolve differently

--state-dir is relative to the folder you run from. The files around the configs are not: evaluations run reads .env, tasks/ and environments/ from the parent of --configs. Run openarena evaluations run smoke --configs my-arena/configs from outside my-arena, and the keys and Harbor tasks come from my-arena/, but the run lands in ./.open-arena/smoke/, not in my-arena/.open-arena/. A later openarena leaderboards run from inside my-arena will not find it.

items.title: Global options
items.text: The top-level command takes only --help. There is no global --configs, no --version and no config file of its own: each option belongs to the command that uses it, and goes after the command (openarena evaluations run smoke --configs DIR, not openarena --configs DIR evaluations run smoke).

items.title: Exit codes
items.text:
code when 0 the command did what it was asked. For check: no error (warnings are allowed). For evaluations run: the sweep finished and every cell gave a score (a 0 included) 1 an error the command reports as Error: ...: no configs folder, an unknown evaluation or leaderboard name, files in the way of init, no finished runs to rank, an invalid evaluation config, a ${NAME} whose variable is not set, a leaderboard entry that does not validate. Also evaluations run when a cell ended FAILED or INVALID, check finding at least one error, a crash inside a run (a traceback), and an interrupt (Ctrl-C prints Aborted!) 2 a usage error, found before anything runs: an unknown command or option, a missing NAME, --batch-size 0, an unknown --template

A run that exits 1 still wrote its results

openarena evaluations run runs every cell, whatever fails. A cell that gave no score (a hard error, an agent whose MCP servers gave no tools, no row answered because of a missing key or an unreachable model) is printed as <model> failed: <why> and recorded in result.json with value: null and a status other than COMPLETED. After writing result.json and printing the table, the command prints N cell(s) failed: <model> × <dataset>, ... and exits 1. A cell where only some rows failed completes, with those rows at 0, and does not change the exit code: read the warnings for those (Reading results).

items.title: Environment variables
items.text:
The CLI has no environment variables of its own. openarena evaluations run loads the workspace's .env (beside configs/) before anything else, and never overrides a variable your shell already set; when it finds one it prints Read <path>/.env. No other command loads .env; openarena check only reads it to look up the ${NAME} references a config holds.

Any string in a registry may name a variable as ${NAME} (an agent's headers, a server's env). The run replaces each one after loading .env, and refuses to start, naming each variable and where it is used, when one is not set. The snapshot config.yaml keeps the references. See Secrets in configs.

What a run reads from the environment, through that file or your shell:

variable for OPENAI_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, GEMINI_API_KEY, ... the hosted models your models.yaml ids call (Models) OLLAMA_API_BASE, HOSTED_VLLM_API_BASE local model servers not on their default address E2B_API_KEY, ARENA_HARBOR_SANDBOX, ARENA_HARBOR_WORKDIR Harbor trials: the sandbox provider, and where task folders and trials go (Environments) MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI, MLFLOW_EXPERIMENT_NAME, ARENA_MLFLOW_TRACING MLflow tracing, for the arena app and run_sweep called from Python; openarena evaluations run does not switch tracing on

The full list, with what each one does, is in The workspace.

In CI, prefer the shell

Set the keys as CI secrets in the environment. They win over .env, so a .env left in the folder cannot override them.

items.title: openarena init
items.text:
Writes a ready-to-use workspace: every registry file with each field explained in comments, an example Harbor task, an environment's build context, and what a coding agent needs to work in the folder.

openarena init [DEST] [--template NAME] [--force]
argument / option type default effect DEST folder . (here) where to write; created if missing --template NAME choice default the template to copy. default is the only one shipped today --force flag off overwrite files already there

It writes:

DEST/
  configs/          one registry per file: models, rewards, datasets, mcp_servers,
                    a2a_agents, environments, evaluations, leaderboards
  tasks/            Harbor task folders (task.toml, instruction.md, environment/,
                    tests/test.sh, solution/solve.sh)
  environments/     an environment's build context
  .agents/skills/   the openarena Agent Skills, one per action
  AGENTS.md         the guide a coding agent reads first; CLAUDE.md links to it
  README.md  .env.template  .gitignore

Then it prints a table of the files and the entries each registry holds, and the next steps. .sh files are made executable, since Harbor runs them as they are. CLAUDE.md is a symbolic link to AGENTS.md; where links cannot be made, it is a copy.

Without --force, init is all or nothing. If any file it would write already exists, it writes nothing, names every file in the way, and exits 1.

When to use it. Once per workspace, into a fresh folder. Use --force on an existing workspace only to reset it to the template: it overwrites your configs/*.yaml, AGENTS.md and the example tasks with the template's, and leaves files the template does not have alone. To pick up newer Agent Skills after an upgrade without touching your configs, run init into an empty folder and copy its .agents/skills/ over.

openarena init my-arena               # a new folder
openarena init                        # the current folder
openarena init my-arena --force       # back to the template; your configs are overwritten

See The workspace for what each file holds.

items.title: openarena check
items.text:
Validates registry files against the same schema a run loads, and every reference between them (a dataset's reward, an evaluation's models). Each problem is printed with its line, the dotted path to the field, what is wrong and the edit that fixes it.

openarena check [PATH] [--configs DIR]
argument / option type default effect PATH folder or file configs a configs folder (every <registry>.yaml in it), or one registry file --configs DIR folder the file's own folder only for a single file: the folder whose registries its references are checked against. Ignored when PATH is a folder

A file's registry is read off its name only (datasets.yaml holds datasets); a file with any other name is an error, whatever its top-level key. In a folder, any other .yaml or .yml file is reported too, since nothing reads it.

exit when 0 no error; warnings are printed but allowed 1 at least one error; or PATH does not exist; or the folder has no registry files

When to use it. After every edit, and as the first step of any CI job: a run refuses a config check rejects, and check is fast, offline and free. It reads files only. It does not call a model, download a dataset or start a sandbox, so a wrong dataset path or a missing key still shows up at run time. It does look each ${NAME} up in your shell and the workspace's .env, and warns (without failing) about one set in neither.

openarena check                                  # ./configs
openarena check configs/datasets.yaml            # one file, references against configs/
openarena check draft/datasets.yaml --configs configs   # a draft, against the real registries

Use the last form to validate a file before you move it into configs/. See Checking configs for how to read the output.

items.title: Registry listings
items.text:
openarena models list         [--configs DIR]
openarena rewards list        [--configs DIR]
openarena datasets list       [--configs DIR]
openarena mcp-servers list    [--configs DIR]
openarena a2a-agents list     [--configs DIR]
openarena environments list   [--configs DIR]
openarena evaluations list    [--configs DIR]
openarena leaderboards list   [--configs DIR]

Each prints one registry of the configs folder as a table, a row per entry. They read the YAML as it is, without validating it: run openarena check for that. A registry with no file prints an empty table.

option type default effect --configs DIR folder configs the configs folder to read; exits 1 if it does not exist command columns guide openarena models list model (the litellm id), type, description Models openarena rewards list type, direction, description Rewards openarena datasets list type, reward, description Datasets openarena mcp-servers list transport, command, url MCP tools openarena a2a-agents list url, description A2A agents openarena environments list docker_image, cpus, memory_mb, network_mode Environments openarena evaluations list language_models, datasets, description Running evaluations openarena leaderboards list title, datasets, models, description; an empty scope shows as all Leaderboards

When to use them. To find the exact name to pass to openarena evaluations run or openarena leaderboards run, or to see which model id a name calls before you spend money on it.

openarena evaluations list
openarena models list --configs ../other-arena/configs

items.title: openarena evaluations run
items.text:
Runs the evaluation saved as NAME: every model of its language_models on every dataset of its datasets, one cell per pair.

openarena evaluations run NAME [--configs DIR] [--state-dir DIR] [--no-cache]
                               [--batch-size N] [--json FILE] [-v | -vv]
argument / option type default effect NAME text required a key of evaluations.yaml; an unknown name exits 1 and lists the ones there --configs DIR folder configs the configs folder. Its parent is where .env, tasks/ and environments/ are read --state-dir DIR folder .open-arena where the run is kept, in <state-dir>/NAME/; relative to the current folder --no-cache flag off drop the run's saved state and start every cell over --batch-size N integer, at least 1 the evaluation's batch_size, else each dataset's own, else 1 rows sent at once, for every dataset of this run --json FILE file none also write the result to FILE; parent folders are created -v, --verbose count silent -v a progress bar per cell, -vv a line per batch

What it does, in order:

  1. Loads .env from the parent of --configs, without overriding your shell.
  2. Gathers the evaluation and every entry it names (its datasets, their rewards and MCP servers, Harbor environments, A2A agents; all models) into one config, replaces each ${NAME} with its variable, and validates it. An invalid config, or a variable that is not set, exits 1 before any call.
  3. Writes that config to <state-dir>/NAME/config.yaml: the exact record of what ran, with the ${NAME} references rather than their values.
  4. Copies the Harbor folders the run uses beside it, fresh each time: environments/<name>/ for each Harbor environment, and the folder of each harbor_tasks dataset (tasks/). A file deleted from the source is gone from the copy too.
  5. Runs the sweep, every cell whatever fails. It prints each dataset, then each model as it starts and finishes with its metrics, then <model> failed: <why> for any cell that failed.
  6. Writes <state-dir>/NAME/result.json, prints a table per dataset (a row per model, a column per metric, — where a cell has no value), and writes --json FILE if asked.
  7. If any cell ended FAILED or INVALID, prints N cell(s) failed: <model> × <dataset>, ... and exits 1.
.open-arena/NAME/
  config.yaml            what ran
  result.json            the scores
  tasks/ environments/   copies of the Harbor folders, for Harbor datasets
  harbor/                Harbor trials, for Harbor datasets

Check first

The run validates only the entries the evaluation names. Run openarena check before it to catch every problem at once, with the fix.

items.title: Resuming, and when to use --no-cache
items.text:
The run keeps each cell's state in <state-dir>/NAME/. Running the same NAME again with the same --state-dir skips every cell that completed, reading its scores back, and re-runs the cells that failed, were interrupted or were never reached. So:

  • Interrupted (Ctrl-C, a closed laptop, a crash): run the same command again.
  • A cell failed (<model> failed: <why>): fix the cause, run the same command again. Only the failed cells run. A missing key, a model server that was down or an unknown model id fails the cell (no row got an answer: ...), so this covers them too: no --no-cache.
  • Some rows scored 0 in a finished cell (a rate limit, a flaky call): the cell is kept as it is. To score those rows again, run with --no-cache.
  • You changed what a finished cell depends on (a dataset's rows or templates, a reward, a model's params, the model list): add --no-cache. Without it, the old cells are reused and the table mixes old and new.

--no-cache throws away finished work

It deletes the saved state before starting, so every cell is paid for again. Never add it to resume a run, and do not leave it in a script you rerun after a failure.

items.title: Choosing --batch-size
items.text:
A batch is the rows sent at once, so it is the concurrency knob. Higher is faster, until you hit a provider's rate limit, a local server's memory, or the number of sandboxes you can start for Harbor rows. The order of precedence is --batch-size, then the evaluation's batch_size, then each dataset's own, then 1.

situation batch size a local model on one GPU (Ollama, vLLM) low, 1 to 4; raise it while the server keeps up a hosted API with a generous rate limit 8 to 32 rate-limit errors in the failed cells lower it, then rerun: only the failed cells run Harbor tasks, where each row is a sandbox as many sandboxes as your provider or Docker host can hold debugging one row's answer 1, so errors are easy to follow

Use the flag for a one-off change; put a value you want every time in evaluations.yaml.

items.title: --verbose and --json
items.text:
Without -v, a run prints one line when each cell starts and ends: enough for CI logs. -v adds a progress bar per cell, useful in a terminal on a long dataset. -vv prints a line per batch, useful to see where a run stalls.

result.json is always written in the run folder. --json FILE writes the same content to a path you choose: an artifact path for CI, or a dated file to keep a history. Its format is in Reading results.

items.title: When to use which setup
items.text:
goal command a first smoke run, on a few rows (limit: 5 on the datasets) openarena evaluations run smoke -v resume after an interruption or a fixed failure openarena evaluations run smoke (the same command, no --no-cache) rerun after editing a dataset, reward or model openarena evaluations run smoke --no-cache a fast run on a hosted API openarena evaluations run compare --batch-size 16 CI: a clean run with a result to archive openarena evaluations run nightly --no-cache --json out/nightly.json keep two variants' runs apart openarena evaluations run smoke --state-dir .open-arena-b A CI job, step by step 
set -e
cd my-arena
openarena check configs                       # exit 1 on any config error
openarena evaluations run nightly --no-cache --json out/nightly.json
# exit 1 when a cell failed, after writing out/nightly.json
openarena leaderboards run overall --no-eol --json out/ranking.json

The run exits 1 when any cell failed, so set -e stops the job there, with out/nightly.json already written for the artifacts. --no-cache makes each nightly run independent of the last one; drop it if you would rather a retried job resume. --no-eol keeps the ranking from depending on the network. Keys come from CI secrets, which win over any .env.

See Running evaluations for the evaluations.yaml fields, and Harbor tasks for sandboxed runs.

items.title: openarena leaderboards run
items.text:
Ranks the models on the leaderboard saved as NAME, from the runs already finished. It runs no model.

openarena leaderboards run NAME [--configs DIR] [--state-dir DIR] [--no-eol] [--json FILE]
argument / option type default effect NAME text required a key of leaderboards.yaml; an unknown name exits 1 and lists the ones there --configs DIR folder configs the configs folder holding leaderboards.yaml --state-dir DIR folder .open-arena where the runs are; every */result.json under it is read --no-eol flag off leave out eol_days, the days before each model's announced end of life, which is looked up online --json FILE file none also write the ranking to FILE; parent folders are created

It first validates the saved entry as openarena check does; one that does not validate (a share or a budget the schema refuses) exits 1 with the leaderboard 'NAME' does not validate:, each problem and its fix, and a pointer to openarena check configs/leaderboards.yaml. Then it reads every result.json under --state-dir, newest first, keeps the newest score of each cell, applies the leaderboard's scope, weights and budgets, and prints the datasets in scope, the share of each metric, and a table: rank, model, score, each metric with ↑ or ↓ for which way is better, and ★ on the Pareto frontier. Then a line for each model it left out: Not ranked <model>: <why> (not scored on a dataset in scope, or a metric missing) or Over budget <model>: <limit>.

exit when 0 a ranking was printed, even if some models were not ranked 1 no configs folder; no leaderboard NAME; the entry does not validate; no result.json under --state-dir

About --no-eol. End-of-life dates come from litellm's pricing table, Azure's published retirement schedule, and OpenRouter for openrouter/... ids. The online sources are cached for a day, and a shipped snapshot answers when the network does not. Add --no-eol when you want the ranking to depend only on your runs: offline, in CI, or when a model's lifetime is not something you rank on. It removes the eol_days metric entirely, so a share you gave to eol_days in leaderboards.yaml has nothing to weigh.

The JSON. --json FILE writes leaderboard (the saved entry, with its name) and the ranking: datasets, models, shares, axes, rows (each with rank, model, score, values, on_frontier), skipped, gaps and excluded. Use it to feed a dashboard or to diff two rankings.

openarena leaderboards list
openarena leaderboards run overall
openarena leaderboards run math --no-eol --json out/math.json
openarena leaderboards run overall --state-dir ../shared-runs   # rank runs kept elsewhere

One state folder, many evaluations

A leaderboard ranks across every evaluation under the state folder. Run your evaluations into the same --state-dir, and one leaderboard can compare models that never ran in the same evaluation, as long as each is scored on every dataset in scope.

See Leaderboards for scope, shares, budgets and how the score is computed.

items.title: With a coding agent
items.text:
An openarena workspace is plain files: YAML in configs/, results in .open-arena/. That makes it easy work for a coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, ...). It can read every registry, write new entries, check them, run them and report from the result files, the same way you would.

Start the agent in the workspace folder and ask in plain words:

Add Mistral Small and compare it with gpt-4o-mini on GSM8K, then tell me which is better for the money.

This page covers what the agent reads, the skills it uses, the CLI behaviour it relies on, prompts that work, and how to keep it cheap and honest.

items.title: What the agent reads
items.text:
openarena init writes three things for an agent next to the configs (see The workspace for the rest of the layout):

file what it is why it is there AGENTS.md the guide an agent reads first: the layout, the rules, the commands, which skill to read for what, how to report so the agent starts from the workspace's rules instead of guessing CLAUDE.md a link to AGENTS.md (a copy where links cannot be made, as on Windows without the right) agents that look for CLAUDE.md find the same guide .agents/skills/ one Agent Skill per action, copied from the package the YAML of each registry, field by field, and the commands that go with it

The rules in AGENTS.md are the ones that most often trip an agent up:

  • Refer to entries by name. An evaluation lists models.yaml keys, not model ids. The id appears once, in models.yaml.
  • Invent no field. Entries refuse unknown fields. The skills list the real ones, and openarena check names the valid choices.
  • Templates render JSON. Pipe every value through | tojson, and give an input_schema / output_schema. Look at real rows first.
  • Check after every edit, run small before big. limit: 5 on a dataset first, then the full size.
  • Do not start or stop model servers or Docker. If one does not answer, say so.
  • Report from the files. Rewards from result.json, the ranking that leaderboards run printed, and what failed with the error. Never from memory.

Edit AGENTS.md for your project

It is your file once init has written it. Add what the agent should know about your work: which models are off limits, a cost ceiling, which evaluation is the reference one. The agent reads it before anything else.

items.title: The skills
items.text:
Each skill is a folder with a SKILL.md. Its description starts with "Use when ...": the agent reads the descriptions and opens the skill whose situation matches the task. The body teaches the YAML entry field by field, with examples the test suite checks against the engine, and the commands to run after.

skill the agent opens it when what it teaches openarena-init-workspace starting a project from nothing, or it needs the general rules openarena init, the layout, how every registry file is written, the edit, check, run loop openarena-check-configs after any YAML edit, or when a command fails on a config openarena check, reading each problem and applying its fix, looping until clean openarena-add-model adding, changing or choosing a model a models.yaml entry: the litellm id, type, params, the provider prefix and its API key openarena-add-reward a dataset needs something to score its answers exact comparison or a judge model; the catalog types and the kwargs each accepts openarena-add-dataset a benchmark has to become a dataset the provider config, the Jinja2 templates, the schemas, what answers each row, the reward openarena-add-mcp-tools models should answer by calling tools an MCP server in mcp_servers.yaml and an agent: dataset that uses it openarena-compare-a2a-agents comparing remote A2A agents instead of models a2a_agents.yaml, an a2a dataset, an evaluation whose axis lists agents openarena-add-environment ordinary rows should be worked by an agent in a sandbox a Harbor environment in environments.yaml and a harbor: dataset over it openarena-create-harbor-task a terminal or codebase task, checked by a script, has to be written a Harbor task folder, file by file, and the harbor_tasks dataset that runs it openarena-run-evaluation models have to be evaluated on datasets an evaluations.yaml entry, openarena evaluations run, resuming, cost openarena-rank-leaderboard finished runs have to become a ranking a leaderboards.yaml entry, openarena leaderboards run, why a model is unranked openarena-read-results a run finished or failed result.json, why a cell failed or scored 0, Harbor trial logs

A typical task touches several. "Add GSM8K and compare two models" goes through add-dataset, add-reward, check-configs, run-evaluation and read-results, in that order.

arena-import: a skill that is shipped but not installed

The package also holds arena-import. It is for the arena web app, not the CLI: it converts results computed elsewhere (an HTML dashboard, a CSV or JSON from another tool) into the JSON the app's Leaderboards → Import takes, and checks it against the app's validator. init copies only the openarena-* skills, so a workspace does not get it. Copy it by hand (below) if you import results into the app.

items.title: Installing the skills
items.text:
In a new workspaceIn an existing projectFor every project

Nothing to do. openarena init copies every openarena-* skill into .agents/skills/, and AGENTS.md tells the agent to read the one that fits before acting.

openarena init my-arena
cd my-arena

The skills ship inside the package, under openarena/skills/. Find the folder and copy (or link) what you need into the folder your agent reads skills from:

SKILLS=$(python -c "import openarena, pathlib; print(pathlib.Path(openarena.__file__).parent / 'skills')")
mkdir -p .agents/skills
cp -r "$SKILLS"/openarena-* .agents/skills/

Prefix python with uv run when openarena is installed in a uv project.

Copy the folders into your user-level skills folder, for example ~/.claude/skills/ or ~/.agents/skills/, depending on which one your agent reads.

Where your agent looks

.agents/skills/ is where init puts the skills, and AGENTS.md points the agent there by name, so it finds them either way. If your agent also loads skills on its own from another folder, you can link that folder to .agents/skills/ so they load as native skills. Check your agent's documentation for the folder it uses.

Refreshing the skills after an upgrade

The skills change with the engine: a new reward type or dataset field lands in the skill too. After upgrading openarena, copy the folders again as in the "existing project" tab. Do not use openarena init --force for this: it overwrites every template file as well, your configs/ and AGENTS.md included.

items.title: What makes the CLI agent-friendly
items.text:
The CLI has no prompts and no interactive mode. Every command takes its input from arguments and files, so an agent can run it as is. The behaviours an agent leans on:

behaviour command what the agent does with it exit code 1 on an error openarena check edit, check, read the problems, fix, check again until it exits 0. Warnings alone exit 0 exit code 1 on a failed cell evaluations run every cell still runs and result.json is written; the last line names each failed <model> × <dataset> a line, a location and a fix per problem openarena check the fix line is often the YAML to write, so the agent does not guess field names refuse instead of overwrite openarena init writes nothing and names every file in the way; --force is the only way past it errors that name the choices evaluations run, leaderboards run an unknown evaluation or leaderboard name fails with choose one of: ...; a leaderboard entry that does not validate is refused with its problems a listing per registry openarena <registry> list what is already defined, before adding a duplicate results as JSON on disk evaluations run writes .open-arena/<name>/result.json; --json FILE on both run commands writes another copy the agent reads numbers from JSON with a short script, not from a printed table the exact config that ran .open-arena/<name>/config.yaml when a result looks wrong, compare what ran with what was meant resume by default evaluations run a rerun after fixing a key only pays for the cells that failed or did not finish

The printed output is tables for people. The JSON files are what an agent should read, and the openarena-read-results skill tells it to read them with a script, not by eye.

A failed cell fails the command, after the others ran

openarena evaluations run runs every cell whatever fails, writes result.json, prints the table, and exits 1 if any cell failed, with N cell(s) failed: <model> × <dataset>, .... Each failed cell also printed <model> failed: <why> after its dataset and has value: null and a status other than COMPLETED in result.json. Exit 0 does not mean every row answered: a cell where only some rows failed completes with those rows at 0. Ask the agent to read the warnings and every cell's reward, not just the exit code.

Two more details to know:

  • .env is read for evaluations run, from the folder above configs/, never over a variable already set. The agent does not need to export keys, and should never print or commit .env (the workspace's .gitignore already leaves it out). A secret a config field must carry (an agent's headers) is written as ${NAME} and set in .env (Secrets in configs); check warns when a ${NAME} is set nowhere.
  • The cache does not notice config changes. After changing a dataset, a model's params or a reward, a rerun reuses old cells unless it gets --no-cache. See Running evaluations.

items.title: The loop
items.text:
flowchart LR
    A[read AGENTS.md<br/>and the skill] --> B[edit configs/]
    B --> C[openarena check]
    C -- errors --> B
    C -- clean --> D[smoke run<br/>limit: 5]
    D -- failed cells --> E[read result.json<br/>and the errors]
    E --> B
    D -- looks right --> F[full run]
    F --> G[report from<br/>result.json]

The smoke step is the one to insist on. It catches a wrong template, a missing key or a reward that scores everything 0 for the price of a few rows.

items.title: Example prompts
items.text:
Prompts work best when they name the outcome, the size and what to report. The agent picks the skills.

Add a datasetRun a sweepRead resultsRank runs

Add the test split of openai/gsm8k from Hugging Face as a dataset called gsm8k-test, scored on the final number. Look at a few real rows first, use limit: 5 for now, check it, and run it on gpt-4o-mini only. Show me the reward and one row's answer.

The agent uses add-dataset (provider, templates, schemas), add-reward (an exact comparison on the number), check-configs, then run-evaluation with a one-model evaluation. Asking for one answer makes it show you what the model actually returned, which is where template and reward mistakes show.

Compare qwen38 and gpt-4o-mini on gsm8k-20. Tell me how many rows times models that is before you run it. Run a smoke version with limit: 5 first, then the full one.

The agent writes an evaluation, states the size, runs the small version, checks every cell's status, then raises the limit and runs again with --no-cache (the limit changed what the cells depend on).

The math-compare run finished. Which model is best on reward, and which is cheapest? List every cell that failed and the error it gave. Quote numbers from result.json only.

The agent uses read-results: reads result.json with a script, reports the frontier and the failed cells with their printed errors.

Write a leaderboard over all finished runs that weighs reward 70% and cost 30%, leaves out any model whose cost is over 0.05, and print it. Tell me which models were not ranked and why.

The agent uses rank-leaderboard (shares and a budget), runs openarena leaderboards run, and quotes the "Not ranked" and "Over budget" lines it prints.

qwen38, gpt-4o-mini and gsm8k-20 are entries of the example workspace; use the names in yours.

items.title: Guarding cost
items.text:
Every row is at least one model call per model, plus one per judge reward. A Harbor row is a whole agent session in a sandbox. An agent that runs the full size on its first try can spend real money on a broken config.

guard how when limit on the dataset limit: 5 in the dataset's config every new or changed dataset, before the first run a smoke evaluation a second evaluation with one cheap or local model before adding paid models to the sweep batch_size on the evaluation, or --batch-size N for one run lower it for a local model, a rate-limited key, or Harbor on a small machine ask for the size first "tell me rows times models before you run" in the prompt or in AGENTS.md any run with paid models or judges resume, do not restart rerun the same name after a fix; --no-cache only when the config changed after a missing key or a server that was down: those cells failed, and a plain rerun runs them again

A dataset with a limit looks like this (other fields left out):

datasets:
  gsm8k-test:
    type: huggingface
    reward: exact-match
    config:
      limit: 5     # raise to the full size once the smoke run looks right
      # ...

And a smoke evaluation next to the real one:

evaluations:
  math-smoke:
    description: One local model, to check the datasets before paying for the sweep.
    language_models: [qwen38]
    datasets: [gsm8k-20]
    batch_size: 4
  math-compare:
    description: The real comparison.
    language_models: [qwen38, gpt-4o-mini]
    datasets: [gsm8k-20]

Put the budget in AGENTS.md

A line such as "never run more than 200 rows times models without asking" in AGENTS.md applies to every session, not just the one where you remembered to say it.

items.title: When to let it drive, when to do it yourself
items.text:
let the agent do it do it yourself writing and fixing YAML until check is clean putting keys in .env mapping a benchmark's columns to templates and schemas starting Ollama, a vLLM server or Docker smoke runs and reading why a cell failed approving the full run when it uses paid models or judges reading result.json and summarising the numbers deciding what the reward should measure writing a leaderboard and printing it deciding which results you publish

The agent is good at the mechanical part: field names, template syntax, the check loop. The judgment calls stay yours, and what counts as a correct answer is the main one. A reward that scores the wrong thing still gives clean numbers.

items.title: Reviewing what it changed
items.text:
Keep the workspace in git and git diff configs/ shows everything the agent did. What to look at:

  • Model ids and params in models.yaml. A wrong provider prefix is a different model, and a changed temperature changes every result.
  • Rewards. The type, its kwargs, and direction. A reward that compares the wrong field can score 0 everywhere, or 1 everywhere.
  • Templates and schemas. Does the input template send what the benchmark means to ask? Does the output schema allow the answer form the reward expects?
  • limit. Still at the smoke value when you meant the full run, or removed when you meant a smoke run.
  • Evaluations. The model and dataset lists you asked for, nothing more.

Then compare .open-arena/<name>/config.yaml with the diff: it is what actually ran, every entry gathered. (.open-arena/ is git-ignored, so it is not in the diff.)

Report what failed

A failed cell says why. A missing key or a model server that is not running is yours to fix, not the agent's to work around. If it swapped a model, dropped a dataset or loosened a reward to get a green run, the diff shows it.

items.title: See also
items.text:
• The workspace: the layout init writes.
  • Checking configs: what check reports and what it does not.
  • Running evaluations and Reading results.
  • CLI reference: every command and option.

items.title: Introduction
items.text:
openarena answers one question: which model, or agent, does this job best, at what cost? You describe the candidates and the job in YAML. openarena runs every candidate on every dataset, scores each answer, and ranks them.

Use it when you have to pick, or keep picking: a cheaper model for a task that already works, a local model to replace a hosted one, the model that uses your MCP tools best, the deployed agent that answers your users best, the coding agent that solves your tasks in a sandbox. It measures on your data, on your machine, and keeps every score so the next comparison builds on the last one.

This page is the mental model: the pieces, how they name each other, what a run does, and which setup fits which goal. The guides then go through each piece field by field.

items.title: The pieces
items.text:
Everything is declared in registries: one YAML file per kind of thing, under configs/, each a mapping of names to entries.

registry an entry is it names it is named by models a litellm model id, its type (llm or embedding) and its params nothing evaluations, judge rewards, leaderboards rewards a catalog reward (type), its kwargs (config), and which way is better (direction) its judge model, if any datasets datasets where the rows come from, how each row becomes a question and an expected answer, what answers it, and the reward that scores it a reward, MCP servers, an environment evaluations, leaderboards mcp_servers a tool server, reached over stdio, streamable_http, sse or websocket nothing datasets with an agent: block, environments a2a_agents a remote agent reached over A2A: a URL, headers, a timeout nothing evaluations over a2a datasets environments a sandbox: a Docker image or a Dockerfile, resources, network MCP servers datasets with a harbor: block evaluations a sweep: the models (or agents) × the datasets to run models or A2A agents, datasets openarena evaluations run leaderboards a way to rank finished runs: a scope and each metric's share of the score datasets, models openarena leaderboards run

Harbor tasks are the one piece that is not a registry entry. They are folders under tasks/, each with its instruction, its sandbox and its own tests, read by a dataset of type: harbor_tasks.

items.title: How they reference each other
items.text:
flowchart LR
  E[evaluation] -->|language_models| M[models]
  E -->|"language_models (a2a sweep)"| A[a2a_agents]
  E -->|datasets| D[datasets]
  D -->|reward| R[rewards]
  R -->|config.language_model| M
  D -->|agent.mcp_servers| S[mcp_servers]
  D -->|harbor.environment| V[environments]
  V -->|mcp_servers| S
  D -->|"type: harbor_tasks"| T[(tasks/ folders)]
  E ==>|evaluations run| O[(.open-arena/*/result.json)]
  L[leaderboard] -.->|reads| O
  L -.->|scope| D

The evaluation is the root: it says what to run, and everything else is reached from it by name. A leaderboard is not tied to an evaluation. It reads the results every run left behind and ranks the models in its scope.

items.title: Names are the glue
items.text:
Every reference is a registry name, never a provider id. A dataset's reward is a rewards key. An evaluation's language_models are models keys. A judge's language_model is a models key too, and must be a chat model. Names match ^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9_.-]*$, up to 128 characters.

This has consequences worth knowing:

  • Two entries calling one id are two models. gpt-4o-mini and gpt-4o-mini-hot can both call openai/gpt-4o-mini with a different temperature, and are compared as two candidates. That is how you compare settings, not only models.
  • Scores are stored under the name. A leaderboard joins runs by model and dataset name. Rename an entry and its earlier scores no longer line up with its new ones. Point an entry at another id while keeping its name, and new runs score something else under the old name.
  • A typo is caught before anything runs. openarena check configs resolves every reference across the registry files and says which line to fix. See Checking configs.

items.title: A minimal workspace
items.text:
The smallest set of entries that runs and ranks, shown together here but kept in models.yaml, rewards.yaml, datasets.yaml, evaluations.yaml and leaderboards.yaml. Follow the names: math-compare names two models and a dataset, the dataset names a reward, and the leaderboard scopes the dataset.

models:
  qwen38:
    model: ollama/qwen3.8:27b-mlx
    params: {temperature: 0}
  gpt-4o-mini:
    model: openai/gpt-4o-mini
    params: {temperature: 0}

rewards:
  exact-match:
    type: exact_match
    direction: max

datasets:
  gsm8k-20:
    type: huggingface
    config:
      path: openai/gsm8k
      name: main
      split: test
      limit: 20
      input_template: '{"question": {{ question | tojson }}}'
      output_template: '{"answer": {{ answer.split(''####'')[-1] | replace('','', '''') | trim | tojson }}}'
      input_schema:
        type: object
        properties: {question: {type: string}}
        required: [question]
      output_schema:
        type: object
        properties: {answer: {type: string, description: The final number only}}
        required: [answer]
    reward: exact-match

evaluations:
  math-compare:
    language_models: [qwen38, gpt-4o-mini]
    datasets: [gsm8k-20]

leaderboards:
  math:
    title: Math, quality only
    datasets: [gsm8k-20]
    shares: {reward: 100}

openarena init writes a workspace with entries like these and more, each file explaining its own fields in comments. See The workspace.

items.title: What a run does
items.text:
openarena evaluations run math-compare
  1. Reads .env beside configs/, never over a variable already set. That is where provider keys go, and the values of any ${NAME} a config uses (Secrets in configs).
  2. Gathers the evaluation: the entry, the datasets it lists, and the rewards, MCP servers, environments and A2A agents those name. Every model is kept, since rewards and metrics name their models by key.
  3. Validates it whole, each ${NAME} replaced by its variable. An unset variable, an unknown name, a judge that is not a chat model, a chat model on an embedding dataset, a Harbor agent that cannot call the model: the run stops here, before any call.
  4. Writes a snapshot to .open-arena/<evaluation>/config.yaml, and copies the environments' build folders and the harbor_tasks folders beside it. That snapshot is exactly what ran, with the ${NAME} references kept rather than the secrets.
  5. Prepares each dataset: reads its rows, renders each through input_template (the question) and output_template (the expected answer), and builds what answers it, once per model.
  6. Runs the grid model by model: every dataset for the first model, then the next, so a local server loads each model once. One cell is one model on one dataset. Rows go in batches of batch_size: the --batch-size option, else the evaluation's, else the dataset's, else 1.
  7. Scores every answer with the dataset's reward, from 0 to 1. The cell's reward is the mean over its rows; the cost and tokens the calls used are recorded beside it, with any extra metrics.
  8. Writes result.json next to the snapshot, and prints one table per dataset: a row per model, a column per metric.
flowchart LR
  rows[(dataset rows)] -->|input_template| q[question]
  rows -->|output_template| ref[expected answer]
  q --> m{{model or agent}}
  m --> a[answer]
  a --> r[reward]
  ref --> r
  r --> cell[cell: reward, cost, tokens]
  cell --> res[(result.json)]
  res --> board[leaderboard]

A finished cell is kept. Run the same evaluation again and it resumes: cells that completed are read back, cells that failed or never ran are run. This is what makes a long sweep cheap to fix: correct a key or a template, run again. When you change something finished cells depend on (the model list, a dataset's reward or metrics), add --no-cache to start over. See Running evaluations and Reading results.

A failed cell is a result, not a crash

One model failing does not stop the others: every cell runs, and every failure is reported. A cell that cannot give a score (a template naming a missing column, an agent whose MCP servers give no tools, a missing key or a model server that is down, so that no row got an answer) prints <model> failed: <why> and shows — in the table, and the command exits 1 once the table is printed. A plain rerun runs those cells again. A cell where only some rows failed finishes, and those rows score 0. Read the warnings and the failed lines before the scores.

items.title: Ranking is a separate step
items.text:
openarena leaderboards run math

A leaderboard reads every result.json under .open-arena/, takes the newest score of each model on each dataset, and ranks the models in its scope. Each metric is normalized per dataset against the models in scope, weighted by its share, and the result averaged over the datasets. With no shares, the reward weighs most and the other measurements break ties. Budgets (cost at most 0.05, say) are hard limits: a model breaking one is left out of the ranking and listed as over budget. A model not scored on every dataset in scope is listed as not ranked.

Keeping the two steps apart is deliberate. You pay for a run once and rank it as many ways as you need: quality only, quality per dollar, one domain, every domain. And runs add up: a model run this week on math and next week on code ranks on both. See Leaderboards.

items.title: What answers each row
items.text:
A dataset says what answers its rows with at most one block. That choice decides what is under test, what the answer looks like, and which rewards make sense.

block what is under test what the reward scores the evaluation's language_models guide none, or generator: a chat model, one call per row the model's structured answer chat models Datasets tools: a chat model's tool calls, one call, nothing executed the calls it made chat models Datasets agent: a chat model working with real tools over MCP, in a loop the agent's final answer chat models MCP tools a2a: {} a remote agent, whatever is inside it the agent's reply A2A agents A2A agents harbor: with an environment a model driving a Harbor agent (terminus-2, claude-code, codex, ...) in a sandbox, on your rows what it wrote to answer_file, else its last message chat models Environments harbor: on type: harbor_tasks the same, on task folders with their own tests the score the tests gave chat models Harbor tasks embedding: an embedding model retrieving the row's passages the passages it returned embedding models Datasets

items.title: Which one fits your goal
items.text:
Plain model QATool callingAgent with MCP toolsRemote agentsSandboxed tasksRetrieval

Block: none, or generator: for instructions and chain_of_thought.

Pick it when the job is a question in, an answer out: extraction, classification, math, summaries, multiple choice. It is the cheapest and fastest setup, one call per row, and the easiest to score exactly.

It does not tell you how the model behaves with tools or over many steps.

Block: tools: with tool_schemas.

Pick it when you want to know whether a model picks the right function with the right arguments, without running a tool server. Nothing executes, so it is fast, repeatable and safe. Score it with tool_calls_accuracy against the expected calls.

It does not tell you whether the model recovers from a tool's error or uses a result well: there is no result. For that, use agent:.

Block: agent: naming mcp_servers.

Pick it when the job needs real tools: search, a database, your own API. The model calls the tools, reads the results and decides, until it answers. This measures the model as an agent over your tools.

Trade-offs: each row is several calls, so it costs more and takes longer. The servers must be reachable from your machine. A tool whose answers change over time makes scores drift between runs.

Block: a2a: {}, and the evaluation lists a2a_agents keys.

Pick it when what you compare is an agent already deployed behind the A2A protocol, built with any stack. Each row is sent as one message and the reply is scored. openarena does not see or choose the model inside.

Constraint: an evaluation's axis is either models or A2A agents, so a2a datasets go in an evaluation of their own.

Block: harbor:.

Pick it when the job is done by acting, not replying: editing files, running code, working a terminal. The model drives a Harbor agent in a sandbox. Over your rows, name an environment and score the answer with any reward. Over task folders (type: harbor_tasks), each task's own tests score it, read by the harbor_verifier reward.

Trade-offs: the slowest and most expensive setup: a sandbox per row, many calls per row. It needs Docker, or a sandbox provider's key.

Block: embedding:.

Pick it when you choose an embedding model for search. Each row brings a query and its passages, the model under test ranks them and returns the top k, and retrieval_recall scores how many of the expected passages came back.

Constraint: an embedding dataset runs in an evaluation of its own, over embedding models.

flowchart TD
  start{What do you compare?} -->|deployed agents| a2a["a2a: {}"]
  start -->|embedding models| emb["embedding:"]
  start -->|chat models| acts{Is the job done by acting?}
  acts -->|"no, by answering"| tools{Does it need tools?}
  tools -->|no| gen["generator (or no block)"]
  tools -->|"the call, not its result"| tc["tools:"]
  tools -->|real tools| ag["agent: + mcp_servers"]
  acts -->|"yes: files, code, a terminal"| hb{Task folders with tests?}
  hb -->|yes| ht["harbor: on harbor_tasks"]
  hb -->|no| he["harbor: + environment"]

items.title: Choosing a reward
items.text:
Every dataset names one reward, the primary score of its cells. It scores one answer from 0 to 1, and its direction says which way is better on a leaderboard.

kind examples how it scores pick it when watch out for deterministic exact_match, answer_accuracy, tool_calls_accuracy, retrieval_recall compares the answer with the fields output_template renders, each field whole (a list of calls, a nested object); what else the program returns stays out of the score there is one right answer: a number, a label, a choice, a call an answer right in substance but different in form scores 0 ("42" and "42.0"); tighten the output_schema a model judges lm_as_judge, rubrics_as_judge, multi_judge_panel, ... a judge model (a models key) reads the answer, with the expected answer when there is one the answer is open text: a summary, an explanation, an agent's report every row costs a judge call; a judge has its biases; changing the judge changes every score the task's own tests harbor_verifier reads the score a Harbor task's tests/ wrote type: harbor_tasks datasets the tests are the spec: a weak test passes a wrong solution

Prefer deterministic when you can

A deterministic reward is free, instant and gives the same score every time, so a gap between two models is a gap between the models. Shape the answer so it can be compared: the final number only, a letter, a label from an enum in the output_schema. Reach for a judge when the answer cannot be reduced to a value.

Keep the judge out of the race

A judge that is also under test grades its own style. Name a judge model that is not in the evaluation's language_models, and keep it the same across the runs you want to compare.

With a judge, output_template is optional: without a reference, the judge grades the answer on the question and its instructions. A dataset can also record extra scores beside its reward with metrics:; they show as columns and can weigh on a leaderboard. See Rewards.

items.title: Designing evaluations
items.text:
An evaluation is a grid: every model on every dataset. A few rules of thumb:

  • One evaluation per question you want answered. math-compare, support-agents: small grids are quick to run and to resume. Leaderboards bring them back together.
  • Start small. A dataset's limit caps its rows. Run 20 rows, read the answers and the failures, then raise it. A template bug then costs 20 calls, not 2,000.
  • One kind of axis per evaluation. Chat models, embedding models and A2A agents each need an evaluation of their own.
  • batch_size is concurrency. A batch is sent at once: larger batches finish sooner and hit rate limits sooner, and a local model server may need it low.
  • seed is not determinism. It seeds the engine's own randomness, not the provider's sampling. For steadier answers, set temperature: 0 on the model.

items.title: What runs where
items.text:
• Models are called through litellm. Any provider it routes (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Mistral, Ollama, vLLM, ...) works, with that provider's key in the environment or in .env. Each call is priced from litellm's table, completed before the run from other price sources; a model on a local server (ollama/, vllm/) costs nothing.
  • Runs happen on your machine, one cell after another. No server is needed, and a run's state stays under .open-arena/<evaluation>/.
  • MCP servers are spawned by the run (stdio) or reached by URL from your machine.
  • Harbor trials run in a sandbox: the provider named by ARENA_HARBOR_SANDBOX, E2B by default (with an E2B_API_KEY), and the local Docker when that provider has no credentials.

items.title: The arena
items.text: openarena is the engine of the arena, a web app that edits the same registries from forms, runs the same evaluations, and shows the leaderboards. A workspace written by openarena init is a workspace the arena opens as it is. This site documents the engine and its command; the app has its own documentation in the repository.

items.title: Where to go next
items.text:
• New here: the Quickstart, then The workspace.
  • Writing entries: Models, Rewards, Datasets, then the guide for the block you picked.
  • Running and reading: Running evaluations, Reading results, Leaderboards.
  • Working with a coding agent: With a coding agent.
  • Every command and option: CLI reference.

items.title: The workspace
items.text:
A workspace is a plain folder. Everything a comparison needs is a file in it: the registries under configs/ say what to compare, the Harbor folders beside them say what sandboxes and tasks look like, .env holds the keys, and every run writes its results under .open-arena/. There is no database and no server: files in, files out. You can read it, diff it, commit it and hand it to a colleague or a coding agent.

This page explains each part of that folder: what it is for, how the openarena command finds it, what it writes, and what belongs in git. The fields of each registry have their own guides (links below).

flowchart LR
  subgraph ws[workspace folder]
    env[.env]
    cfg[configs/*.yaml]
    tasks[tasks/]
    envs[environments/]
  end
  env -->|keys, endpoints| run((openarena evaluations run NAME))
  cfg -->|the evaluation NAME and every entry it names| run
  tasks -->|copied| run
  envs -->|copied| run
  run --> out[.open-arena/NAME/<br/>config.yaml, result.json, trial state]
  out --> lb((openarena leaderboards run))
  cfg -->|the leaderboard| lb

items.title: Start one
items.text:
openarena init my-arena        # DIR defaults to the current folder

init copies a template into the folder, then copies the engine's Agent Skills (every openarena-* skill) into .agents/skills/. The result runs as it is, given the keys or local servers its examples need (see What the example runs).

option what it does when to use it DIR where to write; created if missing a new project folder, or . to turn the current folder into a workspace --template NAME the template to copy; default is the only one shipped leave it --force overwrite files that are already there to refresh the skills or reset an example file; it replaces your edits to those files

Without --force, init checks every target file first. If any one exists, it writes nothing at all and names every file in the way. So init on an existing workspace is safe: it cannot half-overwrite it.

--force overwrites, it does not merge

--force copies the template's configs/*.yaml over yours as well as the skills. To pick up newer skills after upgrading the package, run init into an empty scratch folder and copy .agents/skills/ across, or commit first and restore the files you edited with git.

items.title: Layout
items.text:
my-arena/
  configs/                          the registries, one YAML file each
    models.yaml                     name -> litellm id, type, params
    rewards.yaml                    name -> catalog reward, its kwargs, direction
    datasets.yaml                   name -> rows, templates, what answers, reward
    mcp_servers.yaml                name -> MCP tool server
    a2a_agents.yaml                 name -> remote A2A agent
    environments.yaml               name -> Harbor sandbox
    evaluations.yaml                name -> models x datasets, the sweep to run
    leaderboards.yaml               name -> how to rank finished runs
  tasks/hello-world/                a Harbor task folder
  environments/python/environment/  the `python` environment's build context
  .agents/skills/                   Agent Skills for a coding agent, one per action
  AGENTS.md                         the guide a coding agent reads first
  CLAUDE.md                         a link to AGENTS.md
  README.md                         the quickstart
  .env.template                     every key and endpoint a run may read
  .gitignore                        keeps .env and .open-arena/ out of git
  .env                              your keys (you create it from the template)
  .open-arena/                      runs, created by the first one
part written by read by commit it? configs/ you, or a coding agent every command yes: it is the experiment tasks/, environments/ you evaluations run, for Harbor datasets yes local data files (JSONL, CSV, ...) you local and folder datasets yes if small and shareable, else keep them elsewhere .agents/skills/, AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md init coding agents yes, so everyone's agent works the same way README.md, .env.template, .gitignore init people yes .env you evaluations run; check looks up ${NAME}s in it never: it holds secrets .open-arena/ evaluations run leaderboards run, you no, by default (see Versioning)

items.title: configs/: the registries
items.text:
Each registry is one file, named after it, holding one top-level key with the same name. Entries are keyed by a name you choose, and other entries refer to them by that name.

# configs/<registry>.yaml
<registry>:              # the one top-level key, the file's own name
  <name>:                # an entry; others refer to it by this name
    <field>: <value>
