items.title: MultiJudgePanel
items.text:
MultiJudgePanel(panel_language_models=None, smart_language_model=None, agreement_threshold=0.2, prompt_template=None, examples=None, instructions=None, name='multi_judge_panel', in_mask=None, out_mask=None, reduction='mean', in_mask_pattern=None, out_mask_pattern=None, program=None)

Judge panel: multiple small LMs vote, smart LM breaks ties.

Each (y_true, y_pred) is scored in parallel by every model in panel_language_models. If the spread between the lowest and highest panel scores is <= agreement_threshold, the panel is treated as in agreement and the panelist whose score is closest to the mean wins. If the spread exceeds the threshold, smart_language_model is invoked and its verdict overrides the panel.

Example:

program.compile(
    reward=MultiJudgePanel(
        panel_language_models=[
            "ollama/llama3.2",
            "ollama/mistral",
            "ollama/qwen",
        ],
        smart_language_model="openai/gpt-4o",
        agreement_threshold=0.2,
        instructions="Score 0.0–1.0 on factual correctness.",
    ),
)

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default panel_language_models list

The panelists, each given as a LanguageModel, a config dict, or a string identifier (e.g. "ollama/llama3.2"). Required.

None smart_language_model

Escalation model used on disagreement. Same forms as panelists. Required.

None agreement_threshold float

Maximum allowed (max - min) panel score spread for the panel to be deemed "in agreement" (default 0.2).

0.2 prompt_template str

The default jinja2 prompt template forwarded to every panelist and the smart judge.

None examples list

The default examples forwarded to every judge.

None instructions str

The default judging-task instructions forwarded to every judge (same prompt, different LMs).

None name str

Optional. string name of the reward instance (default "multi_judge_panel").

'multi_judge_panel' in_mask list

Optional. list of keys to keep to compute the reward.

None out_mask list

Optional. list of keys to remove to compute the reward.

None reduction str

Optional. How per-sample rewards are reduced over a batch — one of "mean" (default), "sum", "min", "max", "none".

'mean' in_mask_pattern str

Optional. Regex; fields whose names match are kept (OR-combined with in_mask).

None out_mask_pattern str

Optional. Regex; fields whose names match are dropped (OR-combined with out_mask).

None

items.title: RetrievalRecall
items.text:
RetrievalRecall(name='retrieval_recall', in_mask=None, out_mask=None, in_mask_pattern=None, out_mask_pattern=None)

Recall of the target's list fields in the prediction's.

items.title: ToolCallsAccuracy
items.text:
ToolCallsAccuracy(name='tool_calls_accuracy', in_mask=None, out_mask=None, in_mask_pattern=None, out_mask_pattern=None)

How many of the gold tool calls the model made, with the right arguments and nothing extra.

items.title: HarborVerifier
items.text:
HarborVerifier(key='reward', name='harbor_verifier', in_mask=None, out_mask=None, in_mask_pattern=None, out_mask_pattern=None)

The verifier's score for the row: rewards[key] of the Harbor trajectory.

items.title: A2A agents
items.text:
Most evaluations compare models: openarena calls each model itself, with the prompt, tools and settings you wrote. An A2A evaluation compares deployed agents instead. Each agent is a running service that speaks the Agent2Agent protocol at its own URL. openarena sends it each row as a message, waits for its answer, and scores that answer with the dataset's reward, exactly as it would score a model's.

What is under test is the whole service: its prompts, its model, its tools, its memory, its guardrails. openarena sees none of that. It sees the question it sent and the text that came back.

Three files are involved:

file what it holds for A2A configs/a2a_agents.yaml one entry per agent: where it is, how to authenticate, how long a row may take configs/datasets.yaml a dataset with an empty a2a: {} block: its rows go to agents configs/evaluations.yaml an evaluation whose language_models lists agent names, not model names 
flowchart LR
  R[row] -->|input_template| Q[JSON question]
  Q -->|one user message| A[A2A agent]
  A -->|message, or task + artifacts| T[answer text]
  T -->|read into the output shape| S[reward]
  S --> C[cell: agent x dataset]

items.title: A2A agent or model + MCP tools?
items.text:
openarena can evaluate an agent two ways. Over A2A, you point it at the service you already run. With an agent: dataset, openarena is the agent: it gives a model of models.yaml the tools of MCP servers and runs the loop itself.

A2A agent model + MCP tools what is tested the deployed service, as its users reach it a model's ability to use the tools you give it what you can vary which deployment (version, environment, vendor) the model, its params, the tools the evaluation's axis agents (a2a_agents keys) models (models keys) cost, tokens, latency not measured: the agent spends on its side measured per cell what openarena sees the final answer the answer, from a loop it runs itself needs a running, reachable A2A endpoint the MCP servers, a tool-calling model

Choose A2A when the thing you ship is the agent, and you want to know how that exact build behaves: a release candidate against the current release, two vendors' agents on the same questions, a regression check before a deploy. Rebuilding such an agent as model + tools would test your copy of it, not the agent.

Choose model + MCP tools when the question is which model to put inside an agent, or how models handle a given set of tools. Only then can you swap the model, read its cost and tokens, and hold everything else fixed.

items.title: Registering an agent
items.text:
a2a_agents:
  support-prod:
    url: https://support-agent.example.com       # required: the agent's base URL
    headers:                                      # sent on every request, the card's included
      Authorization: Bearer ${SUPPORT_PROD_TOKEN}   # read from the environment or .env
    timeout_sec: 120                              # one row, from sending to the last word (default 300)
    description: The support agent, current release.
    tags: [support, prod]
  support-staging:
    url: https://support-agent.staging.example.com
    card_path: /a2a/agent.json                    # the card is not at the well-known path
    headers:
      Authorization: Bearer ${SUPPORT_STAGING_TOKEN}
    description: The support agent, release candidate.
    tags: [support, staging]

The key (support-prod) is the agent's name everywhere else: in an evaluation's language_models, in result.json, on a leaderboard.

field required default what it does url yes the agent's base URL; must start with http:// or https://; a trailing / is dropped card_path no the well-known path where the agent card is, relative to url, when it is not at <url>/.well-known/agent-card.json headers no {} HTTP headers sent on every request to the agent, the card request included timeout_sec no 300 how long one row may take, in seconds, from sending the message to the agent's last word; above 0 description no for you and openarena a2a-agents list; the run does not read it tags no [] labels for browsing; the run does not read them

No other field is accepted. In particular there is no streaming switch, no retry count and no rate limit: see what a row does.

items.title: url and the agent card
items.text:
On the first row of a cell, openarena reads the agent's card from <url>/.well-known/agent-card.json, or from card_path under url when you set it. The card says which interfaces the agent serves and at which address. openarena opens a client on the interface the card prefers and sends every message there.

Look at the card before you register an agent:

curl -s https://support-agent.example.com/.well-known/agent-card.json
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://support-agent.example.com/.well-known/agent-card.json

Messages go where the card says, not to url

url is only where the card is read. The messages go to the address in the card's interfaces. An agent behind a proxy or a tunnel often advertises its internal address (http://localhost:9999, a container name): the card reads fine, then every message fails to connect. Fix the card the agent serves; openarena has no field to override it.

Set card_path only when the agent publishes its card somewhere other than the well-known path, for example an older agent serving /.well-known/agent.json. It is a path under url, not a full URL.

items.title: headers: authentication
items.text:
Every request to the agent goes through one HTTP client that carries these headers: the card request, each message, each poll of a running task. Use them for whatever the agent's gateway expects: Authorization, an API key header, a tenant header.

a2a_agents:
  vendor-agent:
    url: https://agents.vendor.example.com/support
    headers:
      X-Api-Key: ${VENDOR_API_KEY}
      X-Tenant: arena-eval

Header names cannot contain whitespace, and values are strings: quote a value YAML would read as a number.

Keep tokens out of the file with ${NAME}. When a run reads its config, after it has loaded the workspace's .env, each ${NAME} in a value is replaced by the environment variable NAME:

# .env, beside configs/
VENDOR_API_KEY=...
  • a2a_agents.yaml and the run's copy, .open-arena/<evaluation>/config.yaml, keep ${VENDOR_API_KEY}, not its value, so either can be committed.
  • A variable set neither in your shell nor in .env stops the run before it starts, naming the variable and where it is used; openarena check warns about it first.
  • $${NAME} writes a literal ${NAME}.

Any string value takes a reference, url included (url: ${SUPPORT_AGENT_URL}). Still use a key made for evaluation, scoped to the least it needs and easy to revoke.

items.title: timeout_sec: how long a row may take
items.text:
timeout_sec bounds one whole row: sending the message, waiting for the answer, and polling a task until it ends. It is also the timeout of each HTTP request, the card's included. A row that runs past it gets no answer and scores 0, with a warning; the cell goes on (see when a row fails).

Set it from the agent's real behaviour, measured on a few rows:

agent where to start answers in one turn, no tools 30 to 60 calls a few tools, searches 120 to 300 (the default) long tasks: research, code, multi-step workflows above 300

Too low scores a slow row 0, as if the agent had answered wrong. Too high only costs time when the agent hangs: the run waits that long before it says so. Rows of a batch are sent at once, so an agent under load is slower than the same agent answering one question alone: measure with the batch_size you will use.

items.title: Staging or production
items.text:
Register each deployment as its own entry, as above. The name is what results and leaderboards show, so put the environment in it.

StagingProductionLocal

The default for evaluation. You can run as often as you like, at any batch_size, without real users feeling the load or real systems seeing the questions. Compare support-staging (the candidate) with support-prod (the release) before promoting.

Measures what users actually get, with the production model, data and configuration. But every row is real traffic: it counts against the agent's rate limits and quotas, costs money on its side, may land in its logs and analytics, and may trigger side effects if the agent can act (open tickets, send mail). Use a small limit, a low batch_size, and questions that do not make the agent act.

An agent you run on your machine (url: http://localhost:9999), for a quick check while developing it. Its card must advertise an address the run can reach too.

items.title: The dataset: a2a: {}
items.text:
A dataset whose rows go to A2A agents carries an empty a2a: block. It takes no settings: which agents answer is the evaluation's choice, not the dataset's.

datasets:
  support-questions:
    type: local
    config:
      path: support.jsonl              # {"question": "...", "expected": "..."}
      limit: 20
      input_template: '{"question": {{ question | tojson }}, "reply_format": "a JSON object with one string field, answer, and nothing else"}'
      output_template: '{"answer": {{ expected | tojson }}}'
      input_schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          question: {type: string, description: The customer's question}
          reply_format: {type: string, description: How to reply}
        required: [question, reply_format]
      output_schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          answer: {type: string, description: The answer to give the customer}
        required: [answer]
    a2a: {}                            # always empty: the agents come from the evaluation
    reward: judge

The provider, the templates, limit and batch_size work as for any dataset (Datasets). What changes is how the question reaches the agent and how its answer is read back.

items.title: What the agent receives
items.text:
The row's rendered input, a JSON object, is sent as the text of one user message: the agent literally reads {"question": "...", "reply_format": "..."}. Nothing else goes with it: no system prompt, no schema, no earlier rows. Each row is a new message, not linked to the ones before.

So write the input_template for the agent as a user would. Most agents read a JSON object fine; if yours expects prose, render one field that holds the whole prompt.

items.title: What openarena reads back
items.text:
The answer the agent must give depends on the dataset's output_template.

With an output template and schemaWithout an output template

The agent must answer a JSON object. Its whole reply is parsed as JSON; a reply that is a single fenced block (```json ... ```) is unwrapped first. The object is the answer the reward compares with the expected one.

This is what lets you score against a reference: exact_match, answer_accuracy, or a judge that reads the expected answer. The agent never sees your output_schema, so tell it the format in the input, as reply_format does above.

A reply that is not a JSON object gets no answer: the row scores 0, with a warning, and the cell goes on. Use this only with an agent that follows the instruction every time, or the zeros measure its formatting, not its answers.

An inputs-only dataset: leave out output_template and output_schema. The agent's text is taken as it is, as one chat message ({"role": "assistant", "content": "..."}). Nothing has to parse.

There is no expected answer, so only a judge can score it: say what a good answer is in the judge's instructions. This suits agents whose replies are free text you cannot force into JSON.

datasets:
  support-open:
    type: local
    config:
      path: support.jsonl
      input_template: '{"question": {{ question | tojson }}}'
      input_schema: {type: object, properties: {question: {type: string, description: The customer's question}}, required: [question]}
    a2a: {}
    reward: judge

An output template without an output schema

The expected answer is then a chat message, and the agent must answer a JSON object of that shape ({"role": ..., "content": ...}) too: free text scores the row 0. Give an output_schema, or drop the output_template.

items.title: Message or task
items.text:
An A2A agent replies in one of two ways, and openarena handles both:

  • A message: its text is the answer.
  • A task: openarena asks for the task again every second until it ends. When it ends completed, the answer is the text of the task's artifacts, joined by new lines, or, when they hold no text, the text of the task's final status message. When it ends any other way (failed, canceled, rejected, input required, auth required), the row gets no answer and scores 0, with a warning saying what the agent said, e.g. the agent's task ended input required: Which order?.

Only text parts are read. An agent that answers with file or data parts only gives an empty answer.

One turn only

An agent that asks a clarifying question (input required) scores the row 0: openarena does not answer back. Put everything the agent needs in the row.

items.title: The evaluation: agents on the axis
items.text:
An evaluation over A2A datasets lists agents in language_models, by their a2a_agents key:

evaluations:
  support-release-check:
    description: The release candidate against the current release.
    language_models: [support-staging, support-prod]   # a2a_agents keys
    datasets: [support-questions]
    batch_size: 2                                      # rows sent to an agent at once

Every dataset of such an evaluation must be an a2a dataset. A run cannot mix them with model datasets, because its axis is either agents or models; it refuses with an A2A dataset cannot share a run with other kinds of dataset; run it on its own. Run agents and models as two evaluations.

The cells run one agent after another; within a cell, batch_size rows are sent at once. See Running evaluations for the run itself and for resuming.

items.title: What a row does
items.text:
sequenceDiagram
  participant O as openarena
  participant A as A2A agent
  Note over O,A: first row of the cell only
  O->>A: GET the card (url + card_path, with headers)
  A-->>O: agent card: interfaces, skills
  loop each row, batch_size at once
    O->>A: send message: the rendered input as text
    alt the agent answers a message
      A-->>O: message
    else the agent answers a task
      A-->>O: task (still working)
      loop every second, until it ends or timeout_sec
        O->>A: get task
        A-->>O: task state, artifacts
      end
    end
    O->>O: answer text, output shape, reward
  end
  • The card is read once per cell, and the same client serves all of its rows; it is closed when the run ends.
  • openarena does not stream, even when the card says the agent can: it sends, then waits for the reply or polls the task.
  • There is no retry inside a cell. A row the agent does not answer (an HTTP error, a reply that is not JSON where JSON is expected, a task that does not complete, the timeout) is warned about as A2A agent <url>: <why> and scores 0; the other rows still count. When no row of a cell got an answer, the cell fails instead, with no row got an answer: ... and the first error, and the next run of the same command runs it again.

items.title: What is recorded
items.text:
what where each cell's reward (the mean over its rows) and status .open-arena/<evaluation>/result.json (Reading results) why a cell failed the run's output: <agent> failed: <why> why a row scored 0 without an answer the run's output: A2A agent <url>: <why> the first rows of each cell: input, expected answer, the agent's answer as scored handed to the caller of the run, which is how the arena app shows them; the CLI keeps scores only

What is not recorded: the agent's intermediate steps, its tool calls, the task's status history, non-text parts. openarena only sees the final answer, so it cannot score how the agent got there. To score a trajectory (tool_correctness, step_efficiency), the agent must put it in its answer, or you evaluate it as model + MCP tools, where openarena runs the loop.

items.title: Scoring an agent
items.text:
The reward is the dataset's, as for models (Rewards):

your agent answers reward a short field you can compare exactly (a category, an id, yes or no) exact_match or answer_accuracy, with an output schema free text, and you have a reference answer a judge (lm_as_judge, rubrics_as_judge), with an output schema and a reply instruction in the input free text, no reference a judge on an inputs-only dataset, its criteria in instructions several qualities to report apart (correct, polite, on policy) rubrics_as_judge

A judge's calls are made by openarena, with its own model, and counted as reward_cost.

items.title: Comparing agents fairly
items.text:
Same rows, same reward, same load. Agents in one evaluation share the dataset, its order and its reward, so their cells compare directly. Keep batch_size the same between runs you compare: load changes how fast an agent answers, and an agent that times out under load loses the cell.

Against a plain model. One evaluation cannot hold both. Write two datasets over the same rows, one with a2a: {} and one with generator: (or agent:), with the same reward, and run them as two evaluations. Their rewards are on the same scale, but they are two datasets: a leaderboard normalizes each dataset against its own agents or models. Read the two result.json side by side.

Two things make that comparison uneven; say so when you report it:

  • Cost. A model's cell reports its cost and tokens; an agent's cannot, since it spends on its own side. A cost share or budget on a leaderboard means nothing for agents.
  • Instructions. The model gets the dataset's generator.instructions and output_schema with each call; the agent only gets what the input says. Put the same instructions in the agent's input, or the model starts ahead.
Ranking agents on a leaderboard

A leaderboard ranks agents like models, by the names in result.json. Leave models: [] to take every agent scored. When you list agent names in models:, openarena check warns that each one is not in models; the warning does not stop the leaderboard. Weight reward and your own metrics, not cost.

items.title: Rate limits and cost
items.text:
openarena does not rate-limit agents. What it sends:

  • one card request per cell;
  • per row, one message, plus one task request per second while a task runs;
  • batch_size rows at once.

Keep batch_size within the agent's quota, and low for production. Start with limit: 5 on the dataset, read the answers, then run the full size. The agent's own spend (its model calls, its tools) is not in the results: read it on the agent's side.

items.title: Checking and debugging
items.text:
openarena check configs validates a2a_agents.yaml, the a2a block and the evaluation's references, without contacting any agent (Checking configs).

you wrote openarena check reports fix url: localhost:9999 `url` must start with http:// or https:// write the scheme: http://localhost:9999 no url `url:` is missing, fix add `url: http://localhost:9999` add the agent's base URL streaming: true, retries: 3, any field not in the table not a field of a a2a_agents entry remove it; an entry reads card_path, description, headers, tags, timeout_sec, url timeout_sec: 0 Input should be greater than 0, fix set `timeout_sec:` to more than 0 a positive number of seconds a ${NAME} in a value whose variable is set nowhere a warning: `${NAME}` is not set in your shell or in <workspace>/.env; a run that reads it refuses to start add NAME=... to .env, or export it a header name with a space header '...' must not contain whitespace rename it a header value YAML reads as a number Input should be a valid string quote it a2a: {agent: helper} `a2a:` takes no settings write a2a: {}; list agents in the evaluation a2a: {} beside generator: or agent: `generator`, `a2a` are mutually exclusive keep one an agent name not in a2a_agents.yaml an error on evaluations.<name>.language_models[i] add the agent, or fix the name an a2a dataset beside a model dataset in one evaluation an A2A dataset cannot share a run with other kinds of dataset two evaluations

items.title: When a row fails
items.text:
check reads files only. Whether the agent is up, accepts your token and answers in the expected shape shows only when the run reaches it. A row the agent does not answer scores 0 and the run warns A2A agent <url>: <why>; the cell goes on. A cell where no row got an answer (the agent is down, every request is refused) fails with no row got an answer: all N row(s) failed; the first error: <why>, and openarena evaluations run exits 1. Fix the cause and run the same command again: failed cells run again, cells already scored are kept. A cell that scored with some rows at 0 is kept too: rerun it with --no-cache once the cause is fixed.

the run says likely cause fix a connection error or timeout on the first row the agent is down, or its card advertises an address the run cannot reach curl the card; check its interface URLs an HTTP 401 or 403 missing or wrong headers test the token with curl -H an HTTP 404 on the card the card is elsewhere set card_path a timeout on later rows timeout_sec too low for this agent, or too many rows at once raise timeout_sec, lower batch_size the agent did not answer JSON for the dataset's output schema free text where the output template needs a JSON object add a reply instruction to the input, or make the dataset inputs-only the agent's JSON answer is not an object a JSON list or string ask for an object in the instruction the agent's task ended failed: ... (or canceled, rejected, input required, auth required) the agent gave up, or wanted a second turn read its message; put what it needs in the row the agent sent no answer the agent closed the reply with no message or task on the agent's side

items.text:
• Datasets: providers, templates, schemas, limit, batch_size
  • Rewards: judges and their instructions

  • A2aAgentEntry: the schema of an entry
  • Coding agents: the openarena-compare-a2a-agents skill

items.title: Checking configs
items.text:
openarena check reads your registry files and reports everything wrong with them, before anything runs. Each problem comes with the file, the line, the dotted path to the field, what is wrong, and a fix you can apply as written.

It uses the same strict schema the engine and the arena app load. A field the engine would refuse is refused here first, in seconds, instead of when a sweep starts.

openarena check                                 # ./configs, every registry file in it
openarena check configs/datasets.yaml           # one file, references checked against its folder

items.title: Why run it
items.text:
A run already validates its config. The check is still worth running, because it covers more and says more:

  • It reads every entry. evaluations run loads only the evaluation you name and the entries it selects. A typo in a dataset no evaluation uses yet waits there until the day you add it. check reads all of them.
  • It reports every problem at once. A run stops at the first thing it refuses. check keeps going, so one pass lists everything to fix.
  • It gives the line and the fix. A run's error names the rule. check names the line, and the rename, value or snippet that fixes it.
  • It costs nothing. It reads files only. No model is called, no dataset is downloaded, no sandbox starts, no key is needed. The one thing it reads besides the configs is the workspace's .env, without loading it, to tell you whether each ${NAME} a config uses is set.

items.title: When to run it
items.text:
When Why After every edit to configs/ The fastest way to catch a typo, an unknown field, a broken reference. Before every evaluations run A run refuses what check rejects, but only once it starts loading. After renaming or removing an entry Every name is a key other files refer to. check finds each place that still uses the old name. In CI, on every pull request A broken config never reaches the main branch. It exits 1 on any error. In a pre-commit hook Same, before the commit exists. After a coding agent edits configs The agent's skill loops on it until clean; run it yourself to confirm. See With a coding agent.

After a rename, check the folder

Renaming exact-match to exact in rewards.yaml breaks every dataset whose reward: still says exact-match. The errors show up in the files that refer to the name, not in the one you edited. So run openarena check configs on the whole folder, not just the file you changed. Each stale reference reads 'exact-match' is not in `rewards`, with a fix naming the closest key.

items.title: Usage
items.text:
openarena check [PATH] [--configs DIR]
Argument / option What it does Default PATH A configs folder, or one registry file. configs --configs DIR For a single file only: the folder whose registries its references are checked against. Ignored when PATH is a folder. the file's own folder

There is one check command for every registry. There is no openarena datasets check. The CLI reference lists every command.

A folderOne fileA file elsewhere 
openarena check configs

Checks each <registry>.yaml in the folder, each one's references against the others. Any other .yaml or .yml file in the folder is an error, since nothing reads it. A folder with no registry file fails with no registry files in configs; write some with `openarena init`.

Use this by default, in CI, and after renames.

openarena check configs/datasets.yaml

Checks one file, its references against the other registry files of its own folder. Shorter output while you work on one registry. It does not tell you about other files that refer to this one: after a rename, check the folder.

openarena check drafts/datasets.yaml --configs configs

Checks a file that lives outside the workspace (a draft, a file from a colleague) against the registries of a real configs folder, before you copy it in. References are checked against DIR only, not against the file's own folder.

items.title: Exit codes
items.text:
Code When 0 No error in any file. Warnings are allowed. 1 At least one error; or nothing at PATH (nothing at <PATH>; pass a configs folder or a registry file); or a folder with no registry file.

Warnings never fail the command. To fail CI on warnings too, use the Python API.

items.title: Which registry a file holds
items.text:
A registry is read only from the file named after it: models.yaml, rewards.yaml, datasets.yaml, mcp_servers.yaml, a2a_agents.yaml, environments.yaml, evaluations.yaml, leaderboards.yaml. That file holds one top-level key, the registry's own. See The workspace for the layout.

A file with any other name is an error, not a registry file: a registry is read only from `<registry>.yaml`, even when its top-level key is right. When the name is close, the fix says what to call it: my-models.yaml and dataset.yaml get rename it to `models.yaml` and rename it to `datasets.yaml`. A run follows the same rule: it never reads my-models.yaml.

items.title: Reading the output
items.text:
A clean file is one line:

✓ configs/models.yaml: 2 models, no problems

A file with problems gets a header, then one block per problem:

✗ configs/rewards.yaml: 3 rewards, 3 errors

  error    line 3  rewards.exact-match.type
           unknown reward 'exact_matsh'
     fix   change 'exact_matsh' to 'exact_match'

  error    line 8  rewards.judge.config.instruction
           lm_as_judge does not take `instruction`
     fix   rename `instruction:` to `instructions:` under rewards.judge.config

  error    line 7  rewards.judge.config.language_model
           'openai/gpt-4o-mini' is not in `models`
     fix   name the entry that calls it: 'gpt-4o-mini'
Part Meaning ✓ / ✗ / ! Clean / at least one error / warnings only. header How many entries the file holds, then how many errors and warnings. level error or warning. See Levels. line N The line in the file. For a key that is missing, the line of the nearest part of its path that is written. Left out when the problem has no place in the file (a registry missing beside it). where The dotted path to the field: <registry>.<entry>.<field>, list items as [i], e.g. datasets.agent.agent.mcp_servers[0]. A file-level problem shows the registry or the file name. message What is wrong, in one sentence. fix The change to make. Apply it as written. A multi-line fix is a snippet to paste.

A fix takes one of a few shapes:

  • a rename: rename `pth:` to `path:` under datasets.d.config;
  • a replacement value: change 'hugingface' to 'huggingface';
  • a removal: remove `provider:`; the provider is read off the model id;
  • an addition: add `url: https://<host>/mcp`;
  • what is accepted, when nothing is close: use one of the rewards: ...;
  • a snippet, when a shape is easier shown than said:
  error    line 4  models.qwen38.temprature
           not a field of a `models` entry
     fix   move it under `params:` (spelled `temperature:`):
             params:
               temperature: 0

The "did you mean" suggestions are near misses against what is actually accepted: the registry's fields, the provider's settings, the reward's arguments, the keys of the registry referred to. When nothing is close enough, the fix lists the accepted values instead.

No JSON output

The command prints for people only. For a machine-readable result, call the checker from Python: see From Python.

items.title: Levels
items.text:
There are two levels, error and warning. There is no info level.

Level Meaning Blocks a run? Fails check? error The engine or the app would refuse this. Yes, when the run loads that entry. Yes, exit 1. warning It loads, but likely not as you meant, or something could not be checked. No. No, exit 0.

Warnings come from a few places only:

Warning Why it is not an error What to do A leaderboard names a dataset or model not in its registry: 'retired' is not in `datasets`; only scores from runs made before it was removed can be ranked A leaderboard ranks finished runs, which outlive the entries that made them. Scoping a board to a retired dataset is legitimate. Keep it if you want the old scores ranked. Otherwise fix the name. A registry the file refers to is not beside it: no `rewards` registry to check references against; they are not checked Nothing is wrong in this file; the check cannot see the other one. Keep the file in its configs folder, or pass --configs DIR. A registry beside the file does not parse: does not read; its entries are not used for references That file's own check reports the real error. Fix it first: the fix gives the command. An evaluation names an entry that does not validate: not validated whole: `datasets` it names does not read The error belongs to that entry and is reported in its own file. Fix that registry, then check again: the fix names its file. A ${NAME} set neither in your shell nor in the workspace's .env: `${SUPPORT_BOT_TOKEN}` is not set in your shell or in .env; a run that reads it refuses to start The value is a secret you may keep out of the machine that checks (CI). The rest is checked as written; only the field holding the reference skips its own rule (a url's scheme), since its value is not known yet. Add NAME=... to .env, or export it, before running.

A missing-registry warning means not checked

When check cannot see a registry, it skips every reference to it. A result with no error but a no ... registry warning means "references not checked", not "references correct". Check the whole folder, or point --configs at it.

items.title: What it checks
items.text:
The check runs in layers. Each finds what the one before cannot see.

flowchart TD
    A["1. The file<br/>YAML, name, shape"] --> B["2. Each entry<br/>strict schema, catalog, provider"]
    B --> C["3. References<br/>names that point at other files"]
    C --> D["4. The evaluation, whole<br/>as a run would load it"]
    A -. "YAML error or wrong top-level key" .-> X["stop: nothing else in the file is read"]

items.title: 1. The file
items.text:
Check Message The file exists. no file at <path> Its name is a registry's. not a registry file: a registry is read only from `<registry>.yaml` It is valid YAML. not valid YAML: <what the parser found> (<context>) No key is written twice in one mapping. Plain YAML keeps the last one silently; check and runs refuse it. 'a' is written twice in one mapping (in the mapping at line 2); YAML would keep only the last The top-level key is the registry's. no `rewards:` at the top of the file (it holds `models:`) No other top-level key. A models: block inside rewards.yaml is never read. not read from rewards.yaml: it holds `rewards:` only The registry maps names to entries. `datasets:` maps each name to its entry Each name starts with a letter or a digit, then letters, digits, _, . or -. a name starts with a letter or a digit, then letters, digits, `_`, `.` or `-` Each entry is a mapping of fields. an entry is a mapping of its fields

A YAML error or a wrong top-level key stops the check of that file, since nothing below can be read. For a wrong shape, the fix includes a working example entry to copy.

items.title: 2. Each entry
items.text:
Every entry is validated against its registry's strict schema, the same one the app's registries use. Strict means a field the schema does not know is an error, not something silently ignored. That is what catches typos.

Registry Checked beyond types, bounds and required fields models No unknown field. A param the model's type takes, written beside model: (temperature, max_tokens, reasoning_effort for a chat model, dimensions for an embedding one), gets a fix that moves it under params:. A call option it does not take (top_p, seed, ...) is reported as not supported, with the params that type takes. api_base, base_url and api_key are refused, beside model: or under params:: they are set in the environment (OLLAMA_API_BASE, ...). provider: is refused: the provider comes from the model id. See Models. rewards type is a reward in the catalog, and one an entry can build: agent_as_judge is refused (it needs tools, which an entry cannot give), and the fix names rlm_as_judge, deep_agent_as_judge or a judge over the agent's messages. Each key of config: is an argument that reward takes; reduction only on a reward that takes it (a judge does, exact_match does not). An argument written beside type: gets a fix that moves it under config:. name and direction are not inside config:. rubrics_as_judge has rubrics; multi_judge_panel has panel_language_models and smart_language_model. Every model a reward names (language_model, smart_language_model, sub_language_model, embedding_model, panel_language_models) is a models key of the right type. See Rewards. datasets type is a known provider. config: has every setting the provider requires and nothing it does not take (unless the provider accepts any setting); that includes braintrust's project (or project_id) and dataset_name, and mlflow's name (or dataset_id), which it refuses to load without. config.input_template is set and not blank. config: holds no top-level key (reward, metrics, a kind block). Only one of generator, agent, a2a, embedding, tools, harbor. a2a: {} takes no settings. tools: lists at least one tool_schemas entry. agent: names at least one MCP server and does not set language_model or tools. A harbor_tasks dataset has harbor:, and no harbor.environment, harbor.answer_file or harbor.instructions (a task folder is run and scored as written); a harbor: dataset over rows has harbor.environment. harbor.agent is a known Harbor agent. See Datasets. mcp_servers transport is known. A stdio server has command; any other transport has a url starting http://, https://, ws:// or wss://. No field the transport does not read (url on a stdio server, command on an sse one). No whitespace in env or headers keys. See MCP tools. a2a_agents url is set and starts http:// or https://. Header values are text. timeout_sec is above 0. See A2A agents. environments Exactly one of docker_image and dockerfile. network_mode: allowlist needs allowed_hosts, and allowed_hosts needs allowlist. No whitespace in env keys. See Environments. evaluations Types and bounds, e.g. batch_size is 1 or more. See Evaluations. leaderboards title is set. Each share is 0 or more, and at least one is above 0 when shares: is set. Group and dataset weights are 0 or more. See Leaderboards.

Tags follow one rule on every registry, the app's: written as a list, each at most 40 characters, at most 32 of them. A tag the app only tidies (Local, Open Weights) passes. One it would refuse gets the spelling it takes, e.g. write it as `bad-tag`.

items.title: 3. References
items.text:
Names are how files point at each other. Each reference is checked against the registry beside the file:

From Field Must be a key of datasets reward rewards datasets agent.mcp_servers[i] mcp_servers datasets harbor.environment environments datasets models named in metrics[i] models, of the right type rewards config.language_model and the other model arguments models, of the right type environments mcp_servers[i] mcp_servers evaluations datasets[i] datasets evaluations language_models[i] models; a2a_agents when every dataset it selects is an a2a dataset evaluations default_language_model, default_embedding_model, models named in metrics[i] models, of the right type leaderboards datasets[i], models[i] datasets, models (a warning, not an error)

A model reference is a models key, never a raw model id. Writing language_model: openai/gpt-4o-mini in a reward is an error. When an entry already calls that id, the fix names it: name the entry that calls it: 'gpt-4o-mini'. "Of the right type" means a judge names a language model and an embedding argument names an embedding model: 'vectors' is an embedding model; this setting needs a language model.

Dataset and evaluation references are checked even when the entry failed its schema, so one pass shows both kinds of problem.

items.title: 4. The evaluation, whole
items.text:
When an evaluation has no error so far and the datasets registry is there, it is validated whole, as evaluations run would: gathered with every entry it names, then checked across them. This finds rules no single entry can see:

Message Fix given a Harbor dataset cannot share a run with other kinds of dataset; run it on its own. (the same for A2A and embedding datasets) split it in two evaluations: one for the datasets of that kind, one for the others `evaluation.language_models:` 'vectors' is an embedding model; this sweep needs language models. list only models of the type the datasets need in language_models:, or move the others to their own evaluation dataset 'x' has no `reward:`; set one before evaluating on it. set reward: on that dataset (a rewards key), or leave it out of this evaluation

It also checks that a Harbor dataset's agent can drive each model on the axis, and that a Harbor environment's MCP servers resolve. See Harbor tasks.

items.title: The most common problems
items.text:
Message Usual cause Fix not a field of a `models` entry on temperature Call options written beside model:. Move them under params:; the fix shows the snippet. not a field of a `models` entry on provider Copied from another tool's config. Remove it. The provider is the prefix of the model id (openai/...). not a field of a `models` entry on top_p, fix it is not supported A call option the model's type does not take. Remove it; the fix lists the params that type takes. not a field of a `models` entry on api_base A server address on the model. Remove it and set the provider's variable in .env (OLLAMA_API_BASE, HOSTED_VLLM_API_BASE). not a field of a `<registry>` entry A typo, or a field from another registry. Rename to the suggested field, or remove it; the fix lists what an entry reads. unknown reward 'exact_matsh' Typo in type:, or a reward that does not exist. Change to the suggested name. Rewards lists the catalog. lm_as_judge does not take `instruction` A misspelled reward argument. Rename as suggested (instructions). exact_match does not take `reduction` reduction on a reward that does not take it. Remove it. config cannot set direction: use `type` and `direction` direction: written inside config:. Move it beside config:. 'openai/gpt-4o-mini' is not in `models` A raw model id where a models key is expected. Name the models entry that calls it. 'vectors' is an embedding model; this setting needs a language model The wrong model type for a judge or a sweep. Name a model of the right type. unknown provider 'hugingface' Typo in a dataset's type:. Change to the suggested provider. not a setting of the local provider on pth Typo in a provider setting. Rename as suggested (path). A misspelled required setting is reported once, as the rename. the huggingface provider needs `path` A required provider setting is missing. Add it under config:. no `config.input_template`: nothing says what each row asks A row-based dataset without a question template. Paste the snippet the fix shows, then adapt the column names. `config` cannot contain arena-level keys ['reward'] reward:, metrics: or a kind block written inside config:. Move it to the dataset's top level. `generator`, `agent` are mutually exclusive Two ways of answering in one dataset. Keep one block. 'exact-mach' is not in `rewards` Typo, or the entry was renamed or removed. Change to the suggested key, or add the entry. a stdio server needs a `command` to spawn / a sse server needs a `url` Transport and fields do not match. Add the missing field, or change transport:. a stdio server does not take ['url']; it reads [...] A field the transport does not read. Remove it, or switch to a transport that reads it. an environment is a `docker_image` or a `dockerfile`, not both Both set. Keep one. an `allowlist` network lets nothing through without `allowed_hosts` network_mode: allowlist alone. Add allowed_hosts, or use network_mode: public. Input should be greater than or equal to 1 on batch_size batch_size: 0. Set it to 1 or more. no metric carries weight Every leaderboard share is 0. Give one metric a share above 0, or remove shares: for the default. 'a' is written twice in one mapping A copy-pasted entry whose name was not changed. Delete one, or rename it. not valid YAML: ... Bad indentation, an unclosed bracket or quote, an unquoted :, or a value starting with {. Fix the syntax on that line.

Quote templates

A Jinja template such as {"question": {{ question | tojson }}} starts with {, so YAML reads it as a mapping unless it is quoted. Put it in single quotes, and double any single quote inside it ('').

items.title: What it does not check
items.text:
It reads files only. These pass check and show up when a run reaches them (see Reading results):

  • Keys and environment. check does not look for OPENAI_API_KEY or any other provider variable; a missing key fails the cell at run time. The only variables it looks up, in your shell and in the workspace's .env (read, not loaded), are the ${NAME}s your configs use, and one set nowhere is a warning. See The workspace for keys.
  • Reachability. A model id is not tried. An MCP server is not started or connected to. An A2A agent's URL is not called. A Docker image is not pulled or built.
  • Data. A dataset is not downloaded or opened. A wrong Hugging Face path, a missing local file, a harbor_tasks folder that does not exist: all pass. Provider settings are checked by name, not by value.
  • Template syntax and columns. Only that input_template is set is checked. The Jinja is not parsed, and the columns it uses are not matched against the data.

Check, then smoke test

check proves the config is well formed. A run on a small slice proves it works: a few rows (limit: on the dataset) and one cheap model. Do both before a long sweep.

items.title: In CI and pre-commit
items.text:
The exit code is all CI needs: 0 passes, 1 fails. No key is needed, since check never calls a model, and a ${NAME} the CI job does not set is only a warning.

GitHub Actionspre-commit 
# .github/workflows/configs.yml, a sketch: install openarena the way your project does
name: configs
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v5
      - run: uv run openarena check configs

# .pre-commit-config.yaml; `openarena` must be on the PATH (language: system)
repos:
  - repo: local
    hooks:
      - id: openarena-check
        name: openarena check
        entry: openarena check configs
        language: system
        pass_filenames: false
        files: ^configs/

pass_filenames: false matters: the hook checks the whole folder, not just the changed file, so a rename is caught where the old name is still used.

items.title: From Python
items.text:
The same checks are plain functions. Use them for a machine-readable result, or to apply your own policy (for example, fail on warnings too).

from pathlib import Path
from openarena.config.check import check_folder, check_registry

reports = check_folder(Path("configs"))          # one Report per file
for report in reports:
    for p in report.problems:                     # Problem: level, where, message, fix, line
        print(report.path, p.level, p.line, p.where, p.message, p.fix)

failed = any(r.errors for r in reports)           # r.warnings: the warnings only

# A registry held in memory, as the arena app checks one; references against the registries given.
report = check_registry("rewards", {"judge": {"type": "lm_as_judge"}}, registries={"models": {}})

check_folder raises FileNotFoundError when the folder does not exist. check_file(path, beside=DIR) is the single-file check, --configs being beside. check_registry gives no line numbers, since there is no file, and with no registries it checks no reference at all. Signatures are in the API reference.

items.title: Datasets
items.text:
configs/datasets.yaml says, for each dataset, where its rows come from, how each row becomes a question and an expected answer, what answers it, and which reward scores it. An evaluation then names datasets by their key (Running evaluations).

Every row goes through the same steps, whatever the provider:

flowchart LR
  S[(source: file, hub,<br/>platform, table)] -->|provider reads a row| R["row: {column: value}"]
  R -->|input_template| I[input JSON]
  R -->|output_template| O[expected JSON]
  I -->|input_schema| M[model, agent or sandbox]
  M --> P[prediction]
  P --> W{reward}
  O -->|output_schema| W

The provider only decides where rows come from and what their columns are called. Everything after that (the templates, the schemas, the block that answers, the reward) works the same for all of them. So choosing a provider is about where your data lives and how you pin a version of it, not about what you can evaluate.

items.title: An entry, field by field
items.text:
datasets:
  gsm8k-20:                            # the key evaluations and leaderboards use
    type: huggingface                  # the provider
    description: GSM8K test split, 20 rows.
    tags: [math]                       # for browsing; the run ignores them
    config:                            # the provider's settings, the templates, the schemas
      path: openai/gsm8k
      name: main
      split: test
      limit: 20                        # the first 20 rows; leave out for all
      batch_size: 4                    # rows sent to the model at once
      input_template: '{"question": {{ question | tojson }}}'
      output_template: '{"answer": {{ answer.split(''####'')[-1] | replace('','', '''') | trim | tojson }}}'
      input_schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          question: {type: string, description: The question to answer}
        required: [question]
      output_schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          answer: {type: string, description: "The final number only, no units or commas"}
        required: [answer]
    generator:                         # what answers: a model, in one call
      chain_of_thought: true
      instructions: Solve the problem. Reply with the final number only.
    reward: exact-match                # a rewards.yaml key; required to run
field values default effect the key letters, digits, _, ., -; starts with a letter or digit the name evaluations and leaderboards refer to type a provider (below) required where rows are read from config the provider's settings, the templates, the schemas {} how rows are read and rendered description text none shown when browsing; not read by the run tags list of labels [] lower-cased and de-duplicated; for browsing only generator, agent, a2a, embedding, tools, harbor at most one block a generator what answers each row (below) reward a key of rewards.yaml none the dataset's score; an evaluation refuses a dataset without one metrics list [] extra columns beside the reward (below)

reward, metrics and the answering block always sit at the entry's top level, never inside config. openarena check says so and tells you to move them up.

items.title: Settings every provider takes
items.text:
These live in config, next to the provider's own settings.

field values default effect input_template Jinja2 rendering a JSON object required (not for harbor_tasks) what the model receives for a row output_template Jinja2 rendering a JSON object none the expected answer the reward compares with; leave out for an inputs-only dataset input_schema JSON Schema, as YAML or a JSON string chat messages the shape input_template renders output_schema JSON Schema, as YAML or a JSON string one chat message the shape output_template renders, and the structure the model answers in limit integer all rows read at most this many rows, the first ones in the source's order batch_size integer 1 rows in flight at once repeat integer, at least 1 1 each row is sent this many times in a row, each copy scored as a row

batch_size is the concurrency knob. openarena evaluations run --batch-size and an evaluation's own batch_size override every dataset's: the flag wins, then the evaluation's, then the dataset's. Keep it low for a local model or a rate-limited key; raise it for a hosted model with headroom.

repeat sends the same row several times. Use it to see how much a sampled model's answers vary on a small set. Leave it at 1 for a benchmark score: repeated rows weigh each question more without adding questions.

items.title: Templates: from a row to JSON
items.text:
Both templates are Jinja2 over one row: each column of the row is a variable. Each must render to a JSON object, which is then read against its schema.

  • input_template is what the model receives: {"question": ...} for question answering.
  • output_template is the expected answer. A judge can score without one; exact_match and the other deterministic rewards cannot. Leave it out and the dataset is inputs-only: its rows carry no expected answer.

Pipe every value through | tojson. It quotes and escapes strings, and keeps numbers, lists and objects as JSON. Never write "{{ question }}": it breaks on the first quote or newline in a question.

you write for {{ question \| tojson }} a column {{ input.question \| tojson }} a field of a column holding an object {{ answers.text[0] \| tojson }} an item of a list {{ answer.split('####')[-1] \| trim \| tojson }} Python string methods and Jinja filters {{ "ABCD"[answer] \| tojson }} an index turned into a letter {{ answer \| string \| tojson }} a number compared as text {{ hint \| default("") \| tojson }} a column some rows lack {{ metadata.difficulty \| tojson }} a platform item's metadata, carried into the input

Quoting in YAML

Write a template as a single-quoted YAML string, and double every single quote inside it: split(''####'') in YAML is split('####') in Jinja. Double quotes need no escaping.

Templates are strict: a variable the row does not have is an error, not an empty string. That catches a misspelled column on the first row instead of scoring a whole run against blanks. When a column really is optional, say so with | default(...).

Look at real rows before writing a template. For a Hugging Face dataset:

python -c "import datasets; print(next(iter(datasets.load_dataset('openai/gsm8k', 'main', split='test', streaming=True))))"

For a local file, head -n 1 data/qa.jsonl. For a platform, open one item in its UI: the template variables are the provider's fields (table below), and your data sits inside them.

items.title: Worked examples
items.text:
Messy answer columnMultiple choiceSeveral columnsPlatform itemsChat messages

GSM8K's answer holds the worked solution, then ####, then the number, sometimes with a thousands separator. The expected answer keeps only the number:

datasets:
  gsm8k-clean:
    type: huggingface
    config:
      path: openai/gsm8k
      name: main
      split: test
      limit: 20
      input_template: '{"question": {{ question | tojson }}}'
      # "... #### 1,234" becomes "1234"
      output_template: '{"answer": {{ answer.split(''####'')[-1] | replace('','', '''') | trim | tojson }}}'
      input_schema: {type: object, properties: {question: {type: string, description: The question to answer}}, required: [question]}
      output_schema: {type: object, properties: {answer: {type: string, description: The final number only}}, required: [answer]}
    reward: exact-match

MMLU has the question, a list of choices and the index of the right one. The input lists the choices under the question; the expected answer is the letter:

datasets:
  mmlu-math:
    type: huggingface
    config:
      path: cais/mmlu
      name: high_school_mathematics
      split: test
      limit: 50
      input_template: '{"question": {{ (question ~ "\n" ~ (choices | map("string") | list | join("\n"))) | tojson }}}'
      output_template: '{"answer": {{ "ABCD"[answer] | tojson }}}'
      input_schema: {type: object, properties: {question: {type: string, description: The question to answer}}, required: [question]}
      output_schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          answer: {type: string, enum: [A, B, C, D], description: The letter of the correct choice}
        required: [answer]
    generator:
      instructions: Answer with the letter of the correct choice only.
    reward: exact-match

The enum keeps "Option B" out where "B" is expected.

A support-ticket CSV with subject, body, product and expected_team. Every CSV value is text. The input carries what the model needs as separate keys, and the label is normalised:

datasets:
  ticket-routing:
    type: local
    config:
      path: data/tickets.csv
      input_template: '{"ticket": {{ (subject ~ "\n\n" ~ body) | tojson }}, "product": {{ product | tojson }}}'
      output_template: '{"team": {{ expected_team | trim | lower | tojson }}}'
      input_schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          ticket: {type: string, description: The ticket's subject and body}
          product: {type: string, description: The product the ticket is about}
        required: [ticket, product]
      output_schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          team: {type: string, enum: [billing, technical, sales], description: The team to route the ticket to}
        required: [team]
    reward: exact-match

Platforms store an item's input and expected output as objects. With Langfuse a row is input, expected_output, metadata and id, so your fields are one level down:

datasets:
  support-golden:
    type: langfuse
    config:
      dataset_name: support-golden
      input_template: '{"question": {{ input.question | tojson }}, "tier": {{ metadata.tier | default("free") | tojson }}}'
      output_template: '{"answer": {{ expected_output.answer | tojson }}}'
      input_schema: {type: object, properties: {question: {type: string}, tier: {type: string}}, required: [question, tier]}
      output_schema: {type: object, properties: {answer: {type: string}}, required: [answer]}
    reward: judge

If the items were stored as plain strings, drop the field: {{ input | tojson }}.

Without schemas, a row is read as chat messages. The input renders {"messages": [...]}, the expected answer one message:

datasets:
  chat-replies:
    type: local
    config:
      path: data/chats.jsonl         # {"prompt": "...", "reply": "..."} per line
      input_template: '{"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": {{ prompt | tojson }}}]}'
      output_template: '{"role": "assistant", "content": {{ reply | tojson }}}'
    reward: judge

Use this for free-form conversation scored by a judge. For anything with a structured answer, write schemas.

There is no metadata template: a row is an input and, optionally, an expected answer. When the source carries metadata the model should see, put it in the input. When you only want it to select rows, select at the source (Opik's filter_string, Phoenix's splits) or keep a separate file.

Column names

A column is a template variable, so its name must be a valid identifier. A column called expected answer or gold-label cannot be named in a template: rename it in the file or at the source.

items.title: Schemas
items.text:
input_schema and output_schema are the JSON Schemas of what the templates render. With an output_schema the model answers in that structure, and each field's description is the instruction for that field. An enum holds the model to the exact labels the expected answer uses.

Give both whenever a template renders anything but chat messages, which is nearly always. Without input_schema a row is read as chat messages ({"messages": [...]}), and without output_schema the expected answer is read as one chat message ({"role": ..., "content": ...}), so {"question": ...} and {"answer": ...} fail when the run reads the rows. A free-text answer still gets a schema: one string field, no enum.

Every object in a schema is closed for you (additionalProperties: false, unless you set it otherwise), because some model providers refuse structured output on an open object. List required yourself.

Two kinds of dataset get their shapes for you: an embedding dataset gets the retrieval shapes, and a harbor_tasks dataset has fixed templates and schemas.

An output_schema without an output_template is refused when the run loads the dataset: there is nothing for the schema to describe.

items.title: Choosing a provider
items.text:
Pick the provider for where the rows already live, then pin a version.

flowchart TD
  A{Where are the rows?} -->|a benchmark on the Hugging Face Hub| HF[huggingface]
  A -->|files in the workspace| B{one file or one per row?}
  B -->|one table: jsonl, json, csv, parquet| L[local]
  B -->|one record per file| F[folder]
  A -->|curated in an LLM-ops platform| P[langfuse, langsmith, opik,<br/>phoenix, braintrust, mlflow]
  A -->|a governed lakehouse table| U[unity_catalog]
  A -->|Harbor task folders| H[harbor_tasks]
provider choose it when pin with extra to install huggingface a public benchmark (GSM8K, MMLU), or a team dataset on the Hub revision none local you own the rows and keep them in git beside the configs git none folder each case is a file people edit (a YAML per case, a Markdown prompt) git none langfuse items curated in Langfuse, often from traces version (a time) langfuse langsmith examples curated in LangSmith as_of (a version tag) langsmith opik items in Opik, selected with server-side filters version (a version name) opik phoenix examples in Phoenix, divided into splits version_id phoenix braintrust records in a Braintrust project version (a transaction id) braintrust mlflow an MLflow evaluation dataset nothing none unity_catalog a Delta or Parquet table governed by Unity Catalog version or as_of unity-catalog harbor_tasks tasks an agent works in a sandbox, scored by their own tests git none

The trade-offs:

  • A file in git (local, folder) is the most reproducible. The dataset changes only in a commit, and anyone with the workspace can run it without an account anywhere. Prefer it for a small, hand-made set.
  • The Hub is right for public benchmarks, so others compare on the same rows. Pin revision: a dataset's main can change under you.
  • A platform is right when the rows are curated there, for instance production traces promoted to a golden set. Reading it directly avoids a stale export, but the dataset moves as people curate it. Pin a version, or results two weeks apart compare different questions.
  • Unity Catalog is right when the evaluation data is a governed table others maintain. Pin a Delta version.

items.title: Providers
items.text:
Each tab gives the provider's settings, the variables a row exposes to the templates, what it reads from the environment, how to pin it, and its pitfalls. openarena check refuses a setting a provider does not take, except on huggingface, which forwards unknown settings to the Hugging Face loader. Keys and endpoints go in the workspace's .env (Workspace), never in datasets.yaml.

huggingfacelocalfolderlangfuselangsmithopikphoenixbraintrustmlflowunity_catalogharbor_tasks

Reads a dataset from the Hugging Face Hub, row by row.

datasets:
  gsm8k-pinned:
    type: huggingface
    config:
      path: openai/gsm8k               # the repo
      name: main                       # the subset
      split: test
      revision: main                   # a commit hash for a frozen benchmark
      streaming: true                  # download rows as they are read
      limit: 50
      input_template: '{"question": {{ question | tojson }}}'
      output_template: '{"answer": {{ answer.split(''####'')[-1] | replace('','', '''') | trim | tojson }}}'
      input_schema: {type: object, properties: {question: {type: string}}, required: [question]}
      output_schema: {type: object, properties: {answer: {type: string}}, required: [answer]}
    reward: exact-match
field values default effect path a repo id (openai/gsm8k) or a loader name required which dataset name a subset none which configuration of a multi-subset dataset (main, high_school_mathematics) split train, test, validation, ... none the split; without one, every split is read in turn revision a commit hash, branch or tag latest the version of the repo streaming true, false true true reads rows as they download; false downloads the split first anything else e.g. data_files, token, trust_remote_code passed to datasets.load_dataset

Row variables: the dataset's columns, as its card shows them.

When to use it: public benchmarks, and team datasets on the Hub. Keep streaming: true when you take a few rows of a large dataset: rows are read only until limit is reached.

Pitfalls

  • Without split, every split is read in turn, so limit: 20 takes the first 20 rows of the first split, often train.
  • Without name, a multi-subset dataset fails to load: the Hub asks which configuration you mean.
  • Without revision, an upstream update changes your score with no change to your config. Pin the commit hash for anything you publish.
  • Unknown settings are passed on, so check cannot catch a misspelled one here: it fails when the run loads the dataset.

Reads one file: one row per record.

datasets:
  qa-local:
    type: local
    config:
      path: data/qa.jsonl              # {"question": "...", "answer": "..."} per line
      # format: jsonl                  # only when the extension does not say
      limit: 5
      input_template: '{"question": {{ question | tojson }}}'
      output_template: '{"answer": {{ answer | string | tojson }}}'
      input_schema: {type: object, properties: {question: {type: string}}, required: [question]}
      output_schema: {type: object, properties: {answer: {type: string}}, required: [answer]}
    reward: exact-match
field values default effect path a file required the file format json, jsonl, csv, parquet from the extension how to read it

The extension decides the format: .jsonl and .ndjson are JSON lines, .json is JSON, .csv comma-separated, .tsv tab-separated, .parquet Parquet. Set format only for another extension.

format a row is note JSON lines one object per line blank lines are skipped JSON an item of the top-level list, or of the one list an object holds ({"data": [...]}) an object holding two lists is refused CSV, TSV one line, keyed by the header every value is a string Parquet one record read in row groups, so a large file need not fit in memory

Row variables: the record's keys, or the header's columns.

When to use it: your own set, small enough to keep in git. It is the simplest dataset to pin: its version is the commit.

Pitfalls

  • A relative path is read from the directory you run openarena in. Run from the workspace root, or give an absolute path.
  • CSV values are text: {{ score | int }} to use one as a number, {{ answer | trim }} against stray spaces.
  • A .txt, or any other extension, is refused until format says how to read it.

Reads a folder where each file is one row. Files are read in alphabetical order.

datasets:
  cases:
    type: folder
    config:
      path: data/cases                 # one YAML per case: {question: ..., answer: ...}
      pattern: "*.yaml"
      recursive: false
      input_template: '{"question": {{ question | tojson }}, "case": {{ _stem | tojson }}}'
      output_template: '{"answer": {{ answer | tojson }}}'
      input_schema: {type: object, properties: {question: {type: string}, case: {type: string}}, required: [question, case]}
      output_schema: {type: object, properties: {answer: {type: string}}, required: [answer]}
    reward: judge
field values default effect path a folder required where the files are pattern a glob * which files are rows recursive true, false false also look in sub-folders format json, yaml, text from each file's extension how to read every file encoding a text encoding utf-8 how files are decoded

Row variables

file variables .json, .yaml, .yml holding an object its keys .json, .yaml, .yml holding anything else record .txt, .md, or any file under format: text text every file _filename (case-01.yaml), _stem (case-01), _path (relative to path)

When to use it: cases written and reviewed by people, one per file, so a pull request shows exactly which case changed. Also prompts kept as Markdown, read as text.

Pitfalls

  • The default pattern * takes every file, a stray README.md included. Narrow it to *.yaml or *.json.
  • A file with any other extension stops the run until format says how to read it.
  • limit takes the first files in alphabetical order: number them (001-...) when the order matters.

Reads a Langfuse dataset, a page of items at a time.

datasets:
  lf-golden:
    type: langfuse
    config:
      dataset_name: support-golden
      version: "2026-04-15T00:00:00Z"  # the items as they were then
      streaming: true
      page_size: 50
      input_template: '{"question": {{ input.question | tojson }}}'
      output_template: '{"answer": {{ expected_output.answer | tojson }}}'
      input_schema: {type: object, properties: {question: {type: string}}, required: [question]}
      output_schema: {type: object, properties: {answer: {type: string}}, required: [answer]}
    reward: judge
field values default effect dataset_name the dataset's name required which dataset version an ISO 8601 time; UTC when it has no zone latest the items as they were at that time streaming true, false true true fetches a page at a time; false fetches every item first page_size integer 50 items per page when streaming

Row variables: input, expected_output, metadata, id.

Environment: LANGFUSE_PUBLIC_KEY, LANGFUSE_SECRET_KEY, LANGFUSE_HOST.

Extra: langfuse.

Pinning: Langfuse versions a dataset by time, not by name. Set version to the moment you froze the set; items added later are left out.

Reads the examples of a LangSmith dataset.

datasets:
  ls-golden:
    type: langsmith
    config:
      dataset_name: support-golden
      as_of: golden-2026-04            # a version tag
      input_template: '{"question": {{ inputs.question | tojson }}}'
      output_template: '{"answer": {{ outputs.answer | tojson }}}'
      input_schema: {type: object, properties: {question: {type: string}}, required: [question]}
      output_schema: {type: object, properties: {answer: {type: string}}, required: [answer]}
    reward: judge
field values default effect dataset_name the dataset's name required which dataset as_of a version tag latest the examples as tagged

Row variables: inputs, outputs, metadata, id. Note the plurals: these are LangSmith's names, not Langfuse's.

Environment: LANGSMITH_API_KEY, LANGSMITH_ENDPOINT.

Extra: langsmith.

Pinning: tag a version in LangSmith and set as_of to the tag. Moving a tag (prod) moves every evaluation that names it, which suits "the current golden set" but not a published result: use a tag you never move for those.

Reads the items of an Opik dataset, optionally filtered by Opik.

datasets:
  opik-regressions:
    type: opik
    config:
      dataset_name: support-golden
      version: v1                      # a named version
      filter_string: 'tags contains "regression"'
      input_template: '{"question": {{ input.question | tojson }}}'
      output_template: '{"answer": {{ expected_output.answer | tojson }}}'
      input_schema: {type: object, properties: {question: {type: string}}, required: [question]}
      output_schema: {type: object, properties: {answer: {type: string}}, required: [answer]}
    reward: judge
field values default effect dataset_name the dataset's name required which dataset version a version name (v1) latest the items of that version filter_string an Opik filter expression none only the items it matches, filtered by Opik

Row variables: the item's fields: input, expected_output, metadata, id, and any custom field the item was created with.

Environment: OPIK_API_KEY, OPIK_WORKSPACE, OPIK_URL_OVERRIDE.

Extra: opik.

When to use it: filter_string makes several datasets out of one (the regressions, one product's items) without copying items. limit is sent to Opik, so only that many items are fetched.

Reads the examples of an Arize Phoenix dataset.

datasets:
  phoenix-golden:
    type: phoenix
    config:
      dataset_name: support-golden
      version_id: <version id>         # from the Phoenix UI
      splits: [test]
      input_template: '{"question": {{ input.question | tojson }}}'
      output_template: '{"answer": {{ output.answer | tojson }}}'
      input_schema: {type: object, properties: {question: {type: string}}, required: [question]}
      output_schema: {type: object, properties: {answer: {type: string}}, required: [answer]}
    reward: judge
field values default effect dataset_name the dataset's name or id required which dataset version_id a version id latest the examples of that version splits list of split names all only the examples in these splits

Row variables: id, input, output, metadata. The expected answer is output here.

Environment: PHOENIX_API_KEY, and PHOENIX_COLLECTOR_ENDPOINT or PHOENIX_HOST with PHOENIX_PORT.

Extra: phoenix.

Pitfall: Phoenix returns the whole version in one call, and limit is applied after. To evaluate a slice of a large dataset, give the slice its own split.

Reads the records of a Braintrust dataset.

datasets:
  bt-golden:
    type: braintrust
    config:
      project: support
      dataset_name: golden
      version: "1000192656880881099"   # a transaction id
      input_template: '{"question": {{ input.question | tojson }}}'
      output_template: '{"answer": {{ expected.answer | tojson }}}'
      input_schema: {type: object, properties: {question: {type: string}}, required: [question]}
      output_schema: {type: object, properties: {answer: {type: string}}, required: [answer]}
    reward: judge
field values default effect project the project's name project or project_id is required where the dataset is project_id the project's id instead of project dataset_name the dataset's name required which dataset version a transaction id latest the records as of that transaction org_name an organization BRAINTRUST_ORG_NAME for an account in several organizations fetch_batch_size integer the SDK's records per request to Braintrust; not the run's batch_size

Row variables: id, input, expected, metadata. The expected answer is expected here.

Environment: BRAINTRUST_API_KEY, and optionally BRAINTRUST_APP_URL, BRAINTRUST_ORG_NAME.

Extra: braintrust.

Pitfall: the provider loads nothing without a project and a dataset name. openarena check reports either one missing (the braintrust provider needs `project` or `project_id`).

Reads an MLflow evaluation dataset.

datasets:
  mlflow-golden:
    type: mlflow
    config:
      name: qa_golden_set              # or dataset_id
      input_template: '{"question": {{ inputs.question | tojson }}}'
      output_template: '{"answer": {{ expectations.answer | tojson }}}'
      input_schema: {type: object, properties: {question: {type: string}}, required: [question]}
      output_schema: {type: object, properties: {answer: {type: string}}, required: [answer]}
    reward: judge
field values default effect name the dataset's name name or dataset_id is required which dataset dataset_id the dataset's id when the name is ambiguous tracking_uri an MLflow URI see below the server to read from

Row variables: inputs, expectations, outputs, tags, record_id.

Environment: the server is tracking_uri when set, else MLFLOW_SOURCE_TRACKING_URI, else the tracing server, MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI. Set the first variable when the datasets live on one MLflow server and runs are traced to another.

Extra: none.

Pitfalls

  • With an output_template, every record needs expectations; one without stops the run. Leave output_template out to read an unlabelled set, for a judge that scores without a reference.
  • Evaluation datasets need an MLflow server backed by a database, not a plain ./mlruns folder.
  • There is no version to pin: the dataset is read as it is now.
  • Without name or dataset_id there is nothing to read: openarena check reports the mlflow provider needs `name` or `dataset_id`.

Reads a Delta (or Parquet) table registered in Unity Catalog, straight from its object storage, in batches.

datasets:
  uc-questions:
    type: unity_catalog
    config:
      table: main.evals.questions      # catalog.schema.table
      version: 3                       # a Delta version
      # as_of: "2026-04-15T00:00:00Z"  # or a time; not both
      input_template: '{"question": {{ question | tojson }}}'
      output_template: '{"answer": {{ reference_answer | tojson }}}'
      input_schema: {type: object, properties: {question: {type: string}}, required: [question]}
      output_schema: {type: object, properties: {answer: {type: string}}, required: [answer]}
    reward: judge
field values default effect table catalog.schema.table required the table version an integer Delta version latest the table at that version as_of an ISO 8601 time latest the table at that time; not with version storage_path an s3://... path looked up in the catalog read this path and skip the catalog read_batch_size integer 10000 rows per read from storage; not the run's batch_size

Row variables: the table's columns.

Environment

variable for UNITY_CATALOG_API_URL the catalog's REST API, /api/2.1/unity-catalog included; not read with storage_path UC_TOKEN its bearer token; not read with storage_path AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY the object storage AWS_DEFAULT_REGION its region; fr-par when unset S3_ENDPOINT an S3-compatible store (MinIO, Scaleway)

Extra: unity-catalog.

Pinning: set version to the Delta version you evaluated. version and as_of apply to Delta tables only: a table the catalog reports as Parquet is read as it is now.

Pitfalls

  • table must have exactly three parts, and version must be an integer, 3 and not "3".
  • With storage_path, nothing tells the provider the table's format, and it reads the path as a Delta table.

Reads Harbor task folders: every sub-folder of path holding a task.toml is a row, run in its own sandbox and scored by its own tests.

datasets:
  my-tasks:
    type: harbor_tasks
    config:
      path: tasks                      # relative to the workspace; the run copies it
      tasks: [hello-world]             # only these folders; leave out for every task
    harbor:
      agent: terminus-2
    reward: harbor-tests               # type: harbor_verifier
field values default effect path a folder of task folders required where the tasks are tasks list of folder names every task, sorted by name only these tasks

No templates and no schemas: they are fixed, and each task's tests score it.
