The entry needs a harbor: block without environment, since each task brings its own, and without instructions or answer_file: a task says what the agent is told in its instruction.md and is scored by its own tests/, so check refuses both. limit, batch_size and repeat work as for the other providers. Harbor tasks covers the folders, the agents and the trials.

items.title: What each provider calls a row
items.text:
The quickest way to write a template over a platform's items is to know which variable holds what:

provider the input the expected answer also huggingface, local, unity_catalog your columns your columns folder the file's keys, or text, or record the file's keys _filename, _stem, _path langfuse input expected_output metadata, id langsmith inputs outputs metadata, id opik input expected_output metadata, id, custom fields phoenix input output metadata, id braintrust input expected metadata, id mlflow inputs expectations outputs, tags, record_id

items.title: Installing a provider's SDK
items.text:
The platform providers need their SDK, which openarena installs only when asked, as an extra named after the provider:

provider extra installs langfuse langfuse langfuse langsmith langsmith langsmith opik opik opik phoenix phoenix arize-phoenix-client braintrust braintrust braintrust unity_catalog unity-catalog deltalake all of the above all every one 
uv tool install "openarena[langfuse] @ git+https://github.com/Atena-IT/open-arena"
uv add "openarena[langfuse]"          # in a project

Without it, the run stops when it loads the dataset and names the extra to install. openarena check does not need the SDK, so a config can check clean on a machine that cannot run it.

items.title: Reproducibility: pin the version
items.text:
A score means something only if the rows behind it can be read again. Pin every dataset you publish or compare over time:

provider pin with example huggingface revision the dataset repo's commit hash local, folder, harbor_tasks git commit the files with the configs langfuse version "2026-04-15T00:00:00Z" langsmith as_of a tag you never move, golden-2026-04 opik version v3 phoenix version_id the version's id braintrust version a transaction id unity_catalog version 3 mlflow nothing export it to a local file to freeze it

Change the key with the version

A run keeps finished cells by dataset key and reuses them when run again. After changing a pinned version (or a template, or limit), give the dataset a new key (golden-v3 to golden-v4), or run with --no-cache (Resuming). A new key also keeps the old scores readable beside the new ones.

items.title: Smoke subsets
items.text:
Start small, read the answers, then scale. limit caps the rows a dataset reads, and is the quickest way to get there.

datasets:
  gsm8k-smoke:                         # 5 rows: do the template, the schema and the reward work?
    type: huggingface
    config:
      path: openai/gsm8k
      name: main
      split: test
      limit: 5
      input_template: '{"question": {{ question | tojson }}}'
      output_template: '{"answer": {{ answer.split(''####'')[-1] | replace('','', '''') | trim | tojson }}}'
      input_schema: {type: object, properties: {question: {type: string}}, required: [question]}
      output_schema: {type: object, properties: {answer: {type: string}}, required: [answer]}
    reward: exact-match
  gsm8k-full:                          # the same source, every row
    type: huggingface
    config:
      path: openai/gsm8k
      name: main
      split: test
      input_template: '{"question": {{ question | tojson }}}'
      output_template: '{"answer": {{ answer.split(''####'')[-1] | replace('','', '''') | trim | tojson }}}'
      input_schema: {type: object, properties: {question: {type: string}}, required: [question]}
      output_schema: {type: object, properties: {answer: {type: string}}, required: [answer]}
    reward: exact-match

Keep the smoke entry and the full one side by side under different keys, and point a smoke evaluation at the first. Editing limit on one entry back and forth makes a resumed run reuse cells computed at the other size.

limit is not a sample

limit takes the first rows in the source's order; nothing shuffles them. When a dataset is sorted (by topic, by difficulty), its first 20 rows are not representative. For a representative subset, make one: a local file of rows you picked, a Phoenix split, an Opik filter_string, or a subset on your platform.

How each provider applies limit:

provider what is fetched huggingface (streaming), langfuse (streaming), local, folder, unity_catalog rows are read in order until limit opik limit items, asked of Opik phoenix, mlflow, langfuse with streaming: false the whole dataset, then cut

items.title: What answers each row
items.text:
At most one block. Without one, a model answers in one call.

block answered by the evaluation's language_models are none, or generator: a model in one call; instructions, chain_of_thought models agent: a model calling MCP tools (MCP tools) models a2a: {} remote agents (A2A agents) A2A agents embedding: retrieval with an embedding model (below) embedding models tools: one call with tool declarations, nothing executed (below) models harbor: an agent the model drives in a sandbox (Environments, Harbor tasks) models

Two blocks on one entry are refused: a dataset is answered one way. To compare a model alone with the same model using tools on the same rows, write two entries over the same source.

items.title: Retrieval
items.text:
The input renders a query and the chunks to search, the expected answer the gold chunks. The embedding model under test ranks the chunks, the top k are returned, and retrieval_recall scores them. No schemas to write: an embedding dataset gets these shapes by default.

datasets:
  passages:
    type: local
    config:
      path: retrieval.jsonl            # {"query": "...", "passages": [...], "gold": [...]}
      input_template: '{"query": {{ query | tojson }}, "chunks": {{ passages | tojson }}}'
      output_template: '{"chunks": {{ gold | tojson }}}'
    embedding:
      k: 3
    reward: recall                     # type: retrieval_recall

items.title: Tool calls
items.text:
The model gets the declared functions and answers with the calls it would make; nothing is executed. The expected answer renders the gold tool_calls, each {name, arguments}, with an output_schema saying so. That schema only shapes the expected answer: the model's answer is its chat message, tool calls included.

datasets:
  weather-calls:
    type: local
    config:
      path: calls.jsonl                # {"question": "...", "calls": [{"name": "get_weather", "arguments": {"city": "Paris"}}]}
      input_template: '{"question": {{ question | tojson }}}'
      output_template: '{"tool_calls": {{ calls | tojson }}}'
      input_schema: {type: object, properties: {question: {type: string, description: The question to answer}}, required: [question]}
      output_schema: {type: object, properties: {tool_calls: {type: array, description: The gold calls}}, required: [tool_calls]}
    tools:
      instructions: Call the function that answers the question.
      tool_schemas:
        - type: function
          function:
            name: get_weather
            description: The weather in a city.
            parameters: {type: object, properties: {city: {type: string}}, required: [city]}
    reward: tool-calls                 # type: tool_calls_accuracy

items.title: Extra metrics
items.text:
metrics: adds columns beside reward. Each is a catalog reward, averaged over the rows, or a plain metric (accuracy, f1_score, ...): a bare name, or a mapping with class, an alias (the column's name, never reward), a direction and the type's settings (Rewards).

datasets:
  gsm8k-20:
    # ...
    reward: exact-match
    metrics:
      - answer_accuracy
      - {class: lm_as_judge, alias: judged, language_model: gpt-4o-mini}

Cost, tokens and latency reach result.json only when listed here or on the evaluation, by their measurement names. Their direction is set for you: a metric written without direction: is min when it measures cost, tokens or latency (cost, total_tokens, avg_latency, ...) and max otherwise. Write direction: to override it; the leaderboard ranks by the direction the run recorded (Running evaluations).

items.title: Common mistakes
items.text:
openarena check configs catches what the file gets wrong (Checking configs). It reads no rows, so what depends on the data shows up when the run loads the dataset.

mistake caught by what you see a misspelled provider, hugginface check unknown provider, with the fix "change 'hugginface' to 'huggingface'" a misspelled setting, pth: check not a setting of the provider, with the fix "rename pth: to path:" a setting the provider does not take, as_of: on langfuse check the list of settings the provider takes a required setting missing, table: on unity_catalog check the provider needs it, with a placeholder to fill in no project or dataset name on braintrust, no name or dataset_id on mlflow check the braintrust provider needs `project` or `project_id`, with a placeholder to fill in no input_template check "nothing says what each row asks", with templates to paste reward: inside config: check arena-level keys in config, with the fix to move them up two answering blocks check the blocks are mutually exclusive harbor_tasks without harbor: check it needs a harbor: block, with harbor: {agent: terminus-2} to add instructions or answer_file in a harbor_tasks dataset's harbor: check they have no effect on task folders, with where each belongs instead a column the row does not have the run the template fails on the first row a value not piped through tojson the run the template renders invalid JSON a template that does not match its schema, or no schema the run the row is refused when read a missing SDK the run the extra to install a wrong Hugging Face path, a bad key, an unreachable server the run Reading results

Every mistake caught by the run is also caught by a smoke run with limit: 5, in seconds rather than after a full sweep.

Imported scores are not datasets

Scores computed by another tool can be imported and ranked on a leaderboard. They appear as <import>/<dataset>, so they never collide with the datasets of this file, but they are results, not rows: nothing in datasets.yaml describes them (Leaderboards).

items.title: Environments
items.text:
An environment is a sandbox definition: the image an agent works in, the resources it gets, what network it may reach, and the tools it is handed. On its own it does nothing. A dataset whose harbor: block names it turns each of its rows into a Harbor task in that sandbox: the row's question becomes the task's instruction, the model under test drives an agent that works there with a terminal and files, and the agent's answer is scored by the dataset's own reward.

Environments live in configs/environments.yaml, one entry per name.

items.title: Do you need one?
items.text:
An environment is the most expensive way to ask a question: every row starts a sandbox, and the agent makes many model calls to answer it. Use one only when the answer should be worked out, not just stated.

you want to measure use the answer a model gives in one call a plain dataset (Datasets) a model calling tools you serve a dataset with MCP tools (MCP tools) ordinary questions (GSM8K, your CSV) solved with a shell, Python, files an environment and a dataset over it (this page) tasks that each bring their own files, setup and tests Harbor tasks: each task folder carries its own environment, and no entry here is needed

Harbor tasks bring their own

A type: harbor_tasks dataset reads each task's [environment] from its own task.toml. An environments: entry is that same section, written once in YAML and shared by every row of a dataset, under the same field names.

items.title: How a row runs
items.text:
flowchart LR
    R[dataset row] -->|input_template| Q[question]
    Q --> T["task folder<br/>task.toml + instruction.md<br/>+ environment/"]
    E["environments.<name>"] --> T
    T --> S["sandbox started<br/>image built or pulled"]
    S --> A["agent works,<br/>driven by the model"]
    A --> F[answer_file read back]
    F --> W[dataset's reward scores it]

For every row, and every model of the evaluation:

  1. The row's question, after the block's instructions, is written as the task's instruction.md.
  2. The environment entry is written as the task's task.toml [environment] section. A copy of the environment's build context goes into the task's environment/ folder, and a dockerfile is written there as Dockerfile.
  3. Harbor starts a sandbox from it with the configured provider, waits for the healthcheck, and lets the agent work.
  4. When the agent is done, or its timeout_sec runs out, the answer_file is copied out of the sandbox. Without one, the agent's last message is the answer.
  5. The dataset's reward scores the answer on your machine, not in the sandbox.

What is isolated. Each row is its own trial, with its own sandbox: one row's files, installed packages and processes never reach another row, nor another model's run of the same row. The sandbox does not see your machine's files, only the image and its build context. What crosses the boundary is what you put there: the env: variables, the MCP servers, and whatever the network mode lets through.

items.title: A first environment
items.text:
environments:
  python:
    description: Python 3.12 with tmux.   # shown when browsing
    tags: [python]
    dockerfile: |                          # the image is built from this...
      FROM python:3.12-slim
      RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends tmux && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
      WORKDIR /app
      COPY requirements.txt /tmp/requirements.txt
      RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r /tmp/requirements.txt
    # docker_image: python:3.12-slim      # ...or pulled from this; one of the two
    workdir: /app                          # where the agent starts; the image must have it
    cpus: 1                                # blank: the provider's default
    memory_mb: 2048
    network_mode: public                   # public | no-network | allowlist

The COPY requirements.txt above reads from the environment's build context, a folder beside configs/:

my-arena/
  configs/
    environments.yaml
  environments/
    python/
      environment/          the build context: whatever the Dockerfile COPYs
        requirements.txt

When a run starts, environments/<name>/ is copied beside the run's own config, fresh each time: a file you removed since the last run does not linger. A docker_image environment needs no folder.

items.title: Fields
items.text:
field type default what it sets docker_image string none a prebuilt image to pull, e.g. python:3.12-slim dockerfile string none a Dockerfile to build from the build context os linux or windows linux the sandbox's operating system workdir string the image's the directory the agent starts in cpus integer, 1 or more the provider's CPUs the sandbox gets memory_mb integer, 1 or more the provider's memory, in MB storage_mb integer, 1 or more the provider's disk, in MB gpus integer, 0 or more the provider's GPUs the sandbox gets gpu_types list of strings [] (any) accepted GPU types, e.g. H100 network_mode public, no-network, allowlist public what the sandbox may reach allowed_hosts list of strings [] the hosts an allowlist sandbox may reach env map of string to string {} environment variables set in the container build_timeout_sec number above 0 600 how long building the image may take, in seconds healthcheck mapping none a command that says when the sandbox is ready mcp_servers list of names [] MCP servers the agent is given, by their mcp_servers key description string none a line shown when browsing tags list of strings [] labels for browsing, e.g. python, gpu, offline

Exactly one of docker_image and dockerfile is required. Any other key is an error: a typo like memory: is caught, not ignored.

items.title: The image: docker_image or dockerfile
items.text:
The image is everything the agent can use without the network: the language runtime, the libraries, the command-line tools, the data files.

docker_imagedockerfile 
environments:
  slim:
    docker_image: python:3.12-slim

The image is pulled as it is. Nothing to build, no folder to keep.

environments:
  data:
    dockerfile: |
      FROM python:3.12-slim
      RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends tmux git && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
      WORKDIR /app
      COPY data/ /app/data/
      RUN pip install --no-cache-dir pandas
    workdir: /app

The image is built from environments/data/environment/, which holds data/. The Dockerfile in the YAML is written into that folder as Dockerfile.

When to use which.

  • docker_image when a public or registry image already has what the agent needs. It skips the build and leaves nothing to drift.
  • dockerfile when the agent needs tools, packages or files the base image lacks. Keep it short: every line is something to trust and maintain.
  • A dockerfile that is slow to build, used across many rows and models: build it once yourself, push it to a registry the sandbox provider can pull from, and name it with docker_image. Whether a built image is reused between rows is up to the sandbox provider, not the arena.

tmux and python3

terminus-2, the default agent, works its terminal through tmux. When the image lacks it, terminus-2 tries to install it at the start of every task, which needs a package manager and the network, and fails without them. Install tmux in the Dockerfile. Most agents also run Python: start from an image that has python3.

build_timeout_sec bounds the build (600 seconds by default). Raise it for a heavy build (CUDA bases, large pip installs) rather than letting the rows fail on it; lower it to fail fast on a build that should be quick.

os is linux unless you set windows. Leave it unless your image is a Windows one and your sandbox provider runs those.

items.title: Where the agent starts: workdir
items.text:
workdir is the directory every command in the sandbox starts in, the agent's included. Set it to where the work happens, and put answer_file under it (/app/answer.txt with workdir: /app), so the agent finds both without searching.

The image must have it

With a docker_image, a workdir the image lacks makes every command fail, and so every row. Either create it in a Dockerfile (WORKDIR /app) or leave workdir out to keep the image's own.

items.title: Resources
items.text:
environments:
  heavy:
    docker_image: python:3.12
    cpus: 4
    memory_mb: 8192
    storage_mb: 20480
field blank means cpus, memory_mb on the local Docker: 2 CPUs (no more than the machine has) and 2048 MB. Elsewhere: the provider's default storage_mb, gpus the provider's default gpu_types any GPU type

How to size them. Give the sandbox what the work needs, not what the machine has.

  • Question answering with a shell and Python: 1 to 2 CPUs and 2048 MB.
  • Data work (pandas over a real file, compiling, running test suites): 2 to 4 CPUs and 4096 to 8192 MB. An agent killed for lack of memory scores 0, which looks like a wrong model.
  • storage_mb only when the agent writes large files or installs a lot.
  • gpus only when the task runs a model or GPU code. Not every provider has GPUs: E2B, the default provider, has none, and the arena app refuses such a run before it starts.

Keep resources equal across models

Every model of an evaluation runs in the same environment, so the comparison is fair by construction. Change the resources between two evaluations, though, and their scores no longer compare.

On the local Docker, a container without limits would get the whole machine, and a few at once can freeze it, more so with a local model loading beside them. So the arena fills in 2 CPUs and 2048 MB there when the entry leaves them blank, and runs one trial at a time. What the entry asks for is always kept. The settings below change both defaults.

items.title: Network
items.text:
environments:
  offline:
    docker_image: python:3.12-slim
    network_mode: no-network
  pip-only:
    docker_image: python:3.12-slim
    network_mode: allowlist
    allowed_hosts: [pypi.org, files.pythonhosted.org]
network_mode the sandbox can reach use it when public (default) anything the agent needs to install packages or fetch data, or you are still building the environment no-network nothing the answer must come from the model and the image alone: fair, reproducible, nothing leaks out allowlist only allowed_hosts the agent needs one or two hosts (a package index, your API), and nothing else

Why turn it off. With public, an agent can search the web for the answer to a well-known benchmark question, download a solution, or send data anywhere. For a leaderboard that claims to measure the model, no-network is the honest setting. It is also the safe one when the agent runs code you did not review.

What it costs. The network mode applies to everything in the sandbox, the agent included:

  • terminus-2 runs on your machine and types into the sandbox, so it works with any network mode, as long as the image already has tmux.
  • An agent installed in the sandbox (claude-code, codex, openhands, ...) calls its model from there. With no-network it cannot work at all, and the run refuses the pairing: Harbor agent 'openhands' runs inside the sandbox and calls its model from there, which a no-network environment forbids. With allowlist, its model provider's host has to be on the list. See Agents and models.
  • An HTTP MCP server has to be reachable under the network mode too.

Not every provider can cut or filter the network. E2B can do both; on the local Docker it depends on the host. In the arena app, a run whose provider cannot give the network mode asked for is refused before it starts.

items.title: Environment variables: env
items.text:
environments:
  python:
    docker_image: python:3.12-slim
    env:
      PYTHONUNBUFFERED: "1"
      DATA_DIR: /app/data

Set in the container, so the agent's commands and any stdio MCP server started there see them. Keys must have no whitespace; values are strings, so quote numbers.

Use env for settings the work needs: paths, flags, and a stdio MCP server's variables, which Harbor cannot hand to the server itself.

A value can name a variable of your machine as ${NAME}. When a run reads its config, after it has loaded the workspace's .env, the reference is replaced by the variable's value:

environments:
  search:
    docker_image: python:3.12-slim
    network_mode: public
    env:
      SEARCH_API_KEY: ${SEARCH_API_KEY}   # from your shell or the workspace's .env

The YAML, and the copy of it beside each run's config, keep ${SEARCH_API_KEY}, not the value. A variable set nowhere stops the run before it starts, naming it; openarena check warns about it first. $${NAME} writes a literal ${NAME}.

Anything in env is the agent's

The value is set in the sandbox, so the agent can read every variable, print it, and, with a network, send it anywhere. ${NAME} keeps a key out of your files, not out of the agent's reach. Put in no key you would not hand to the model; prefer one scoped to the evaluation and easy to revoke.

items.title: Healthcheck
items.text:
environments:
  service:
    dockerfile: |
      FROM python:3.12-slim
      RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends tmux curl && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
      # ... and starts the service the agent will query
    healthcheck:
      command: curl -fs http://localhost:8000/health   # exit 0 means ready
      interval_sec: 5
      timeout_sec: 30
      retries: 3

Harbor runs command inside the container until it succeeds, and the agent starts only once the sandbox is ready. Leave it out when the image is ready as soon as it starts, which is the usual case. Add it when the image starts a server, loads a database or warms a cache the agent depends on: without it, the agent's first commands race the service and fail.

field default command required run in the container; exit 0 means ready interval_sec 5 seconds between tries timeout_sec 30 how long one try may take retries 3 how many failed tries are allowed start_period_sec 0 a grace period after the container starts start_interval_sec 5 seconds between tries during that grace period

They are written to the task's [environment.healthcheck] as they are. The command's tools must be in the image: curl is not in python:3.12-slim, hence the install above.

items.title: MCP servers
items.text:
environments:
  web:
    docker_image: python:3.12-slim
    network_mode: public
    mcp_servers: [fetch]          # keys of mcp_servers.yaml

The agent gets these servers' tools beside its terminal. Harbor carries less of a server than a plain dataset does: no websocket, no headers, no stdio env or cwd, and a stdio command runs inside the sandbox, so the image must have it. MCP tools has the details.

items.title: The dataset over it
items.text:
An environment runs only through a dataset that names it:

datasets:
  gsm8k-terminal:
    type: huggingface
    config:
      path: openai/gsm8k
      name: main
      split: test
      limit: 5
      input_template: '{"question": {{ question | tojson }}}'
      output_template: '{"answer": {{ answer.split(''####'')[-1] | replace('','', '''') | trim | tojson }}}'
      input_schema: {type: object, properties: {question: {type: string, description: The question to answer}}, required: [question]}
      output_schema: {type: object, properties: {answer: {type: string, description: The answer only}}, required: [answer]}
    harbor:
      environment: python              # an environments.yaml key
      agent: terminus-2
      instructions: Solve the problem; you may use Python. Write the bare number only.
      answer_file: /app/answer.txt     # the agent is told to write its answer here
      timeout_sec: 300                 # per row
    reward: exact-match
harbor: field default environment none the sandbox every row runs in; required unless the dataset is harbor_tasks agent terminus-2 the Harbor agent the model drives (Agents and models) instructions none said to the agent before every row's question; not on a harbor_tasks dataset answer_file none an absolute path in the sandbox; the agent is told to write its final answer there, and nothing else; not on a harbor_tasks dataset timeout_sec Harbor's how long the agent may work on one row, in seconds

The question must render to {"question": ...}. The prediction is the agent's whole trajectory plus answer: the content of answer_file, else the agent's last message. The reward reads answer, so any reward works. Set answer_file whenever the reward compares strings (exact_match): an agent's last message is often a summary of what it did, not the bare answer.

A Harbor dataset cannot share an evaluation with other kinds of dataset; give it an evaluation of its own (Running evaluations).

items.title: Where it runs: the sandbox provider
items.text:
The environment says what the sandbox is. Where it runs is a setting of your machine, not of the YAML: the same entry runs on any provider that can give what it asks for.

E2B (default)Local DockerOther providers

Remote sandboxes. Set E2B_API_KEY, in your shell or in the workspace's .env. The sandboxes do not run on your machine, and the arena does not hold them to one at a time. no-network and allowlist are supported; GPUs are not.

export ARENA_HARBOR_SANDBOX=docker

Runs on your machine's Docker, with no key. Good for building and debugging an environment, and for private images. One trial at a time by default, 2 CPUs and 2048 MB unless the entry asks otherwise. GPUs and network modes depend on your Docker host.

ARENA_HARBOR_SANDBOX takes any provider Harbor knows, such as daytona, modal, runloop or podman. Each needs its own credentials, which Harbor checks before a trial. A name Harbor does not know is refused, with the list of those it does.

The silent fallback

When the configured provider cannot start (E2B with no E2B_API_KEY), trials run on the local Docker instead. That keeps a first run working, but it also changes the defaults: local resource limits, one trial at a time. When neither can start, the run is refused.

setting default what it does ARENA_HARBOR_SANDBOX e2b the sandbox provider E2B_API_KEY none E2B's key; without it, trials fall back to the local Docker ARENA_HARBOR_LOCAL_CPUS 2 CPUs a local Docker sandbox gets when the entry leaves cpus blank (no more than the machine has) ARENA_HARBOR_LOCAL_MEMORY_MB 2048 memory a local Docker sandbox gets when the entry leaves memory_mb blank ARENA_HARBOR_LOCAL_TRIALS 1 local Docker trials at once ARENA_HARBOR_WORKDIR the run's state where task folders and trials are written; set it when Docker cannot read the default folder

Raise ARENA_HARBOR_LOCAL_TRIALS only when the machine has room for that many sandboxes at once, plus the model if you serve it locally.

Docker installed as a snap

A snap Docker reads neither /tmp nor a hidden folder of your home, so it cannot read the run's state under a hidden folder. The arena then writes task folders and trials under ~/arena-harbor/ instead, unless ARENA_HARBOR_WORKDIR says where.

items.title: Timeouts
items.text:
Three limits, set in three places:

limit where default bounds build_timeout_sec the environment 600 s building the image healthcheck.timeout_sec the environment 30 s one healthcheck try timeout_sec the dataset's harbor: block Harbor's the agent's work on one row

The agent's limit sits on the dataset, not the environment, because the same sandbox can serve quick and slow questions.

items.title: Recipes
items.text:
Offline Python, for a fair leaderboard 
environments:
  offline-python:
    description: Python 3.12, numpy and pandas, no network.
    tags: [python, offline]
    dockerfile: |
      FROM python:3.12-slim
      RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends tmux && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
      RUN pip install --no-cache-dir numpy pandas
      WORKDIR /app
    workdir: /app
    cpus: 1
    memory_mb: 2048
    network_mode: no-network

Everything is in the image, so nothing is needed from the network. Pair it with terminus-2, which runs on your machine.

Package installs only 
environments:
  pip-only:
    dockerfile: |
      FROM python:3.12-slim
      RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends tmux && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
      WORKDIR /app
    workdir: /app
    network_mode: allowlist
    allowed_hosts: [pypi.org, files.pythonhosted.org]

The agent may pip install what it needs, and reach nothing else.

A GPU sandbox 
environments:
  cuda:
    docker_image: registry.example.com/team/cuda-agent:1.0   # your own image, with tmux
    gpus: 1
    gpu_types: [H100, A100]
    memory_mb: 32768

Needs a provider with GPUs, so not E2B. An empty gpu_types accepts any GPU.

items.title: Common mistakes
items.text:
openarena check catches these from the YAML alone:

mistake what check reports fix neither image field an environment needs an image add docker_image: or dockerfile: \| both image fields an environment is a `docker_image` or a `dockerfile`, not both remove one allowlist with no hosts an `allowlist` network lets nothing through without `allowed_hosts` add allowed_hosts:, or use public allowed_hosts with another mode `allowed_hosts` is only read with `network_mode: allowlist`, not 'public' set network_mode: allowlist, or remove the hosts a misspelled field (memory:) not a field of a `environments` entry rename it as the fix says (memory_mb:) a mode that does not exist (off) Input should be 'public', 'no-network' or 'allowlist' use one of the three cpus: 0 Input should be greater than or equal to 1 1 or more, or leave it blank an unknown MCP server 'nope' is not in `mcp_servers` add it to mcp_servers.yaml a dataset naming an unknown environment the dataset's harbor.environment is flagged add the entry, or fix the name a ${NAME} in env whose variable is set nowhere a warning: `${NAME}` is not set in your shell or in <workspace>/.env; a run that reads it refuses to start add NAME=... to .env, or export it

Checking an evaluation as a whole, check and evaluations run also refuse an agent that cannot work with a model or with the environment's network, and an MCP server Harbor cannot carry.

What check cannot see, because it starts nothing: an image that does not exist, a Dockerfile that does not build, a workdir missing from the image, a missing tmux, a provider without the GPUs or network mode asked for. These show up as rows that score 0, or as a cell that fails because no row got an answer. Read the trial's logs (Reading results).

Build an environment on one row

While building an environment, set limit: 1 on the dataset, run on the local Docker, and read the first trial before running the full grid.

items.title: See also
items.text:
• Harbor tasks: the task format, and the agents
  • MCP tools: tools in a sandbox
  • Datasets: templates and schemas
  • Checking configs
  • Reading results: trials and their logs

items.title: Running evaluations
items.text:
An evaluation is a saved sweep, kept in configs/evaluations.yaml. It names models and datasets. Running it evaluates every model on every dataset: one cell per pair. A cell sends each row of the dataset to the model, scores each answer with the dataset's reward, and keeps the mean.

flowchart LR
    M["language_models<br/>qwen38, gpt-4o-mini"] --> G{{"grid<br/>model × dataset"}}
    D["datasets<br/>gsm8k-20, mmlu-50"] --> G
    G --> C1["qwen38 × gsm8k-20"]
    G --> C2["qwen38 × mmlu-50"]
    G --> C3["gpt-4o-mini × gsm8k-20"]
    G --> C4["gpt-4o-mini × mmlu-50"]
    C1 & C2 & C3 & C4 --> R[".open-arena/NAME/result.json"]

Two models on two datasets make four cells. The evaluation holds no rows, no prompts and no scoring rules: those belong to the datasets, the rewards and the models it names. It says what to put on the grid, plus a few settings that apply to every cell.

Why save a sweep instead of passing flags? A saved evaluation is the same experiment every time you run it: the same models, datasets and batch size. Next week you rerun it on a new model by adding one name, and the run's folder records exactly what ran.

items.title: The entry
items.text:
evaluations:
  math-compare:                              # the name you run it by, and its folder under .open-arena/
    description: Local Qwen against the hosted baseline on GSM8K.
    tags: [math, weekly]                     # for listings only
    language_models: [qwen38, gpt-4o-mini]   # the grid's rows: models keys (a2a_agents keys for an A2A sweep)
    datasets: [gsm8k-20]                     # the grid's columns: datasets keys, each with a reward
    batch_size: 4                            # rows in flight at once, for every dataset of this sweep
    metrics:                                 # extra columns, on every dataset
      - cost                                 # what the model under test cost, in USD; lower is better
      - avg_latency                          # seconds per model call; lower is better
      - answer_accuracy                      # a catalog reward, averaged over the rows
    seed: 0                                  # seeds the engine's own randomness, not the model's sampling

The name follows the rule of every registry key: a letter or a digit, then letters, digits, _, . or -. It is also the folder the run writes to, so keep it short.

items.title: Fields
items.text:
field required default what it is language_models yes The models to compare, by their key in models.yaml. At least one. For an A2A dataset, keys of a2a_agents.yaml instead. datasets yes The datasets to run them on, by key. At least one. Each must have a reward:. batch_size no each dataset's own, else 1 Rows sent at once, for every dataset of this sweep. 1 to 1024. metrics no none Columns added beside reward on every dataset. seed no none Seeds the engine's own random number generators before anything is built. default_language_model no none The model a reward or metric uses when its config names none. A models key of type llm, called with its params. default_embedding_model no none The same, for rewards and metrics that need an embedding model. A models key of type embedding. description no One line for listings. tags no Labels for listings, e.g. math, weekly.

Nothing else is accepted: a field the schema does not know is an error, not silently ignored. The sections below take each field in turn.

items.title: language_models: the grid's rows
items.text:
The models you want to compare, by the name you gave them in models.yaml, not by their provider id. That name is what the result tables, result.json and leaderboards show.

A model entry is an id plus its params, so two entries can call the same id with different settings, and they are two rows of the grid. That is how you compare temperature: 0 with temperature: 0.7, or two reasoning_effort levels, on one model:

models:
  gpt-4o-mini:
    model: openai/gpt-4o-mini
    params: {temperature: 0}
  gpt-4o-mini-warm:
    model: openai/gpt-4o-mini
    params: {temperature: 0.7}
evaluations:
  temperature-check:
    language_models: [gpt-4o-mini, gpt-4o-mini-warm]
    datasets: [gsm8k-20]

What a row of the grid must be depends on the datasets:

the datasets are language_models lists plain, generator, agent, tools, harbor models keys of type llm embedding models keys of type embedding a2a a2a_agents keys: the agents themselves are compared (A2A agents)

items.title: datasets: the grid's columns
items.text:
The datasets, by key, in the order the result tables show them. Every one needs a reward: (Datasets). A dataset without one cannot be scored, and the evaluation is refused before anything runs.

Some kinds of dataset cannot share a sweep with other kinds, because the grid's rows are different things for them, or because they run in a sandbox:

kind can share a sweep with plain, generator, agent, tools each other embedding only other embedding datasets a2a only other a2a datasets harbor (including harbor_tasks datasets) only other Harbor datasets

To run GSM8K and a Harbor suite on the same models, write two evaluations. Their scores still meet on a leaderboard, which reads every finished run.

items.title: batch_size: how much runs at once
items.text:
A batch is the group of rows the engine sends at once and evaluates as one step. batch_size is therefore the concurrency knob: with batch_size: 8, up to eight rows are answered at the same time, so eight requests are in flight against the provider (more when a judge reward scores them).

The size a cell uses is the first one set of:

  1. --batch-size N on the command line, for this run only;
  2. the evaluation's batch_size;
  3. the dataset's own batch_size in its config;
  4. 1.

Cells run one after the other, never two at once. A larger batch speeds up each cell; nothing makes two cells overlap.

setup a good starting batch_size why a local model (Ollama, vLLM) on one machine 1 to 4 the server answers a few requests at a time; more just queue, and can time out a hosted model on a new or low-tier key 2 to 4 rate limits are per minute; a burst gets throttled a hosted model on a high-tier key 8 to 32 the provider can take it; the run finishes many times faster a judge reward on top about half of the above each row also makes a judge call an agent dataset 1 to 4 each row is a loop of model and tool calls, and the MCP servers take the load too Harbor, on a laptop 1 each row in flight is a sandbox with an agent session in it

A rate limit does not stop the run: it lowers the score

A model call that fails is retried, up to five attempts, waiting longer between them and honouring a provider's Retry-After. A call that still fails leaves its row without an answer and logs a warning, All retries failed for .... The row scores 0 and the cell carries on. A batch size too high for your key therefore shows up as a reward that is too low, not as an error. If you see those warnings, lower batch_size and run the evaluation again with --no-cache. (When every call of a cell fails, the cell fails instead, and a plain rerun runs it again; see What can fail.)

Where to set it: the dataset's batch_size is a property of the data (a Harbor dataset that should never run more than one sandbox at a time). The evaluation's is a property of the setup you run it on (a sweep of local models that a laptop must survive). --batch-size is for one run: a quick try at a higher speed, or a slower retry after throttling.

items.title: metrics: the columns beside reward
items.text:
reward is always the first column: the mean of the dataset's reward over its rows. metrics adds more columns, on every dataset of the sweep. A dataset can add its own too (Datasets); when both name the same column, the dataset's wins.

Each entry is a bare name, or a mapping:

key default what class required a catalog reward (averaged over the rows), or a measurement such as cost alias the class's name the column's name; never reward, which is taken direction min for a cost, tokens or latency measurement, else max max if higher is better, min if lower is better objective false true puts the column on the dataset's Pareto frontier, beside reward anything else the class's own settings, e.g. a judge's language_model (a models key, called with its params)

The measurements of a run are columns like any other. Only the columns you list are kept in result.json, so only those can be ranked on a leaderboard:

class what it measures over the cell cost USD spent on calls to the model under test reward_cost USD spent on judge calls while scoring embedding_cost USD spent on embedding calls input_tokens, output_tokens, total_tokens tokens consumed avg_latency seconds per model call, on average

Which way is better is read off the name

Without direction:, a metric is min when it measures what the calls spend or how often they fail: a name ending in tokens (but not cached_tokens), token_share, cost, latency, time_to_..., elapsed_time, error_rate, failed_calls or fallback_activations, optionally followed by _per_call. So cost, reward_cost, total_tokens and avg_latency rank the cheaper, faster model first. Anything else is max, rates such as cache_hit_rate included. Write direction: only to override it.

objective: true asks the run for trade-offs. On a dataset with more than one objective, result.json lists the models no other model beats on every objective at once (frontier_by_ds, see Reading results). Use it when the best model is not the cheapest and you want to see which models are worth considering at all.

evaluations:
  quality-vs-cost:
    language_models: [qwen38, gpt-4o-mini, gpt-4o]
    datasets: [gsm8k-20]
    metrics:
      - {class: cost, objective: true}
      - {class: lm_as_judge, alias: judged, language_model: gpt-4o-mini}

Put a metric on the evaluation when you want it on every dataset of the sweep (cost, latency). Put it on the dataset when it only makes sense for that data (an answer_accuracy for numeric answers).

items.title: seed
items.text:
Before anything is built, the run seeds the engine's random number generators with this value. That makes the engine's own choices repeatable. It does not make the models' answers repeatable: sampling happens at the provider, out of reach of this seed. For steadier answers, set temperature: 0 on the models (Models), and still expect small differences between two runs of a hosted model.

Set it on any evaluation you will compare over time: it costs nothing and removes one source of drift.

items.title: default_language_model, default_embedding_model
items.text:
Some rewards and metrics call a model: a judge, a semantic similarity. Their config usually names it (language_model: gpt-4o-mini). When it does not, they use these defaults.

evaluations:
  judged-sweep:
    language_models: [qwen38, gpt-4o-mini]
    datasets: [support-golden]
    default_language_model: judge-4o      # the judge of every reward that names none

Prefer naming the judge on the reward itself (Rewards): the choice then travels with the reward to every evaluation that uses it. Use the default when one sweep should swap the judge of all its rewards at once.

Note

When a run sets a default model, the engine also writes it to its settings file in your home folder. Name the judge explicitly on rewards you care about rather than relying on what an earlier run left behind.

items.title: description, tags
items.text: Shown by openarena evaluations list and in the app's listings. They change nothing in a run. A tag such as smoke or weekly tells a quick check from the real thing at a glance.

items.title: Things that are not evaluation fields
items.text:
If you are looking for one of these on the evaluation, it lives elsewhere:

you want set where fewer rows, for a quick try limit: N in the dataset's config (the first N rows) Datasets each row answered several times, to average out sampling repeat: N in the dataset's config: each row is sent N times, and the reward is the mean over all the answers Datasets temperature, max tokens, reasoning effort the model's params Models a spending limit a leaderboard's budgets:: a model over budget is left out of the ranking. Nothing stops a run while it spends Leaderboards more cells at once not possible within one run: raise batch_size, or run two evaluations side by side A large sweep more or fewer retries not configurable: each model call gets up to five attempts batch_size

repeat gives a steadier mean, not a spread

With repeat: 5, a cell's reward is the mean over five answers per row, which smooths out a lucky or unlucky sample. It does not tell you how much the answers varied. To see the spread between runs, run the same evaluation under different --state-dirs and compare the result.jsons.

items.title: Running it
items.text:
openarena check configs                    # every registry, as the run will read it
openarena evaluations list                 # the saved evaluations
openarena evaluations run math-compare     # run one
option default what --configs DIR ./configs the configs folder to read --state-dir DIR ./.open-arena where runs live, one folder per evaluation --no-cache off start over instead of resuming --batch-size N the batch size for this run, over the evaluation's --json FILE also write the result there -v, -vv a progress bar per cell, or a line per batch

The run first reads the workspace's .env (beside configs/), without overriding a variable your shell already sets. It then gathers the evaluation and every entry it names into one config, replaces each ${NAME} with its variable (Secrets in configs), and validates it whole. It refuses to start on a problem: a ${NAME} not set, an unknown dataset, a dataset without a reward, a model of the wrong type, kinds that cannot share a run. The snapshot it writes keeps the ${NAME} references, not their values.

CLI has every option in detail.

items.title: What happens during a run
items.text:
flowchart TD
    A["read .env, gather the entries, validate"] --> B["write .open-arena/NAME/config.yaml"]
    B --> C["look up a price for every model"]
    C --> D["per dataset: load the rows, build the reward,<br/>read back the cells a previous attempt finished"]
    D --> E["build a program for each cell still to run<br/>(opens MCP servers and A2A clients)"]
    E --> F["run the cells, model by model"]
    F --> G["print a table per dataset, write result.json"]

Every dataset is loaded and every program built before the first cell runs. A broken dataset fails the run in its first minute, not after an hour of model calls. An agent whose MCP servers give no tools (a server down, a command not found, a server with no tools) fails only its own cells, with could not load the MCP tools of [...], and the other cells run.

The cells then run model by model: every dataset for the first model, then every dataset for the second. A local server that holds one model at a time loads each model once, not once per cell.

items.title: Watching it
items.text:
Running math-compare (.open-arena/math-compare/config.yaml)
gsm8k-20
  qwen38 running…
  qwen38 done reward 0.6500, cost 0.0000, avg_latency 2.1043, answer_accuracy 0.7000
  gpt-4o-mini running…
  gpt-4o-mini done reward 0.8500, cost 0.0021, avg_latency 0.8120, answer_accuracy 0.9000

A line when a cell starts, a line with its numbers when it ends. -v adds a progress bar per cell and -vv a line per batch: use them on long cells, to see that something is moving. After each dataset, every failed cell gets a line with the reason: <model> failed: <why>.

At the end, a table per dataset: a row per model, a column per metric, — where a cell has no value.

items.title: Failures
items.text:
Things go wrong at three levels:

level what happens what you see a row a model call fails five times: the row gets no answer and scores 0 All retries failed for ... in the log; a lower reward a cell an error the cell cannot get past (a template naming a missing column, an agent whose MCP servers give no tools), or no row got an answer at all (a missing key, a model server that is down, a model id the provider does not know): the cell is recorded as failed, and the run moves on <model> failed: <why>, for example no row got an answer: all 20 row(s) failed; the first error: <error>; — in the table; a status other than COMPLETED in result.json the run every cell runs, however many fail; then, if any cell failed, the command exits 1 after the table and result.json, N cell(s) failed: <model> × <dataset>, ...

A row an A2A agent does not answer (an error, a task that did not complete, the timeout) is a row-level failure too: a warning, a 0 for that row, and the cell goes on.

Reading results lists the usual causes and their fixes.

items.title: Resuming and starting over
items.text:
A run keeps each cell's state in its folder as the cell finishes. Running the same evaluation again picks up where it stopped:

  • cells that finished are not run again: their scores are read back;
  • cells that failed, or were running when the process stopped, run again;
  • cells never reached run for the first time.

So after a crash or a Ctrl-C, run the same command and only what is missing runs. The same goes for a missing key or a model server that was down: no row of those cells got an answer, so they failed rather than scoring 0, and a plain rerun runs them once the cause is fixed. Only a cell where some rows answered is kept with 0 for the others; rerun it with --no-cache.

The saved state does not record what a finished cell was computed from, so it keeps the cell even when its inputs changed. Use --no-cache to start over:

you changed finished cells are do nothing; the run stopped or a cell failed still right run again --batch-size or batch_size still right run again description, tags still right run again the language_models list possibly stale --no-cache a dataset's rows, templates, limit or repeat stale --no-cache a reward, or any metrics stale --no-cache a model's params or model id stale --no-cache rate limits made rows score 0 finished, but scored too low --no-cache

--no-cache drops every cell of the evaluation

It wipes the saved cells of every dataset in the evaluation, so everything runs, and is paid for, again. To redo only part of a sweep, write a smaller evaluation for that part.

Two evaluations never share saved state: each has its own folder.

items.title: What a run writes
items.text:
.open-arena/math-compare/
  config.yaml              the evaluation and every entry it names, gathered: what ran
  result.json              the scores, written when the run ends
  gsm8k-20/                each dataset's saved cells: what a resumed run reads back
  harbor/                  Harbor trials, for Harbor datasets
  tasks/  environments/    copies of the Harbor folders the run used

config.yaml is written again at every launch, from the configs as they are then, and the Harbor folders are copied again. result.json is written only when the run ends: after an interrupted run, the one there (if any) is from the previous finished run. What is in it, and how to read it: Reading results.

items.title: How a run is priced
items.text:
Each call is priced by litellm from its token counts. Before the first cell, the run looks up a price for every model in models.yaml, the ones under test and the judges, from the first source that knows it:

  1. a local server (ollama/, vllm/, hosted_vllm/, lm_studio/, llamafile/): free, there is no bill;
  2. litellm's pricing table;
  3. OpenRouter's catalogue, which also prices many vendors' direct ids when OpenRouter serves the same model.

An openrouter/ model's answers carry their own cost.

A cost of 0 is not always free

A model that no source prices still runs, but its spend reads 0. If a hosted model shows cost 0.0000, its price is unknown, not zero. Check what you were billed before trusting that column.

To keep the cost in the results and on leaderboards, list it under metrics (above).

items.title: Estimating it before you run
items.text:
Count the calls:

cells          = models × datasets
rows per cell  = limit (or the dataset's size) × repeat
model calls    = cells × rows per cell × calls per row
judge calls    = cells × rows per cell × judges (rewards and metrics that call a model)

A plain or generator row is one call. An agent row is a loop: one call per step, plus the tool calls. A Harbor row is a whole agent session in a sandbox, often dozens of calls. Each judge adds a call per row.

Then measure rather than guess: run the sweep with limit: 5 and cost as a metric, read the cost per cell, and multiply by rows / 5.

items.title: When to use what
items.text:
First run of a new setupComparing modelsA large sweepA noisy taskKeeping runs apart

Smoke it. Set limit: 5 on the datasets, run one cheap model, and read the answers (Reading results), not only the scores. A reward of 0 everywhere usually means a template or an answer format is off, and that is cheap to find on five rows.

evaluations:
  math-smoke:
    tags: [smoke]
    language_models: [gpt-4o-mini]   # one cheap model is enough to test the setup
    datasets: [gsm8k-20]             # with limit: 5 in its config
    batch_size: 1

Then raise limit, add the other models, and run the real evaluation.

Every model on the same datasets, temperature: 0 on each, cost and avg_latency as columns (both rank lower first on their own), a seed. When a new model comes out, add it to the list and run with --no-cache, or give it an evaluation of its own: a leaderboard puts them side by side either way.

Split it into several evaluations: by provider, by kind of dataset, or by size. Each has its own folder, its own saved state, and its failures do not hold the others back. Run them one after the other, or side by side in two terminals when they call different providers, so that their rate limits do not add up. A leaderboard then reads every result.json under .open-arena/ and ranks them together.

When two runs of one model disagree, set repeat: 3 to 5 on the dataset: the reward becomes a mean over several answers per row. It multiplies the cost by the same factor, so try it on a limited dataset first.

--state-dir gives a run a different home. Use it to keep last month's results while running the same evaluation again, or to run it twice and compare.

openarena evaluations run math-compare --state-dir runs/2026-10
openarena leaderboards run overall --state-dir runs/2026-10

openarena leaderboards run reads the --state-dir you give it, so point it at the same one.

items.title: Common mistakes
items.text:
openarena check configs reads each evaluation as a run would, and reports:

mistake openarena check says language_models: [] List should have at least 1 item ...: give it a value batch_size: 0 Input should be greater than or equal to 1: set 1 or more a field the schema does not have (concurrency:, repeats:, limit:) not a field of a evaluations entry, with the fields an entry reads a model or dataset that is not in its registry 'gpt4' is not in models, with the closest name or the ones there a dataset without reward: dataset 'd' has no reward:: set one, or leave the dataset out an embedding model in a text sweep, or the other way round ... this sweep needs embedding models: list only models of the type the datasets need an A2A, embedding or Harbor dataset beside other kinds ... cannot share a run ...: split it in two evaluations an embedding model as default_language_model 'e' is an embedding model; this setting needs a language model

What check cannot see:

  • A missing key. A hosted model without its key fails every call at run time, and its cell fails with no row got an answer: .... Set the key in .env and run the same command again: the failed cell runs, the others are read back.
  • A batch too large for your rate limit. It shows as All retries failed warnings and a low reward, not as an error.
  • Saved cells from before a change. The run reuses them silently. Add --no-cache after changing what they depend on.
  • A ${NAME} set nowhere. check only warns; the run refuses to start and names it.

Checking configs has every check.

Tracing to MLflow

openarena evaluations run does not trace to MLflow. The arena app runs the same sweep with tracing on when MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI is set and the server answers its /health check (ARENA_MLFLOW_TRACING=0 opts out). Each run then gets its own experiment, under MLFLOW_EXPERIMENT_NAME, and each cell one MLflow run named <dataset> · <model>, tagged with the dataset and the model, with a span per model call and its cost. A server that is down never fails an evaluation: the run goes on untraced, with a warning.

items.title: Next
items.text:
• Reading results: result.json, the answers, failed cells.
  • Leaderboards: rank models across runs, with budgets.
  • Checking configs: every check, before you pay for a run.

items.title: Harbor tasks
items.text: A Harbor task is a folder. It holds what the agent is told, the sandbox it works in, the tests that score it, and a reference solution. openarena runs task folders as Harbor defines them: one trial per task, the model under test driving a Harbor agent, and the task's own tests giving the score.

items.title: When to use Harbor tasks
items.text:
A question-and-answer dataset scores what a model says. A Harbor task scores what an agent does: the files it leaves, the code it fixes, the service it gets running. Pick the tool by what you need to check.

you want to measure use a short answer, a label, a number an ordinary dataset (Datasets) tool calls against live servers an agent: dataset (MCP tools) ordinary questions, worked with a terminal, scored on the answer a dataset over an environment work in a sandbox, checked by a script: coding, fixing, configuring Harbor tasks (this page)

Harbor tasks are the right tool when:

  • The result is a state, not a sentence. A test suite passes, a file has the right content, a server answers on a port.
  • Each task needs its own setup. Its own repository, data files, packages or image.
  • The check is code. A script can decide, without a model judging free text.

They cost more. Every row builds or pulls an image, starts a sandbox, and runs a whole agent session of many model calls. A Q&A row is one call. Use Harbor tasks for what a Q&A dataset cannot measure, not as a slower way to ask questions.

Environment or task folders?

When many questions share one sandbox and a reward can score the final answer, use a dataset over an environment. When each task brings its own files and its own tests, write task folders.

items.title: How a trial runs
items.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant O as openarena
    participant S as Sandbox
    participant G as Agent
    participant M as Model under test
    O->>O: copy the task folder for this trial
    O->>S: build environment/ or pull docker_image, start it
    O->>G: instruction.md
    loop until the agent stops or its time runs out
        G->>M: what next?
        M-->>G: a step
        G->>S: run a command
    end
    O->>S: bring in tests/, run tests/test.sh
    S-->>O: /logs/verifier/reward.txt or reward.json
    O->>O: read trajectory.json and the rewards, score the row

For each row (one task), openarena:

  1. Copies the task folder, so a trial never writes into your source folder. The copy is deleted when the trial is done.
  2. Starts one Harbor trial with the dataset's agent and the model on the evaluation's axis.
  3. Lets Harbor build the sandbox, run the agent, then run the verifier (tests/test.sh) in the same sandbox.
  4. Reads back the agent's trajectory and what the verifier wrote. The harbor_verifier reward turns that into the row's score.

items.title: The task folder
items.text:
tasks/<name>/
  task.toml                    the task's settings: timeouts, resources, network
  instruction.md               what the agent is told
  environment/Dockerfile       the sandbox, built from environment/
  tests/test.sh                runs after the agent, writes the score
  solution/solve.sh            what a correct agent does

tasks/ sits beside configs/ in the workspace. openarena init writes a working one, tasks/hello-world/. Copy it to start a new task.

A folder is a task when it holds a task.toml. Other folders under tasks/ are ignored.

items.title: task.toml
items.text:
The task's settings, in Harbor's format.

[metadata]
difficulty = "easy"
category = "general"

[agent]
timeout_sec = 300.0            # how long the agent may work

[verifier]
timeout_sec = 60.0             # how long tests/test.sh may take

[environment]
build_timeout_sec = 600.0
cpus = 1
memory_mb = 1024
# network_mode = "no-network"
# docker_image = "python:3.12-slim"  # a prebuilt image instead of environment/Dockerfile
section key what it does why you set it [metadata] free labels describes the task to sort and read tasks; not used for scoring [agent] timeout_sec how long the agent may work a hard task needs more; a cap stops a looping agent burning tokens [verifier] timeout_sec how long tests/test.sh may take a test suite that compiles or starts a server needs more [environment] build_timeout_sec how long building the image may take a heavy image (compilers, ML packages) needs more [environment] cpus, memory_mb, storage_mb the sandbox's resources a build or test suite that would be slow or killed otherwise [environment] gpus, gpu_types GPUs only for tasks that need them; not every sandbox provider has any [environment] network_mode, allowed_hosts public, no-network, or allowlist to stop the agent fetching the answer, or limit it to a package index [environment] docker_image a prebuilt image instead of environment/Dockerfile a faster start when nothing task-specific is installed [environment] workdir, env where commands start; variables in the container to match what the instruction says

The [environment] keys are the ones openarena writes for an environment entry. That page explains each in more depth.

A task folder is run as written

openarena adds nothing to a task's task.toml. On the local Docker, a dataset over an environment gets default limits (2 CPUs, 2048 MB) when it sets none. A task folder does not, and Docker would give the container the whole machine. Set cpus and memory_mb in every task.

In-sandbox agents need the network

Most agents run inside the sandbox and call the model from there (see Agents and models). A task with network_mode = "no-network" cuts them off. check catches this for an environment entry, but does not read a task folder's task.toml. Use terminus-2 for a no-network task.

items.title: instruction.md
items.text:
Plain text for the agent: what to do, where the inputs are, where the result must go. It is the only thing the agent is told.

  • Name exact paths and formats. "Write the total to /app/total.txt, as a single integer." The tests check those, so the agent must know them.
  • State what the tests check. If they run the project's test suite, say it must pass. Do not hide a requirement the agent cannot guess.
  • Say what must be true at the end, not how to get there. The tests check the outcome, not the commands.

The instruction is also the row's question in the trials log and the answers view.

items.title: environment/
items.text:
The sandbox's build context. Harbor builds environment/Dockerfile from it, unless task.toml names a docker_image.

FROM python:3.12-slim
# terminus-2 works its terminal through tmux.
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends tmux && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
WORKDIR /app
COPY data/ /app/data/
  • COPY paths are relative to environment/. Put the task's input files there (environment/data/).
  • Install what the agent and the tests need. A test that runs python3 or pytest needs them in the image: the tests run in the same sandbox.
  • Do not put the tests or the solution in the image. Harbor brings the tests in after the agent is done, so the agent cannot read them.
  • Pin versions (FROM python:3.12-slim, pip install pandas==2.2.2). An image that changes between runs moves scores for reasons that are not the model.

tmux

terminus-2, the default agent, works through tmux. Without it in the image, it installs tmux at the start of every trial, which needs a package manager and the network, and fails without them. Install it in the Dockerfile.

items.title: tests/: the verifier
items.text:
Harbor runs tests/test.sh in the sandbox after the agent stops. It writes the score to one of two files:

reward.txtreward.json

One number from 0 to 1. 1 is solved, 0 is not, fractions are allowed. It is read as the key reward.

#!/bin/bash
mkdir -p /logs/verifier
if [ "$(cat /app/hello.txt 2>/dev/null)" = "Hello, world!" ]; then
  echo 1 > /logs/verifier/reward.txt
else
  echo 0 > /logs/verifier/reward.txt
fi

Several named numbers. The harbor_verifier reward reads reward unless you point it at another key.

{"reward": 0.75, "builds": 1, "tests_pass": 0.5}

Every value must be a number: a text value fails the row. Always write a reward key, or point the reward at a key you do write.

How the score is held to range:

the verifier wrote the row scores a number in 0–1 that number a number outside 0–1 clamped to 0 or 1, with a warning in the run's log nan or inf 0, with a warning no reward key, or no file 0

items.title: Writing a verifier you can trust
items.text:
The verifier is the whole measurement. A wrong one ranks models on noise.

  • Test the outcome, not the method. Check the file, the output, the exit code. Do not look for the command you expected the agent to run.
  • Never fail on what the instruction did not ask for. If it says "a CSV", do not require a header it never mentioned.
  • Write a score on every path. Write 0 first, then overwrite it. A crash halfway still leaves a score.
  • Make it deterministic. No network calls, no clock, no random data; fix seeds. Give slow checks a generous [verifier] timeout_sec, so a busy machine does not fail a solved task.
  • Give partial credit when the task has parts. 0.6 for "builds and passes 3 of 5 tests" separates models that a 0 for both would not.
  • Keep the sub-scores. Write them to reward.json beside reward, and report them as extra metrics (see A dataset of tasks).

A verifier with partial credit:

tests/test.shtests/check.py 
#!/bin/bash
mkdir -p /logs/verifier
# Written first: if the check crashes, the task still scores 0.
echo '{"reward": 0}' > /logs/verifier/reward.json
python3 "$(dirname "$0")/check.py"

import json
from pathlib import Path

try:
    report = json.loads(Path("/app/report.json").read_text())
except (OSError, ValueError):
    report = None
ok = isinstance(report, dict)
checks = {
    "exists": ok,
    "total": ok and report.get("total") == 42,
    "regions": ok and sorted(report.get("regions") or []) == ["eu", "us"],
}
scores = {name: float(passed) for name, passed in checks.items()}
scores["reward"] = sum(scores.values()) / len(checks)
Path("/logs/verifier/reward.json").write_text(json.dumps(scores))

A pytest file works the same way: test.sh runs it, then writes the score from its result.

items.title: solution/
items.text:
solution/solve.sh is what a correct agent would do. Harbor's oracle agent runs it, and the tests must then give 1. That proves the task can be solved and the tests are right. An evaluation does not run the oracle: it is for checking the task while you write it.

Both scripts must be executable:

chmod +x tests/test.sh solution/solve.sh
Multi-step tasks

A Harbor task may hold a steps/ folder, one sub-folder per step, instead of a top-level instruction.md. openarena runs the folder as Harbor defines it. The row's question, shown in the trials log, is the first step's instruction.md.

items.title: A dataset of tasks
items.text:
A harbor_tasks dataset reads a folder of tasks, one row per task.

datasets:
  my-tasks:
    type: harbor_tasks
    config:
      path: tasks                  # relative to the workspace; the run copies it
      tasks: [hello-world]         # only these folders; none runs every task under path
    harbor:
      agent: terminus-2
      timeout_sec: 600             # per task, over task.toml's [agent] timeout_sec
    reward: harbor-tests
    metrics:
      - {class: harbor_verifier, alias: tests_pass, key: tests_pass}
rewards:
  harbor-tests:
    type: harbor_verifier          # reads what tests/test.sh wrote
field what it does when to set it config.path the folder holding the tasks always. Relative to the workspace (the parent of configs/), and copied beside the run's config at every run. An absolute path is read in place config.tasks only these task folders, by name to run a subset. A name without a task.toml stops the run. Left out, every task under path runs, sorted by name config.limit at most this many tasks a first run on a few tasks config.repeat each task this many times to measure how often a model succeeds, not whether it did once config.batch_size tasks run at once (default 1) on a cloud sandbox, to run trials in parallel harbor.agent the Harbor agent the model drives (default terminus-2) see Agents and models harbor.timeout_sec how long the agent may work on each task one budget for every task, whatever its task.toml says reward a harbor_verifier reward always metrics more harbor_verifier columns, each with its key to report reward.json's sub-scores beside reward

No input_template is needed: each row is the task's name, its folder and its instruction.

The harbor_verifier reward takes one setting, key: the key of reward.json it reads, reward by default.

Not for task folders

harbor.environment is refused: each task brings its own sandbox. harbor.instructions and harbor.answer_file belong to a dataset over an environment, and openarena check refuses them here. A task folder runs as written, so neither would reach its instruction: check says a `harbor_tasks` dataset runs each task as written: `instructions` is never said to the agent (write it in the task's instruction.md) and a `harbor_tasks` dataset is scored by each task's own tests: `answer_file` is never written, and leaves the answer empty (the task's tests/ read what the agent left in the sandbox).

A Harbor dataset cannot share an evaluation with other kinds of dataset. Give it its own evaluation (Running evaluations).

After editing a task, run with --no-cache. The tasks are copied again at every run, but a cell that already finished is reused as it is.

items.title: Agents and models
items.text:
The agent is the program that works in the sandbox. The model on the evaluation's axis is what the agent calls to decide each step.

agent runs calls terminus-2 (the default) on your machine any provider claude-code in the sandbox Anthropic models only codex in the sandbox OpenAI models only gemini-cli in the sandbox Google models only goose, opencode, openhands, mini-swe-agent, swe-agent, cline-cli, cursor-cli in the sandbox any provider

How to choose:

  • Comparing models: keep one agent for all of them. terminus-2 takes any provider, so it is the usual choice.
  • Comparing agents: one dataset per agent over the same tasks, with the same models where the agents allow it.
  • A local model (ollama/..., vllm/...): only terminus-2. An agent in the sandbox cannot reach your machine's localhost.
  • A task with no network: only terminus-2. The others call their model from inside the sandbox.

check and the run refuse a pairing that cannot work, and say why.

The model entry's params reach the agent where it takes them: temperature, reasoning_effort and, for agents that pass call settings through, max_tokens. A param the agent does not take is dropped, with a warning in the run's log. See Models.

items.title: Where it runs
items.text:
ARENA_HARBOR_SANDBOX names the sandbox provider (e2b, docker, daytona, modal, ...), e2b by default. Without E2B_API_KEY, trials fall back to the local Docker. With neither, the run refuses to start. A provider name Harbor does not know fails the run with the list of known ones.

variable default what it does ARENA_HARBOR_SANDBOX e2b the sandbox provider ARENA_HARBOR_LOCAL_TRIALS 1 trials at once on the local Docker ARENA_HARBOR_LOCAL_CPUS, ARENA_HARBOR_LOCAL_MEMORY_MB 2, 2048 default limits for a dataset over an environment, on the local Docker ARENA_HARBOR_WORKDIR the run's state folder where task copies and trials are written

On the local Docker, trials run one at a time unless ARENA_HARBOR_LOCAL_TRIALS says otherwise, whatever the batch_size. A few containers at once, with a local model loading, can freeze the machine.

Docker installed as a snap

A snap Docker reads neither hidden folders (the run's state is under .open-arena/ by default) nor /tmp. When openarena detects one, task copies, trials and temporary files go under ~/arena-harbor/ instead. Set ARENA_HARBOR_WORKDIR to choose the folder yourself.

items.title: What a trial produces
items.text:
The row's prediction is the agent's trajectory, in Harbor's ATIF format, plus two fields openarena adds:

field what it holds steps each step: its source (system, user or agent), its message, its tool_calls and the observation that came back agent, final_metrics, ... the rest of Harbor's trajectory, as the agent wrote it answer the agent's last message with text rewards what the verifier wrote: reward.txt as reward, or the keys of reward.json

The trajectory is read from the trial's agent/trajectory.json. Only agents that write one are offered.

Each trial's logs land under the run's harbor/trials/<trial>/, named after the task, the model and a short id. One line per trial goes to harbor/trials.jsonl:

key trial, dir the trial's name and its logs folder dataset, task, model, agent what ran question the instruction status answered or failed answer, steps, rewards for an answered trial error why it failed, or why an answered trial stopped early seconds, input_tokens, output_tokens, cost_usd time and usage, as the agent reported them

See Reading results for how to read a run.

How failures score:

  • The agent ran out of time: the trial still answered. The verifier scores what the agent left, and error says why it stopped.
  • No trajectory (the sandbox would not start, the agent crashed before its first step): the row scores 0, with Harbor's error in error. One flaky sandbox does not sink the cell.
  • No row of a cell answered: the cell fails. That is the sandbox, the image or a key, not the model, and a 0 would rank it as if it were.

A task that scores 0 for every model

Check the task before blaming the models. Its solution/solve.sh should make its tests give 1, and the trial's logs show what the verifier saw.

items.title: Scoring with the arena's rewards
items.text:
Some tasks have no answer a script can check: a written summary, an explanation. A task folder can then have the arena's rewards score it, a judge model for example.

  • tests/rewards.yaml lists the rewards, written like the workspace's rewards.yaml. Models are named by their models.yaml key.
  • tests/expected.txt, when present, is the expected answer the rewards compare with.
  • tests/test.sh copies the agent's answer to /logs/verifier/answer.txt. Without that file, the answer is the agent's last message.
tests/rewards.yamltests/test.sh 
rewards:
  judge:
    type: lm_as_judge
    config:
      language_model: gpt-4o-mini
      instructions: Score 1 when the summary names the root cause and the fix, else 0.

#!/bin/bash
mkdir -p /logs/verifier
cp /app/summary.md /logs/verifier/answer.txt 2>/dev/null
echo '{"answer_collected": 1}' > /logs/verifier/reward.json

Each reward is one named score, merged into rewards. The first is also reward, unless one of them is named reward, and it replaces any reward the verifier wrote. The dataset's own reward stays harbor_verifier.

A rewards.yaml that is not valid, names an unknown reward type or a model missing from models.yaml stops the run, saying what to fix. One that fails while scoring sets reward to 0 and says why in the trial's error.

A judge costs a model call per trial, on top of the agent's.

items.title: Timeouts and attempts
items.text:
knob where what it limits [environment] build_timeout_sec task.toml building the image [agent] timeout_sec task.toml the agent's work on this task harbor.timeout_sec the dataset the agent's work on every task; overrides task.toml [verifier] timeout_sec task.toml tests/test.sh repeat the dataset's config trials per task (default 1)

How to set them:

  • Agent timeout. Time the solution yourself, then give the agent several times that. Too short and good models fail on the clock; too long and a looping agent spends tokens for nothing. Use harbor.timeout_sec for one budget across tasks, task.toml when tasks differ.
  • Verifier timeout. Be generous. A verifier that times out scores a solved task 0.
  • Build timeout. Raise it for heavy images, or build the image once and use docker_image.
  • Attempts. A failed trial is not retried. repeat: 3 runs each task three times and the cell's score is the mean: the success rate. Agents are not deterministic, so one trial per task says little on a small set.

items.title: Importing existing task sets
items.text:
openarena has no importer. A task set already in Harbor's folder format runs as it is: copy its task folders under tasks/, or point config.path at them, and list them in a harbor_tasks dataset. A set in another format must be converted to this layout first.

Before you run an imported set:

  • Check the agent fits. For terminus-2, the images need tmux, or a package manager and the network to install it.
  • Check the network. A task with network_mode = "no-network" works only with terminus-2.
  • Check the resources. A task that leaves cpus and memory_mb blank gets the whole machine on the local Docker.
  • Run a few first. limit: 3 with one model. Read the trials before you run the whole set.

items.title: Cost and time
items.text:
A Harbor evaluation runs tasks × repeat × models trials. Each trial is an image build or pull, a sandbox start, an agent session of many model calls, and the verifier.

  • Time. On the local Docker, trials run one at a time by default: 50 tasks of 5 minutes each is about 4 hours per model. A cloud provider with a larger batch_size runs them in parallel.
  • Tokens. An agent session makes many model calls, each over a growing history. One task can cost as much as many Q&A rows. The agent's timeout is your cost cap.
