  • What is reported. Tokens and cost are the agent's own count: an agent that reports no cost shows 0. Latency is the agent's seconds per model call, the commands it ran in between included.
  • Plan in steps. One task with one model, then a few tasks, then the set. Finished cells are kept, so a stopped run resumes where it stopped.

See Running evaluations for running and resuming.

items.title: Checklist for a new task
items.text:
1. Copy tasks/hello-world/ to tasks/<name>/ and write the five files.
  2. chmod +x tests/test.sh solution/solve.sh.
  3. Set cpus, memory_mb and the timeouts in task.toml.
  4. Make sure the solution makes the tests give 1, and that doing nothing gives 0.
  5. Add the task to a harbor_tasks dataset, then run openarena check configs (Checking configs).
  6. Run it with one model and read the trial before you scale up.

items.title: Leaderboards
items.text:
A leaderboard turns the scores of finished runs into one ranking. Use one to answer a question like "which model should we use for this job?". It never calls a model. It reads the result.json files that evaluations already wrote, so ranking costs nothing and you can rank the same runs in as many ways as you like.

A leaderboard is a saved entry in configs/leaderboards.yaml. It sets three things:

  • the scope: which datasets and which models are compared;
  • the weights: how much each metric (reward, cost, latency, ...) counts;
  • the limits: hard budgets that leave a model out.
flowchart LR
  runs[".open-arena/*/result.json<br/>newest first"] --> board["board<br/>one cell per model and dataset"]
  board --> scope["scope<br/>datasets, models"]
  scope --> budgets["budgets<br/>drop what breaks a limit"]
  budgets --> norm["normalize<br/>each metric, per dataset"]
  norm --> combine["weighted geometric mean<br/>per dataset, then weighted mean"]
  combine --> out["ranking + Pareto frontier"]

items.title: A first leaderboard
items.text:
leaderboards:
  math-quality:
    title: Math, quality only
    description: Grade-school math. The reward alone decides.
    tags: [math]
    datasets: [gsm8k-20]
    models: []                  # every model scored on gsm8k-20
    shares:
      reward: 100

  math-value:
    title: Math, quality for the money
    description: Reward first, cost second. Nothing above 5 cents a cell.
    tags: [math, value]
    datasets: [gsm8k-20]
    models: [qwen38, gpt-4o-mini, gpt-4o]
    shares:
      reward: 70
      cost: 30
    budgets:
      - {metric: cost, op: lte, value: 0.05}
      - {metric: reward, op: gte, value: 0.5}

openarena check configs
openarena leaderboards list
openarena leaderboards run math-value

The two entries rank the same runs. The first answers "which model is most accurate?". The second answers "which model gives the best accuracy for what it costs, among those we can afford?". Keep one leaderboard per question and don't bend one leaderboard to answer both.

items.title: Fields
items.text:
field type default what it does title text, 1 to 200 characters required the name printed above the ranking description text none printed after the title; say what decision the board supports tags list of tags [] labels for browsing (math, reward-first, weekly); the ranking ignores them datasets list of dataset names [] = every dataset scored the datasets in scope models list of model names [] = every model scored the models in scope shares {metric: number}, each 0 or more {} = the default preset each metric's weight in the score budgets list of {metric, op, value} [] hard limits; a model that breaks one is left out group_shares {group: number}, each 0 or more {} a weight per group of datasets dataset_shares {dataset: number}, each 0 or more {} a weight per dataset; 0 takes it out

Any other key is refused by openarena check.

items.title: title, description, tags
items.text: These fields are for people. leaderboards list shows title and description, and leaderboards run prints them above the table. Write the description as the question the board answers ("cheapest model that still gets math right"). Six months from now, it tells a reader why the weights are what they are. Tags follow the rules shared by every registry: lower case, letters, digits and :+./-, at most 40 characters each.

items.title: datasets: what is compared
items.text:
Set it to the dataset names you used in your evaluations (the keys of datasets.yaml).

  • Empty means every dataset that has at least one scored cell in the state folder. This is convenient while you explore. It is risky once you have run unrelated evaluations, because a model is ranked only when it has a score on every dataset in scope (see Missing runs).
  • A list fixes the scope. A name with no score in any run is silently dropped. If every name you list is unknown, nothing is ranked.

When to list datasets

List them as soon as the board supports a real decision. An empty scope changes meaning every time someone runs a new evaluation. A listed scope keeps the same meaning.

openarena check warns when a listed name is not in datasets.yaml. This is only a warning: runs outlive the entries that made them, so a board can still rank scores from a dataset you have since removed.

items.title: models: who is compared
items.text:
Set it to model names, which are the keys of models.yaml. For an A2A sweep, use the agent names. These are the names the runs recorded, not the provider ids.

  • Empty means every model with a scored cell.
  • A list keeps only those models. A name that never scored is ignored and does not appear in the output at all.

Narrowing models changes more than the rows you see. Scores are relative: each metric is rescaled against the models in scope (see How the score is computed). Adding or removing a model can change the scores of all the others, and sometimes their order. Pick the models that are real candidates for the decision.

items.title: shares: what matters, and how much
items.text:
A share is a metric's weight. Only the proportions count: {reward: 70, cost: 30}, {reward: 7, cost: 3} and {reward: 0.7, cost: 0.3} give the same ranking. The run prints the shares as percents of their total.

you write what happens nothing, or {} the default preset: reward gets weight 9 and every other metric the scope records gets 1. eol_days gets 0 {reward: 100} quality only. Cost and latency don't count {reward: 70, cost: 30} a trade-off; see the arithmetic a share of 0 the metric doesn't count, the same as leaving it out a negative share, or every share at 0 refused by openarena check and by leaderboards run

A metric can carry weight only if every cell in scope records it. A share on any other metric is dropped without an error. This covers a typo (costs), a judge metric that only some datasets have, and eol_days under --no-eol. If every share you wrote is dropped, the board falls back to the default preset.

Read the Shares: line

leaderboards run prints the shares it actually used, for example Shares: reward 70%, cost 30%. If it differs from what you wrote, a metric was dropped. Check its name in the run's meta.metrics (Reading results), and check that every dataset in scope records it.

With the default preset, the reward leads and the other measurements mostly break near-ties. With reward, cost, input_tokens and output_tokens, for instance, the reward gets 9/12 = 75%, and each of the other three gets 1/12, about 8%. The more measurements a run records, the less the reward weighs by default. Write shares explicitly for any board you rely on.

items.title: budgets: hard limits
items.text:
A budget is a pass/fail rule on one metric:

leaderboards:
  under-a-cent:
    title: Under a cent a cell
    budgets:
      - {metric: cost, op: lte, value: 0.01}       # at most
      - {metric: avg_latency, op: lte, value: 5}   # at most, in the unit the run records
      - {metric: reward, op: gte, value: 0.7}      # at least
key values metric a metric name as the run records it op lte: at most value; gte: at least value value a number, in the metric's own unit (USD for cost)

How budgets apply:

  • A budget is checked on each dataset separately, against that cell's value. It is not checked against an average. If a model breaks it on any dataset in scope, the model is out of the ranking, and the run prints it as Over budget <model>: cost at most 0.01.
  • Budgets are applied before normalizing. A model that is far too expensive can't stretch the cost scale and flatten the differences between the models you can afford.
  • A budget can use any metric the cell records, even one with no share.
  • If a cell doesn't record the budget's metric, the budget can't be broken there. A misspelled metric therefore never excludes anyone.

Budget or share?

Use a budget for a requirement you won't trade: "no more than 1 cent a request", "at least 70% correct". Use a share for a preference you will trade: "cheaper is better, but not at any price". A budget answers yes or no. A share moves the score.

A cell's cost covers the whole dataset

cost is what the cell spent: the model under test over all the dataset's rows, not one request. A budget of 0.05 on cost means 5 cents for the dataset. Divide by the number of rows (the dataset's limit) to think per request. If two datasets in scope have very different sizes, one cost limit means different things on each. Rank them on separate boards.

items.title: group_shares and dataset_shares: weighing datasets
items.text:
By default every dataset in scope counts the same, and a model's score is the plain mean of its per-dataset scores. A share left out is 1.

Your own datasets, the ones openarena evaluations run scores, belong to no group. Each one weighs its group_shares entry times its dataset_shares entry, both keyed by the dataset's name:

weight(d) = group_shares[d] × dataset_shares[d]

Imported benchmarks name their suites, and those suites are groups. A group weighs its share whatever the number of datasets in it, split among its datasets in proportion to their dataset_shares:

weight(d) = group_shares[group(d)] × dataset_shares[d] / sum of dataset_shares in group(d)
Weighing your own datasetsWeighing imported suites

Use dataset_shares, keyed by dataset name:

leaderboards:
  support-mix:
    title: Support, weighted by traffic
    datasets: [faq-answers, refund-requests, escalations]
    dataset_shares:
      faq-answers: 6       # 60% of the traffic
      refund-requests: 3
      escalations: 1
    shares: {reward: 80, cost: 20}

group_shares keyed by the same names gives the same weights, since each dataset is weighed by the product of the two. Write one of them, not both, so a reader sees each weight once.

Use group_shares, keyed by suite, to say how much each suite counts, and dataset_shares to weigh the datasets inside one suite against each other. A suite with ten datasets then weighs no more than a suite with two, unless its share says so.

A dataset weighed 0 (through either field) is out of the score and out of the requirement. Models need no score on it to be ranked. Use this to keep a diagnostic dataset in the board's definition while it is not ready yet.

Weigh datasets when they don't matter equally for the decision: traffic share, business risk, or one task being the main job and another a sanity check. Don't weigh them to correct for difficulty. Normalization already puts every dataset on the same 0.05 to 1 scale.

items.title: Metrics you can name
items.text:
shares and budgets use the metric names the runs recorded. A run lists them in meta.metrics of its result.json (Reading results).

metric where it comes from better scale reward the dataset's reward, the mean over its rows the reward's direction (Rewards) linear cost USD the model under test spent on the cell, from litellm's prices, when listed under metrics: lower, unless its direction says otherwise log input_tokens, output_tokens tokens the cell used, when listed under metrics: lower, unless its direction says otherwise log latency when listed under metrics:; use the name in meta.metrics (for example avg_latency) lower, unless its direction says otherwise log an extra metric's alias metrics: on the dataset or the evaluation (Datasets) its direction log, or linear (see below) eol_days days left before the model's announced end of life, looked up when the board is built higher linear

You never write a direction in a leaderboard: each metric's direction comes from the run that recorded it. A metric listed under metrics: without a direction: gets one automatically: min for a cost, tokens or latency measurement (cost, input_tokens, total_tokens, avg_latency, ...), max for anything else. So a cost ranks the cheapest model best with nothing to write.

To read a metric the other way, write direction: where you list it, on the dataset or the evaluation (Running evaluations): an explicit direction: always wins. Then run the evaluation again: the leaderboard reads the direction stored in result.json, which is written from the config at the end of each run.

Linear or log. reward and eol_days are normalized linearly: 0.9 against 0.8 counts as much as 0.6 against 0.5. Every other metric is normalized on a log scale, as long as all its values on that dataset are above zero. On a log scale, 10 times cheaper counts the same wherever it happens: $0.001 against $0.01 weighs as much as $0.10 against $1. This suits cost, tokens and latency, which vary across orders of magnitude. If a value is 0 or negative, for example a local model with a cost of exactly 0, that dataset's column falls back to a linear scale. The free model then gets the top score, and every paid model is placed by its absolute cost.

items.title: eol_days: time to end of life
items.text:
eol_days measures how long you can keep using a model. It is a fact about the model, not about a run, so every cell of a model gets the same value. leaderboards run looks it up each time it builds the board. The lookup uses the model id (model: in models.yaml) recorded in the config.yaml of the newest run that scored the model. It tries these sources:

  1. the provider's own deprecation date, from litellm's model table;
  2. for openai/, azure/ and azure_ai/ ids, Azure's OpenAI retirement schedule. It is fetched online and cached for a day. When the fetch fails, a copy shipped with the package is used;
  3. for openrouter/ ids, OpenRouter's expiration date, when it comes before the vendor's date. OpenRouter ids are also looked up under the vendor's own id.
situation eol_days no date known (open-weight models, most current models) 1825 (five years) a date more than five years out 1825 a date ahead the days until it a date already past negative: the model may already refuse calls

The five-year cap means "no announced end" is treated as "far away", not as "unknown". eol_days is on the board by default but has no weight unless you give it a share. Pass --no-eol to skip the online lookups, for example offline or in CI. A share or budget on eol_days then has no effect.

items.title: Where the scores come from
items.text:
leaderboards run reads every <state-dir>/*/result.json, newest file first. For each pair of model and dataset, it keeps one cell, taken whole from the newest run that scored it. That cell's reward and every metric it recorded come from the same run, and nothing from an older run is mixed in.

What follows from that:

  • Running again replaces. Rerun an evaluation, or run a new one with the same model and dataset names, and the board uses the new cell.
  • A failed cell does not replace. A cell with no reward is not a score. If the newest run failed on a pair, the board keeps the older successful cell for it. Look at the runs field of --json to see which run each cell came from.
  • Names, not ids, identify a model. Cells are matched by the model's registry name. If you point an existing name at a new model: id, cells for the datasets you haven't rerun still hold the old model's scores under that name. See Refreshing.
  • Every run in the state folder counts. Smoke tests, limit: 5 experiments and half-finished sweeps all feed the board, unless a newer cell replaced them.

items.title: How the score is computed
items.text:
flowchart TB
  A[datasets in scope<br/>weight 0 removed] --> B[models in scope]
  B --> C[metrics with a share<br/>that every cell records]
  C --> D{per dataset}
  D --> E[models with a cell here]
  E --> F[budgets: drop breakers]
  F --> G[normalize each metric<br/>to 0.05 to 1 among the rest]
  G --> H[dataset score =<br/>product of normalized^share]
  H --> I[model score =<br/>weighted mean over datasets]
  I --> J[rank: score, then name]
  1. Scope. The datasets in scope, minus those weighed 0. The models in scope.
  2. Weights. Keep the shares of metrics that every cell in scope records, or use the default preset if none are left. Divide each by their sum, so the weights add up to 1.
  3. Per dataset, among the models that have a cell there:
    1. drop the models that break a budget on this dataset;
    2. rescale each weighted metric to [0.05, 1], with 1 for the best value and 0.05 for the worst. When every model has the same value, all get 1;
    3. the dataset score is the weighted geometric mean of the rescaled values: the product of normalized ^ weight.
  4. Overall. The model's score is the mean of its dataset scores, weighted by the dataset weights. It ranges from 0.05 to 1.
  5. Rank. Only models with a score on every dataset in scope and no broken budget are ranked. They are sorted by score, high to low.

items.title: Why a geometric mean
items.text: In a geometric mean, a weak metric pulls the score down: one value at the floor costs a lot, and other metrics can't fully make up for it. A model that is free but always wrong does not win a 50/50 reward/cost board. The floor of 0.05 instead of 0 means that being worst on one metric hurts without zeroing the score.

items.title: How much a share buys
items.text:
Here are three models on one dataset:

model reward cost (USD) reward, normalized cost, normalized cheap 0.5 0.01 0.24 1.0 good 0.9 1.00 1.0 0.174 bad 0.4 2.00 0.05 0.05 shares cheap good bad winner {reward: 50, cost: 50} 0.490 0.418 0.050 cheap default (here reward 90%, cost 10%) 0.277 0.840 0.050 good {reward: 100} 0.24 1.0 0.05 good

At 50/50, being 100 times cheaper outweighs 0.4 of reward. At 90/10, it does not. Before you commit to a set of shares, compute a few of these by hand, or compare the contributions in --json output. Make sure the board picks the model you would pick yourself in the clear cases.

items.title: The Pareto frontier
items.text: The frontier column marks with ★ each ranked model that no other ranked model dominates. A model is dominated when another one is at least as good on every weighted metric and better on at least one. The comparison uses each metric's raw mean over the datasets, and doesn't depend on the shares. The frontier shows the models worth considering under some weighting. With {reward: 100}, only the models with the best reward are on it.

items.title: Edge cases
items.text:
case what happens two models with the same score both are ranked, in alphabetical order, with different rank numbers one model in scope each metric normalizes to 1, so its score is 1 every model has the same value on a metric that metric gives 1 to every model and doesn't change the order a model has no cell on a dataset in scope Not ranked <model>: not scored on <dataset>. It still counts when other models are normalized on the datasets it does have a model breaks a budget on one dataset Over budget <model>: .... It is left out of normalization on that dataset only, and still counts on the others no finished runs in the state folder the command stops with no finished runs under <dir>

Unranked models still shape the scale

A model that misses a dataset, or breaks a budget on one dataset, still counts when the other datasets are normalized. A very cheap model with a gap can still push everyone else's cost scores down. To remove it from the comparison entirely, leave it out of models.

items.title: Running it
items.text:
openarena leaderboards list
openarena leaderboards run math-value
openarena leaderboards run math-value --no-eol --json ranking.json
openarena leaderboards run overall --configs my-arena/configs --state-dir my-arena/.open-arena
option default --configs DIR configs the folder holding leaderboards.yaml --state-dir DIR .open-arena where the runs are, one folder per evaluation --no-eol off skip the end-of-life lookup, which goes online --json FILE none also write the ranking as JSON

leaderboards run validates the saved entry as openarena check does before it ranks anything. An entry that does not validate (a negative share, a budget op that does not exist) is refused, and the command exits 1:

Error: the leaderboard 'math-value' does not validate:
  leaderboards.math-value.budgets[0].op: Input should be 'lte' or 'gte'
    fix: set `op:` to one of 'lte' or 'gte'
see each problem with its line: `openarena check configs/leaderboards.yaml`

Run openarena check configs after editing (Checking configs) to see each problem with its line.

The output, in outline:

Math, quality for the money — Reward first, cost second. Nothing above 5 cents a cell.
Datasets: gsm8k-20
Shares: reward 70%, cost 30%
 #  model        score   reward ↑  cost ↓  frontier
 1  gpt-4o-mini  ...
Not ranked qwen38: not scored on gsm8k-20
Over budget gpt-4o: cost at most 0.05

The Datasets: and Shares: lines show what the board actually used, after the scope and the shares were resolved. Read them first. Each metric column shows the model's raw mean over the datasets, with ↑ when higher is better and ↓ when lower is better.

The --json file 
{
  "leaderboard": {"name": "math-value", "title": "...", "shares": {"reward": 70, "cost": 30}},
  "datasets": ["gsm8k-20"],
  "models": ["qwen38", "gpt-4o-mini", "gpt-4o"],
  "shares": {"reward": 70.0, "cost": 30.0},
  "axes": [{"name": "reward", "direction": "max"}, {"name": "cost", "direction": "min"}],
  "rows": [
    {
      "rank": 1, "model": "gpt-4o-mini", "score": 0.81,
      "values": {"reward": 0.85, "cost": 0.004},
      "contributions": [
        {"metric": "reward", "value": 0.85, "normalized": 1.0, "weight": 0.7, "factor": 1.0}
      ],
      "per_dataset": {"gsm8k-20": 0.81},
      "dataset_contributions": {"gsm8k-20": 0.81},
      "on_frontier": true,
      "runs": ["math-compare"]
    }
  ],
  "skipped": ["qwen38"],
  "gaps": {"qwen38": [{"dataset": "gsm8k-20", "missing": null}]},
  "excluded": [{"model": "gpt-4o", "failed": [{"metric": "cost", "op": "lte", "value": 0.05}]}]
}
key leaderboard the saved entry, with its name datasets, models the scope used: datasets after weight 0 is removed, every model in scope shares, axes the weights used, in percent, and each weighted metric's direction rows[].values raw mean per metric over the datasets rows[].contributions per metric: mean normalized value, weight, and factor (normalized ^ weight) rows[].per_dataset, dataset_contributions each dataset's score, and its part of the total (they add up to score) rows[].runs the run folder each cell came from skipped, gaps the models left unranked, and per dataset why (missing: null = never scored there) excluded the models over budget, and the budgets they broke

The numbers above are placeholders that show the shape.

items.title: Designing a leaderboard for a decision
items.text:
Start from the decision, not from the data. Write down the question, who acts on the answer, and what they won't trade away. Then set the fields.

Quality onlyQuality for the moneyShortlist under limitsA model to keep for years

Use this for research comparisons, or when cost doesn't matter at your volume.

leaderboards:
  reasoning-quality:
    title: Reasoning, quality only
    description: Which model is most accurate on our reasoning sets?
    datasets: [gsm8k-20, logic-puzzles]
    shares: {reward: 100}

Cost and latency play no part. The frontier holds only the models with the best reward.

Use this to pick a production model when spending matters but isn't a hard limit.

leaderboards:
  reasoning-value:
    title: Reasoning, quality for the money
    description: Best accuracy per dollar among the candidates.
    datasets: [gsm8k-20, logic-puzzles]
    models: [qwen38, gpt-4o-mini, gpt-4o]
    shares: {reward: 70, cost: 30}

Start around 70/30 and work out by hand which trade you are making (see How much a share buys). Look at the ★ models: they are the only ones worth arguing over.

Use this when a team has a hard cost ceiling or a quality floor, and wants the best model inside it.

leaderboards:
  reasoning-shortlist:
    title: Reasoning, within budget
    description: Under 2 cents per 20-row dataset, at least 70% correct.
    datasets: [gsm8k-20]
    shares: {reward: 80, avg_latency: 20}
    budgets:
      - {metric: cost, op: lte, value: 0.02}
      - {metric: reward, op: gte, value: 0.7}

The budgets express the requirements. The shares rank the models that pass. The models over budget are listed, so you can see what each limit costs you. Check the latency metric's exact name in meta.metrics.

Use this when switching models later is expensive: tuned prompts, certification, contracts.

leaderboards:
  reasoning-long-lived:
    title: Reasoning, built to last
    description: Accuracy first, but penalize models close to retirement.
    datasets: [gsm8k-20]
    shares: {reward: 70, cost: 15, eol_days: 15}

With eol_days in the shares, a model retiring next quarter loses ground. Don't run this board with --no-eol, or the eol_days share is silently dropped.

items.title: Don't mix incomparable datasets
items.text:
Each dataset is normalized on its own, so each one gives a spread from 0.05 to 1, however large or small the real differences are. On a dataset where every model scores between 0.95 and 0.96, the 0.01 gap still becomes the full 0.05 to 1 spread. On that board, that dataset counts as much as one where scores range from 0.2 to 0.9.

  • Put datasets on one board only if they measure the same capability for the same decision. Use separate boards for "math" and "customer support".
  • Leave out datasets that every candidate saturates. They add noise, not signal.
  • Use the same limit and reward for a dataset across all the runs you rank. A cell scored on 5 rows and one scored on 200 rows look the same on the board.
  • Use dataset_shares (or group_shares for imported suites) to say which datasets matter more. Don't use it to fix a dataset you shouldn't have included.

items.title: Missing runs
items.text:
The board ranks only complete rows: a model needs a score on every dataset in scope. When a model shows up as Not ranked, you can:

choice when run the missing cells (openarena evaluations run with that model and dataset) the model is a real candidate take it out of models it isn't a candidate. This also stops it from shaping the scale narrow datasets the dataset isn't central to this decision weigh the dataset 0 you want to keep it in the definition but not require it yet

If a metric is missing from some cells, for example a judge metric added to one evaluation only, that metric loses its share for the whole board. Add it to every evaluation that feeds the board, and rerun them with --no-cache, or drop it from shares.

items.title: Refreshing a leaderboard
items.text:
A leaderboard is recomputed from the state folder on every run. It is always as current as your runs. Keeping it honest means keeping the runs current:

  • A new model. Add it to models.yaml and to the evaluations that feed the board, and run them. Finished cells are kept, so only the new model's cells run. Add the model to the board's models if you listed them. Expect the other models' scores to move, since the scale now includes the new model.
  • A model changed behind its name. If you point a name at a new model: id, or change its params, rerun every dataset on the board for it with --no-cache. Otherwise the board mixes old and new cells under one name. To compare the old and new versions side by side, give the new one a new name instead.
  • A changed dataset or reward. Rerun with --no-cache for every model. Old cells from the previous version aren't comparable with new ones.
  • End of life. eol_days is shown, in the table and in --json, only when it has a share. Give it a small share on a board you depend on and run the board from time to time without --no-eol. A negative value means the date has passed: retire the model from models and pick its replacement from the board. With a share, the ranking reflects upcoming retirements before they happen.
  • Old runs. Cells from runs you no longer trust (smoke tests, a broken config) stay on the board until a newer cell replaces them. Delete or move their folder out of the state folder.

Keep decision boards stable

For a board that drives a real choice, list datasets and models, write shares explicitly, and keep a --json export of each ranking you act on. The export records the runs behind every cell, so you can explain the decision later.

items.title: MCP tools
items.text:
configs/mcp_servers.yaml holds connections to MCP tool servers: programs that expose tools (fetch a page, query a database, run code) over a standard protocol. A dataset with an agent: block hands those tools to the model under test. On each row the model may call them, read the results, call again, and then answers. The answer is scored by the dataset's reward as usual.

Use this to measure how well models use tools: whether they pick the right one, pass sensible arguments, stop in time, and turn what they read into the right answer. Every model runs the same loop over the same tools, so the comparison is about the model.

flowchart LR
  row[row: input_template] --> step
  subgraph agent["agent loop, up to max_iterations turns"]
    step[model picks tool calls] -->|calls| tools[(MCP servers)]
    tools -->|results| step
  end
  step -->|no more calls, or turns used up| final[model writes the answer]
  final --> reward[dataset reward]

items.title: MCP tools, A2A agents, environments or tools:
items.text:
Four ways to evaluate something that acts. Pick by what you are testing.

you want to test use what runs the axis is models choosing and using live tools, in a loop the arena runs agent: + MCP servers (this page) the arena's tool loop, the real servers models which function a model would call, with which arguments, without running anything tools: one call, nothing executed, tool_calls_accuracy models an agent you built and deploy yourself, as a black box A2A agents your service, its own loop and tools agents a model working in a sandbox: a terminal, files, packages Environments, Harbor tasks a Harbor agent in a container (MCP servers optional) models
  • agent: versus tools:. tools: grades the decision only: the gold calls are in the dataset, so it is cheap, deterministic and needs no server. agent: grades the outcome: the tools really run and the final answer is scored. Use tools: to test function calling itself; use agent: when the answer depends on what the tools return.
  • agent: versus A2A. With agent: the arena owns the loop and the prompt, and only the model changes. With A2A the agent is yours, its prompt, its tools and its model included; the arena only sends a message and scores the reply. Use A2A to compare versions of an agent, not models.
  • agent: versus environments. An agent: row is a few tool calls over a protocol. An environment gives an agent a whole machine, which is slower and heavier. Use an environment when the work is done in a shell or on files; an environment can also take MCP servers (below).

items.title: The server entry
items.text:
One entry per server. Its key is the name datasets and environments refer to, and it also prefixes the server's tool names (see what the model sees).

stdio: a local processstreamable_http: a running serversse: an older serverwebsocket 
mcp_servers:
  fetch:
    transport: stdio                   # the default; spawn a process
    command: uvx                       # required: the executable
    args: [mcp-server-fetch]           # its arguments, one per item
    env:                               # variables the process gets
      USER_AGENT: openarena-eval
    # cwd: /abs/path/to/server         # its working directory
    description: Fetches a URL and returns it as markdown.
    tags: [web, local]

mcp_servers:
  docs:
    transport: streamable_http
    url: http://localhost:8080/mcp     # required: the endpoint
    headers:                           # sent on every request
      Authorization: Bearer ${DOCS_TOKEN}   # read from the environment or .env
    description: Search over the product documentation.
    tags: [search]

mcp_servers:
  legacy-search:
    transport: sse
    url: http://localhost:8000/sse
    headers:
      X-Api-Key: ${SEARCH_API_KEY}

mcp_servers:
  calc:
    transport: websocket
    url: ws://localhost:8765            # ws:// or wss://
field transport transport all stdio (default), streamable_http, sse or websocket command stdio required. The executable to spawn: uvx, npx, python, a path args stdio its arguments, a list; blank items are dropped env stdio environment variables for the process; keys without spaces cwd stdio the process's working directory url streamable_http, sse, websocket required. Starts with http://, https://, ws:// or wss:// headers streamable_http, sse HTTP headers on every request, typically Authorization; keys without spaces description, tags all for listings (openarena mcp-servers list) only

A field another transport reads is an error, not ignored: a url on a stdio server, or headers on a websocket one. Any other field (timeout, tools, ...) is an error too.

items.title: Which transport
items.text:
transport when stdio The server is a package or a script you can launch: most published MCP servers. Nothing to keep running; the run starts it. streamable_http The server runs on its own, locally or remotely, at a URL. The protocol's current HTTP transport: prefer it for any HTTP server that supports it. sse An HTTP server that only speaks the older Server-Sent Events transport. Its URL usually ends in /sse. websocket A server that serves MCP over websockets. No headers, so it cannot carry a key that way. Not usable in a Harbor sandbox.

The server's own docs say which transport it serves and at which path. A wrong transport or path shows when the run connects, not in openarena check.

items.title: stdio: how the process is started
items.text:
A stdio server does not see your .env

The run reads the workspace's .env, but a stdio server does not inherit the run's environment. It gets a short safe list (HOME, LOGNAME, PATH, SHELL, TERM, USER on Linux and macOS) plus what env: sets. A server that needs GITHUB_TOKEN or BRAVE_API_KEY fails unless env: passes it: env: {GITHUB_TOKEN: "${GITHUB_TOKEN}"} hands it the value from your shell or .env (Secrets).

  • One process per tool call. The tool list is read once, when the run prepares a model's program. After that, every tool call opens a fresh connection: for stdio, a new process that serves that one call and exits. Keep start-up cheap (uvx and npx cache their package after the first download), and do not count on anything the server keeps in memory between two calls.
  • Relative paths in command, args and cwd are read from the folder you run openarena in, not from configs/. Use absolute paths, or set cwd:, for a script of your own.
  • PATH is the run's, so uvx, npx or python are found as in your shell.

items.title: Remote servers: url and headers
items.text: The server must be up before the run starts, and reachable from the machine that runs openarena. The run reads every server's tool list while it prepares, before any cell runs. A server that is down, a command that is not found, or servers that list no tools fail the cells of every model on that dataset, with could not load the MCP tools of [...] and the cause, and the run goes on with the other datasets; openarena evaluations run then exits 1. Start the server and run the evaluation again: a plain resume runs the failed cells. A server that goes down mid-run fails the tool call, which the model sees as an error (below).

items.title: Secrets
items.text:
Write a key as ${NAME}, never as its value. When a run reads its config, after it has loaded the workspace's .env, every ${NAME} in a string is replaced by the environment variable NAME:

mcp_servers:
  github:
    command: npx
    args: ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-github"]
    env:
      GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN: ${GITHUB_TOKEN}   # passes the value on to the process
  docs:
    transport: streamable_http
    url: http://localhost:8080/mcp
    headers:
      Authorization: Bearer ${DOCS_TOKEN}

# .env, beside configs/
GITHUB_TOKEN=ghp_...
DOCS_TOKEN=...
  • The file holds no secret. mcp_servers.yaml and the run's copy, .open-arena/<evaluation>/config.yaml, keep ${GITHUB_TOKEN}, not its value, so either can be committed or shared.
  • This is how a stdio server gets a key. It inherits only the safe list above plus its env:, so a variable in .env reaches it only when env: names it: env: {API_KEY: "${API_KEY}"}.
  • An unset variable stops the run before it starts, naming the variable and where it is used. openarena check warns about a ${NAME} set neither in your shell nor in the workspace's .env.
  • $${NAME} writes a literal ${NAME}, for a value that must keep the characters.
  • An HTTP server's token can only go in headers:. Use a key scoped to the evaluation, read-only where the server allows it.

items.title: What there is no field for
items.text:
• No tool filter. The model gets every tool each listed server exposes. To hide tools, run the server in a mode that exposes fewer (many take flags for that, given in args), or put a small server of your own in front.
  • No timeout. There is no per-call or per-row timeout to set; HTTP transports use the client's built-in defaults. A tool that hangs holds its row, so keep your servers' own timeouts sensible.

items.title: The agent: block
items.text:
A dataset with an agent: block is answered by the tool loop. The evaluation's language_models are ordinary models from models.yaml; each must support tool calling, which check cannot know.

datasets:
  web-questions:
    type: local
    config:
      path: questions.jsonl            # {"question": "...", "answer": "..."}
      input_template: '{"question": {{ question | tojson }}}'
      output_template: '{"answer": {{ answer | tojson }}}'
      input_schema: {type: object, properties: {question: {type: string, description: The question to answer}}, required: [question]}
      output_schema: {type: object, properties: {answer: {type: string, description: The answer only}}, required: [answer]}
    agent:
      mcp_servers: [fetch]             # mcp_servers.yaml keys, at least one
      max_iterations: 8                # tool-calling turns per row (default 5)
      instructions: >-
        Answer the question. Fetch the pages you need first; do not answer
        from memory.
    reward: judge
field default mcp_servers required. A list of mcp_servers.yaml keys, at least one. Their tools are merged into one list max_iterations 5 tool-calling turns per row (below) instructions a generic "helpful agent" line the instructions for every turn; say when to use the tools final_instructions instructions instructions for the last call, the one that writes the answer use_chain_of_thought false have the model reason before each tool decision; for non-reasoning models return_inputs_with_trajectory true keep the tool trajectory (messages) beside the answer (scoring) return_inputs false also put the row's input fields in the prediction type function_calling the only loop there is

language_model and tools are set by the run and refused here. Every other key goes to the agent as a setting, so a misspelled one (max_iteration:) passes check and stops the run when the program is built.

Other agent settings

The block also forwards temperature, max_tokens, top_p, top_k, reasoning_effort, examples, use_inputs_schema, use_outputs_schema and prompt_template to the agent. Set here, they apply to every model of the evaluation alike. A model's own sampling params belong in models.yaml (Models); set a param in one place, not both. Leave autonomous at its default: the run needs the agent to execute the tools itself.

items.title: How a row runs
items.text:
sequenceDiagram
  participant R as row
  participant M as model under test
  participant S as MCP servers
  R->>M: the rendered input, the instructions, every tool
  loop at most max_iterations turns
    M->>S: one or more tool calls (run concurrently)
    S-->>M: results, or "error: ..."
  end
  Note over M: stops early when a turn has no tool call
  M->>R: final call: the answer, in the output_schema
  1. Each turn, the model sees the conversation so far and the full tool list, and either calls tools or does not. Several calls in one turn run at once.
  2. A turn without a tool call ends the loop. So does the last allowed turn.
  3. A last call writes the answer from the whole trajectory, shaped by the dataset's output_schema (an answer field above). It is made even when the turns ran out: a model cut off mid-search still answers, usually badly, and is scored for it.
  4. A tool that fails (bad arguments, a server error) does not fail the row. Its result becomes error: <message> in the conversation, and the model may retry or work around it. That is part of what is measured.

items.title: max_iterations
items.text:
Each turn is a model call, plus the final answer call: a row costs up to max_iterations + 1 calls of the model under test, and each call re-sends the whole conversation, tool results included. Tokens grow with every turn.

setting when 1 to 3 one lookup is enough (a single fetch, a calculator); cuts cost and keeps models from wandering 5 (default) a few dependent lookups 8 to 15 multi-hop tasks: search, open, follow a link, compare

Too low, and good models are cut off before they finish: every model scores alike and the evaluation measures the limit. Too high costs money on models that loop. Run a few rows (limit: 5 on the dataset), read the trajectories, and set it a little above what a good model needs.

items.title: What the model sees
items.text: Each tool is named <server key>_<tool name>: the fetch tool of the fetch server is fetch_fetch, and two servers can both expose search without a clash. Its description and parameters are the server's own. Name server keys plainly, since every model reads them.

items.title: What gets recorded and scored
items.text:
A row's prediction is the answer, with the trajectory beside it:

{
  "messages": [
    {"role": "assistant", "tool_calls": [{"id": "c1", "type": "function",
      "function": {"name": "fetch_fetch", "arguments": {"url": "https://example.com"}}}]},
    {"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": "c1", "content": "# Example Domain ..."}
  ],
  "answer": "Example Domain"
}
the dataset has the prediction is an output_schema (the usual case) its fields, plus messages an output_schema, and return_inputs_with_trajectory: false its fields only no output_schema messages only: the trajectory is the answer return_inputs: true the row's input fields as well; an input field named like an answer field, or messages, stops the run before it starts

How each kind of reward reads it:

reward reads use it for exact_match, answer_accuracy, ... the answer fields only: a deterministic reward is limited to the fields the output_template renders, so messages never counts a short, checkable answer lm_as_judge, rubrics_as_judge, ... the whole prediction, trajectory included free-text answers; asking whether the answer is backed by what the tools returned tool_correctness, tool_use, argument_correctness, step_efficiency, agent_loop_detection, task_completion the whole prediction how the model worked, not only the result; good as extra metrics: beside the main reward tool_calls_accuracy a top-level tool_calls not this page: it scores tools: datasets and reads nothing from an agent's messages

Score the answer, watch the process

Make the main reward about the answer, and add one or two tool-use judges under metrics:. A model that gets the right answer in two calls and one that needs eight then show the same reward and a different step_efficiency.

Cost, tokens and latency, when you list them under metrics: (Running evaluations), cover every turn of the loop. Judges are counted apart (reward_cost). Per-row trajectories are not written to result.json, and openarena evaluations run does not trace into MLflow; to keep them, run the sweep from Python with on_sample (Reading results) or from the arena app.

items.title: Fair comparisons
items.text:
The tools are part of the test. Keep them the same for every model, and as few as the task needs.

  • Give only the tools the task needs. Every tool is in every prompt. Extra tools cost tokens on each turn and give weaker models more ways to go wrong. That may be what you want to measure, or may be noise.
  • One evaluation, one tool set. Every model of an evaluation gets the same servers, the same max_iterations and the same instructions. To compare tool sets, write two datasets over the same rows with different agent: blocks, and put both in the evaluation.
  • Pin the server. uvx mcp-server-fetch runs the latest release; a new version can change tool names, descriptions or output between two runs. Pin it (args: [mcp-server-fetch==<version>], npx -y <package>@<version>) for results you will compare later.
  • Live data moves. A web or search tool returns something different next week. Models in one run see nearly the same web; runs a month apart do not. For a benchmark meant to last, point the tools at a fixed copy of the data.

items.title: Servers that keep state
items.text:
Some tools change something: write a file, insert a row, open a ticket. Then what one row did can change what the next row sees.

  • Rows of a batch run at the same time (batch_size), so their tool calls interleave on a shared server.
  • Models run one after the other against the same server: the second model sees what the first left behind.
  • A stdio server is a fresh process per tool call, so in-memory state does not survive from one call to the next, even within a row. State on disk, in a database or in a remote service does.
  • Resuming reruns only the cells that did not finish, against the server as it is now.

To keep results comparable:

approach how read-only tools the safest: expose only tools that read isolate per row have the tools key their state on something the row provides, such as an id in the input reset between runs restore the database or files before each run, and run with --no-cache so every cell starts from the same state one row at a time batch_size: 1 in the dataset's config:, and no batch_size on the evaluation (it would override it)

When each row needs its own clean machine, an environment is the better fit: every Harbor trial gets a fresh sandbox.

items.title: Tools in a Harbor sandbox
items.text:
An environment can hand servers to its agent with mcp_servers: [...]. They are written into the Harbor task, and Harbor carries less than a dataset's agent does:

  • stdio, sse and streamable_http only; websocket is refused.
  • No headers, and no stdio env or cwd: Harbor would drop them, so a server that sets them is refused. Put a stdio server's variables in the environment's env: instead.
  • A stdio command runs inside the sandbox, so the image must have it (uvx needs uv installed in the Dockerfile).
  • An HTTP server must be reachable from the sandbox, not on localhost.

items.title: Common mistakes
items.text:
openarena check configs catches the shape of an entry and every reference by name (Checking configs):

mistake what check reports a stdio server without command a stdio server needs a `command` to spawn url: localhost:8080/mcp `url` must start with http://, https://, ws:// or wss:// command on an HTTP server, headers on a websocket one a <transport> server does not take [...]; it reads [...], and which transport reads it transport: http Input should be 'stdio', 'streamable_http', 'sse' or 'websocket' timeout: or another unknown field on a server not a field of a `mcp_servers` entry, with the fields it reads mcp_servers: [] or mcp_servers: fetch in agent: it cannot be empty; write it as a list agent.mcp_servers naming a server not in mcp_servers.yaml an unknown reference tools: or language_model: inside agent: `agent:` keys [...] are set by the run agent: and tools: on one dataset `agent`, `tools` are mutually exclusive

What check cannot see shows up when the run reaches it (Reading results):

symptom likely cause the dataset's cells fail: no MCP tools loaded from servers [...] the server started but lists no tools the dataset's cells fail: could not load the MCP tools of [...], connection refused the HTTP server is not running, or its URL or transport is wrong the dataset's cells fail: could not load the MCP tools of [...]: FileNotFoundError: ... No such file or directory command is not on PATH, or a relative path read from the wrong folder the run stops while preparing: an unexpected keyword a misspelled agent: setting the run refuses to start: not set in the environment: NAME (at ...) a ${NAME} whose variable is neither exported nor in .env tool results read error: ... about a missing key a stdio server's variable is in .env but env: does not pass it (env: {KEY: "${KEY}"}) every model scores about the same, and low max_iterations too low, or models without tool calling

items.title: Commands
items.text:
openarena mcp-servers list --configs configs   # every server: transport, command, url
openarena check configs                        # shapes and references

To add servers with a coding agent, the workspace's openarena-add-mcp-tools skill walks through it (Coding agents).

items.title: Models
items.text:
configs/models.yaml is the list of models the workspace can call. Each entry gives a model a name and says which litellm id that name calls, with which settings. Everything else refers to the model by that name, never by id: an evaluation's language_models, a judge reward's language_model, a leaderboard's models. Results and rankings are kept under the name too.

flowchart LR
    E["evaluations.yaml<br/>language_models: [gpt-4o-mini]"] --> N
    R["rewards.yaml<br/>language_model: judge"] --> N
    L["leaderboards.yaml<br/>models: [gpt-4o-mini]"] --> N
    N["models.yaml<br/>name → model id + params"] --> P["provider<br/>(read off the id's prefix)"]

The name is the indirection that keeps a sweep comparable: you change what a name calls, or add a second name for the same id with other settings, without touching the evaluations, rewards and leaderboards that use it.

items.title: A model entry
items.text:
models:
  gpt-4o-mini:                       # the name: what every other file refers to
    model: openai/gpt-4o-mini        # required: <provider>/<id>, as litellm routes it
    type: llm                        # llm (the default) or embedding
    params:                          # the settings the type takes; leave one out for the provider's default
      temperature: 0
      max_tokens: 2048
    modalities: [text]               # what it reads: text, image, audio (default: [text])
    description: OpenAI's small model, the hosted baseline.
    tags: [openai, hosted]           # labels for browsing; never sent to the model
  gpt-4o:
    model: openai/gpt-4o             # the larger sibling, for quality comparisons
    params:
      temperature: 0
    tags: [openai, hosted]
  qwen3-local:
    model: ollama/qwen3:8b           # a local Ollama: no key, no bill
    params:
      temperature: 0
      reasoning_effort: disable      # turn native thinking off
    tags: [local, open-weights]
  minilm:
    model: ollama/all-minilm
    type: embedding                  # encodes text into vectors; does not answer
    params:
      dimensions: 384
    tags: [local]
field values default effect name (the key) a letter or digit, then letters, digits, _, ., -; at most 128 characters what every other file and every result calls the model model <provider>/<id>, a litellm id required which provider is called, and which model there type llm, embedding llm what the model does: which params it takes, where it may be named params a mapping, by type (below) {} settings sent with each call; a param left out keeps the provider's default modalities a list of text, image, audio [text] a fact about the model, for listings description text none shown by openarena models list tags a list of labels [] for browsing and filtering lists

An entry refuses any other field. A run and openarena check read it with the same schema: a field check rejects is one the run would refuse.

items.title: The name
items.text:
The name is the model's identity in the workspace. It is what a sweep's results, a run's table and a leaderboard's rows show.

  • Name what you compare, not the vendor's id: gpt-4o-mini, gpt-4o-mini-t07, o4-mini-high. The id is one field below; the name is what people read.
  • Keep it stable. Results of earlier runs keep the name they were made with, so renaming a model splits its history: a leaderboard shows the old runs under the old name and the new runs under the new one. openarena check lists every reference the rename broke in the configs; it cannot rename results.

items.title: model: the id and the provider
items.text:
The id is written the way litellm routes it: a provider prefix, a slash, and the provider's own model id. The prefix picks the provider; there is no provider: field.

prefix example needs openai/ openai/gpt-4o-mini OPENAI_API_KEY anthropic/ anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5 ANTHROPIC_API_KEY gemini/ gemini/gemini-2.5-flash GEMINI_API_KEY mistral/ mistral/mistral-small-latest MISTRAL_API_KEY groq/ groq/llama-3.3-70b-versatile GROQ_API_KEY openrouter/ openrouter/mistralai/ministral-14b-2512 OPENROUTER_API_KEY ollama/ ollama/qwen3:8b a running Ollama; OLLAMA_API_BASE when it is not at http://localhost:11434 vllm/ vllm/Qwen/Qwen3-4B HOSTED_VLLM_API_BASE: your server's OpenAI endpoint, /v1 included

Any provider litellm supports works the same way, with the variables litellm reads for it.

After the prefix, spell the id exactly as the provider does: ollama/qwen3:8b is the tag ollama list shows, vllm/Qwen/Qwen3-4B the name your vLLM server serves the model under.

items.title: Keys and base URLs
items.text:
Keys and server addresses live in the environment, never in models.yaml. openarena evaluations run loads the workspace's .env (beside configs/) before it runs, and never overrides a variable already set in your shell. No other command reads it. The workspace's .env.template lists the usual ones:

cp .env.template .env

# .env
OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...
OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-...
OLLAMA_API_BASE=http://localhost:11434
HOSTED_VLLM_API_BASE=http://localhost:8000/v1

A base URL is per provider, not per model: every vllm/ entry reaches the one server HOSTED_VLLM_API_BASE names. To compare two models served by vLLM, serve them from the same server, or run the sweeps one after the other with the variable changed.

There is no api_base param

params takes only the settings listed below. api_base:, top_p:, seed: or stop: in an entry are refused. Set a server address in the environment.

check does not check keys

openarena check reads files only. A missing key or a server that is down shows up when the run reaches the model: the cell fails and the run says why (Reading results).

items.title: Local or hosted
items.text:
Hosted APIOllamavLLMOpenRouter 
models:
  gpt-4o-mini:
    model: openai/gpt-4o-mini        # needs OPENAI_API_KEY
    params:
      temperature: 0
    tags: [openai, hosted]

Nothing to run on your side. Each call is billed, and the run's cost is counted from the provider's price (Prices). The provider may retire the model (End of life).

models:
  qwen3-local:
    model: ollama/qwen3:8b           # `ollama pull qwen3:8b` first
    params:
      temperature: 0
    tags: [local]

Runs on your machine. No key, and the cost is 0. Pull the model before the run: a model Ollama does not have fails the cell. Speed depends on your hardware, so keep batch_size low on a laptop.

models:
  qwen3-4b:
    model: vllm/Qwen/Qwen3-4B        # the name the server serves it under
    params:
      temperature: 0
    tags: [local, vllm]

A server of your own, local or on a GPU box, reached through its OpenAI endpoint: set HOSTED_VLLM_API_BASE=http://<host>:8000/v1. The cost is 0. It serves many requests at once, so it suits large batches.

models:
  ministral:
    model: openrouter/mistralai/ministral-14b-2512   # needs OPENROUTER_API_KEY
    params:
      temperature: 0
    tags: [openrouter, mistral]

One key for many vendors. Every call to an openrouter/ id is sent with OpenRouter's require_parameters routing: it only goes to a host that honours every parameter sent, tools included. A host that would drop the structured-output call is skipped, and the call fails at once rather than answering in prose.

When to use which. A hosted API for the models you measure against, and for judges, where answer quality matters more than cost. Ollama to iterate on a dataset or a reward on your laptop, at no cost. vLLM to score open-weight models at scale. Mixing them in one evaluation is fine: each name calls its own provider.

Harbor agents and local models

A Harbor agent installed inside the sandbox calls its model from there. It cannot reach an ollama/ or vllm/ model on the arena's machine, and check reports the pair. See Harbor tasks.

items.title: type
items.text:
type what it does where it can be named llm answers prompts: chat, structured output, tool calls, agents an evaluation's language_models; a reward's language_model, smart_language_model, sub_language_model, panel_language_models; default_language_model embedding turns text into vectors the language_models of a sweep over retrieval datasets (embedding: in Datasets); a reward's or metric's embedding_model; default_embedding_model

The type is checked wherever the model is named: a judge set to an embedding model, or an embedding model in the language_models of a sweep over text datasets, is an error. A sweep runs one type, so a retrieval dataset cannot share an evaluation with other kinds of dataset.

items.title: params
items.text:
What params takes depends on the type. A param left out, or set to null, is not sent, and the provider's default applies.

type param values effect llm temperature a number, 0 to 2 how much the model samples; lower is more consistent llm max_tokens an integer, at least 1 the longest answer, in tokens llm reasoning_effort disable, low, medium, high how much the model thinks before answering, where it can embedding dimensions an integer, at least 1 the vector size, where the model lets you pick

items.title: temperature
items.text:
Temperature trades consistency for variety. At 0 the model takes its most likely answer; higher values spread over more answers.

setup when temperature: 0 benchmarks and comparisons. Two runs of the same model stay as close as the provider allows, so a difference between two models is the models, not the dice. left out when you want each model as its vendor ships it. Vendors pick different defaults, so you compare the models plus their defaults. 0.7 to 1 when the task rewards variety (writing, brainstorming), or to measure how stable a model's score is across runs.

Temperature 0 is the default choice for a benchmark

The evaluation's seed seeds the arena's own randomness, not the provider's sampling. Only a low temperature keeps a model's answers steady from run to run. Even at 0, hosted providers do not promise identical answers.

If a provider refuses a param for a model, the cell fails with the provider's message. Remove the param from that entry.

items.title: max_tokens
items.text: The cap on the length of each answer. Set it to bound cost and time per row, or when a provider's default is too short for the task. Too low cuts answers off mid-way: a truncated answer usually fails the reward, so a low score may be the cap, not the model. On a reasoning model, leave room: depending on the provider, the thinking may count against the cap. Leave it out unless you have a reason.

items.title: reasoning_effort
items.text:
How much a model that can think does so before answering.

value effect disable turns native thinking off, for local models that think by default (Ollama's qwen3, deepseek-r1) low, medium, high the effort, where the model supports levels left out the provider's default

More effort usually means better answers on hard rows, at the price of more output tokens, more cost and more latency. That trade-off is what a leaderboard with shares on cost and latency weighs. A model that does not support the param may ignore it or refuse it.

items.title: dimensions
items.text: For an embedding model that lets you choose its vector size. Smaller vectors are cheaper to store and compare; larger ones keep more of the meaning. Leave it out for a model with a fixed size.

items.title: Where the params apply
items.text:
The params travel with the model wherever it is named: as the model under test, as a judge, as a metric's model or as a default.

the model is... its params under test on a generator, agent or tools dataset sent with every call under test on a Harbor dataset given to the Harbor agent where its options take them (temperature, reasoning_effort, max_tokens); what it does not take is logged and left out under test on a retrieval (embedding:) dataset dimensions sent with every embedding call a reward's or metric's model (language_model, embedding_model, a panel, ...) sent with every call the reward or metric makes default_language_model, default_embedding_model sent with every call, as for a reward's model

So a judge entry with temperature: 0 grades at temperature 0. See Choosing a judge.

items.title: modalities
items.text:
What the model reads: text, image, audio. Default [text]; at least one; duplicates dropped. Add image for a vision model.

It is a fact for listings: the run does not read it, and it does not turn image input on or off. What a model is sent comes from the dataset's templates.

items.title: description and tags
items.text:
description is free text, shown as a column by openarena models list. Say what the entry is for and what sets it apart from its neighbours: "high effort", "the hosted baseline", "served from the lab's GPU box".

tags are short labels: what the model is (openai, local, open-weights), what it can do (tools, vision, 128k-context), what it is for (judge, baseline). The engine never reads them, and they are never sent to the model.

rule form a list: tags: [openai, hosted], never tags: openai characters lower-case letters, digits, -, ., :, +, /; starting with a letter or digit folding upper case is lowered, spaces and _ become -: Open AI is stored as open-ai limits at most 40 characters a tag, 32 tags an entry; duplicates dropped

Pick one spelling per idea and keep to it across the workspace, so one filter finds them all.

items.title: Two entries for one id
items.text:
Two entries calling the same id with different params are two models. Each gets its own row in every result and its own place on a leaderboard. This is how you measure what a setting does.

models:
  o4-mini-low:
    model: openai/o4-mini
    params:
      reasoning_effort: low
    description: o4-mini, light thinking.
    tags: [openai, reasoning]
  o4-mini-high:
    model: openai/o4-mini
    params:
      reasoning_effort: high
    description: o4-mini, deep thinking.
    tags: [openai, reasoning]

Then sweep both:

evaluations:
  effort-ablation:
    language_models: [o4-mini-low, o4-mini-high]
    datasets: [gsm8k-20]

Do this when the question is "is the extra thinking worth it?" or "does temperature 0 hurt this task?", or to keep the setting you deploy next to the default. Both entries share the id's price and end-of-life date: only the tokens they spend differ.

Do not duplicate an entry just to label it differently; that is what tags and description are for. A duplicate with identical params doubles the cost of every sweep that names both.

items.title: Choosing a judge model
items.text:
A judge reward (Rewards) names an llm entry of models.yaml, by name.

models:
  judge:
    model: openai/gpt-4o
    params:
      temperature: 0                 # grade the same answer the same way every time
    description: The judge of the free-text rewards.
    tags: [openai, judge]

rewards:
  graded:
    type: lm_as_judge
    config:
      language_model: judge          # a models.yaml name, never an id
      instructions: |
        Score 1.0 when the answer is correct and complete, 0.0 when it is wrong.
  • Stronger than the models it judges. A judge weaker than the model under test misses the errors that matter.
  • Not one of the models under test, when you can avoid it. A model tends to favour answers like its own. Prefer a judge from another vendor, or a panel (multi_judge_panel).
  • One judge for a whole comparison. Scores from two judges are not on the same scale. Change the judge and you rerun every model.
  • A dedicated entry. Name it judge, not gpt-4o: you swap what it calls in one place, and it keeps its own params apart from the gpt-4o you may test.
  • temperature: 0. A judge's params are sent with its calls (above). At 0 it grades an answer the same way from row to row and from run to run, as far as the provider allows, so a difference in score is the answers, not the judge's sampling.
  • Cost. A judge makes a call per row, counted apart as reward_cost. A local judge costs nothing but is usually weaker.

An evaluation's default_language_model is the model a reward uses when its config names none (Running evaluations).

items.title: Prices
items.text:
A run's cost (and reward_cost, embedding_cost) is the sum of each call's price, which litellm counts as the run goes. Before a run, the arena makes sure litellm has a price for every model the run may call, the models under test and the judges, from the first source that knows one:

  1. A local server. An ollama/, ollama_chat/, vllm/, hosted_vllm/, lm_studio/ or llamafile/ id costs 0: there is no bill.
  2. litellm's pricing table. The live one, filled with the rows only the copy shipped in the package has.
  3. OpenRouter's catalogue. For an openrouter/ id, and for a vendor's direct id when OpenRouter routes the same model at the vendor's price.

A source that prices both input and output wins over one that prices one side.

Unpriced is not free

A hosted model that no source prices still runs, but its spend reads 0. On a leaderboard with a share on cost or a cost budget, it looks free. Check a new model's cost after its first run.

The price is per id: two entries for one id share it.

items.title: End of life
items.text:
A leaderboard adds eol_days to every model: the days left before its id stops being served. A model about to be retired is a poor choice to build on, however well it scores. The date comes from the first source that has one:

source for the provider's announced date, as recorded in litellm's table any provider that announces one Azure's OpenAI retirement schedule openai/, azure/, azure_ai/ ids the provider has not dated; fetched once a day, a shipped snapshot answers offline OpenRouter's expiration date openrouter/ ids; it wins when it is earlier than the vendor's

An openrouter/<vendor>/<model> id is also looked up under the vendor's own id: it is the same model, and it stops on the same day.

case eol_days no date known (local and open-weight models, most current models) 5 years: no end of life a date further than 5 years away 5 years a date in the past negative: the provider may already refuse calls

openarena leaderboards run <name> --no-eol leaves eol_days out, for a ranking that asks nothing of the network (Leaderboards).

items.title: Tags and leaderboards
items.text:
A leaderboard's scope is its models: list, by name. Tags do not select models for it: a leaderboard does not read them.

leaderboards:
  local-vs-hosted:
    title: Local against hosted
    models: [qwen3-local, gpt-4o-mini]   # names; empty means every scored model
    datasets: []
    tags: [baseline]

Use tags to find the names to list: give every model of a family or a deployment the same tag, browse the lists by it, and copy the names into the leaderboard's models:. When the set changes, edit the list.

items.title: Common mistakes
items.text:
Run openarena check configs after every edit (Checking configs). What it reports for a model, and the fix:

mistake check says fix a param beside model: (temperature: 0) not a field of a models entry move it under params:; check prints the block an option the type does not take, beside model: (top_p, seed) not a field of a models entry, fix: remove `top_p:`; it is not supported: a chat model takes only reasoning_effort, temperature, max_tokens under `params:` remove it an option the type does not take, under params: (top_p, temperature on an embedding model) Chat models take reasoning_effort, temperature, max_tokens, not top_p remove it a server address or key (api_base, base_url, api_key) not a field of a models entry, fix: remove `api_base:`; a base URL is not a model setting: set it in the environment instead (`.env`) set the provider's variable in .env (OLLAMA_API_BASE, HOSTED_VLLM_API_BASE) provider: openai not a field of a models entry remove it: the provider is read off the id's prefix reasoning_effort: max reasoning_effort: one of disable, low, medium, high use one of those temperature: 3 temperature: between 0 and 2 a value in range modalities: [video] Input should be 'text', 'image' or 'audio' one of those tags: OpenAI `tags:` is a list tags: [openai] a name with a space a name starts with a letter or a digit, ... rename it as check suggests, and update what refers to it a reward naming an id (language_model: openai/gpt-4o-mini) 'openai/gpt-4o-mini' is not in models name the entry that calls it; check names it a judge set to an embedding model 'minilm' is an embedding model; this setting needs a language model name an llm entry a renamed model still named elsewhere 'old-name' is not in models update the reference; on a leaderboard it is a warning

check does not reach the provider. A misspelt id after the prefix, a missing key, a model Ollama has not pulled or a vLLM server that is down fail the cell at run time, with the provider's message.

items.title: Commands
items.text:
openarena models list            # name, id, type and description of ./configs
openarena check configs          # after an edit

See the CLI reference for the options.

items.title: See also
items.text:
• Rewards: judges, and the models they name.
  • Datasets: the dataset kinds, including retrieval over embedding models.
  • Running evaluations: sweeping models, seed, default_language_model, cost and time.
  • Leaderboards: cost, eol_days, budgets and shares.
  • Harbor tasks: which agents can drive which models.

items.title: Reading results
items.text:
A run answers one question per cell: how did this model do on this dataset? This page says where the answers are written, what every number means, and how to get from a surprising number to the rows behind it.

flowchart LR
    run["openarena evaluations run NAME"] --> term["terminal: a line per cell, a table per dataset"]
    run --> dir[".open-arena/NAME/"]
    dir --> cfg["config.yaml: what ran"]
    dir --> res["result.json: the scores"]
    dir --> state["DATASET/trial_N/: trial state, why a cell failed"]
    dir --> harbor["harbor/trials.jsonl: one line per Harbor row"]
    res --> lb["openarena leaderboards run"]
    res --> json["--json FILE: a copy to keep"]

items.title: What a run writes
items.text:
Everything lands in <state-dir>/<evaluation>/, .open-arena/<evaluation>/ by default (--state-dir).

.open-arena/math-compare/
  config.yaml              the evaluation and every entry it names, gathered
  result.json              the scores, one row per model, dataset and metric
  <dataset>/               trial state, one folder per dataset
    oracle.json
    trial_0/trial.json     one trial per model: its status, metrics and error
  harbor/                  Harbor datasets only
    trials.jsonl           one line per row: question, answer, outcome, usage
    trials/<trial>/        that row's logs: agent session, verifier output
  environments/ tasks/     copies of the Harbor folders the run used
file written read it for config.yaml at the start of every run what actually ran: models, params, rewards, templates, after the registries were gathered; a ${NAME} stays a reference, never the secret result.json at the end, only when the sweep finishes the scores; this is what leaderboards read <dataset>/trial_N/trial.json as each cell ends a failed cell's full error; this is also the resume cache harbor/trials.jsonl as each Harbor row ends the row-level view of a Harbor cell

config.yaml is the record of what ran

It is rewritten from configs/ at every launch. To know what produced a number, read this copy, not configs/, which may have changed since.

result.json is replaced, not appended

Running the same evaluation again rewrites its result.json with every cell, the cached ones included. A run that stops before the end writes none, and the previous result.json stays in place. Keep a copy with --json when you want history (Comparing runs over time).

items.title: The terminal
items.text:
While it runs, the CLI prints a line per cell, and after each dataset one line per failed cell:

gsm8k-20
  qwen38 running…
  qwen38 done reward 0.6500
  gpt-4o-mini running…
  gpt-4o-mini done reward 0.8500
  qwen38 failed: <the exception's last line>

done lists every number the cell measured. failed is the last line of the cell's error; the full traceback is in its trial.json (When a cell failed). After the tables, a run with failed cells names them all, N cell(s) failed: <model> × <dataset>, ..., and exits 1.

At the end it prints one table per dataset: a row per model, a column per metric, four decimals, — where a cell has no value. Add -v for a progress bar, -vv for a line per batch.

items.title: result.json
items.text:
{
  "meta": {
    "config": ".open-arena/math-compare/config.yaml",
    "models": ["qwen38", "gpt-4o-mini"],
    "datasets": ["gsm8k-20"],
    "metrics": ["reward", "cost", "output_tokens"],
    "directions": {"gsm8k-20": "max"},
    "metric_directions": {"cost": "min", "output_tokens": "min"},
    "objectives_by_ds": {"gsm8k-20": [["reward", "max"], ["cost", "min"]]},
    "frontier_by_ds": {"gsm8k-20": ["qwen38", "gpt-4o-mini"]}
  },
  "rows": [
    {"model": "gpt-4o-mini", "dataset": "gsm8k-20", "metric": "reward",
     "value": 0.85, "status": "COMPLETED", "direction": "max", "on_frontier": true},
    {"model": "gpt-4o-mini", "dataset": "gsm8k-20", "metric": "cost",
     "value": 0.0021, "status": "COMPLETED", "direction": "min", "on_frontier": true}
  ]
}

items.title: meta
items.text: key meaning config the gathered config the run read models the models (or A2A agents) compared, in the evaluation's order datasets the datasets, in the evaluation's order metrics every column: reward first, then each extra metric's alias, across all datasets directions per dataset, the direction of its reward (max unless the reward says min) metric_directions per extra metric, its direction: as written in metrics:, else min for a cost, tokens or latency measurement and max for anything else objectives_by_ds per dataset, the axes of its Pareto frontier: reward, plus every metric marked objective: true frontier_by_ds per dataset, the models no other model beats on every axis; empty when the dataset has one axis

items.title: rows
items.text:
Long form: one row per model, dataset and metric. Every row carries what it needs to be read alone.

key meaning model, dataset, metric the cell and the column value the number, or null when the cell did not finish or that dataset does not measure that metric status the cell's outcome, the same on all of its rows direction max or min: which way is better on_frontier whether the model is on the dataset's Pareto frontier

status tells "did not run" apart from "ran and scored 0":

status meaning what to do COMPLETED every row was asked and scored read the value FAILED the cell gave no score: no row got an answer (a missing key, a model server down, an unknown model id), an agent's MCP servers gave no tools, a Harbor cell where no task got an answer read the error; it is the setup, not the model. Fix it and run again: the cell runs again INVALID the cell raised any other error: a template, a reward that cannot be built read the error, fix, run again null the cell has no trial the run did not reach it

A 0 is not a failure, and a failure is not a 0

A failed cell has value: null, and leaderboards skip it. A cell that COMPLETED with 0 did run: the model answered and every answer scored 0, or the scoring could not match its form. See Model or infrastructure.

items.title: Reading it
items.text:
The rewardsOnly what failedWith jq 
python - <<'EOF'
import json
r = json.load(open(".open-arena/math-compare/result.json"))
for row in r["rows"]:
    if row["metric"] == "reward":
        print(f'{row["dataset"]:20} {row["model"]:20} {row["value"]} {row["status"]}')
EOF

python - <<'EOF'
import json
r = json.load(open(".open-arena/math-compare/result.json"))
seen = set()
for row in r["rows"]:
    cell = (row["dataset"], row["model"])
    if row["status"] != "COMPLETED" and cell not in seen:
        seen.add(cell)
        print(*cell, row["status"])
EOF

jq -r '.rows[] | select(.metric == "reward") | [.dataset, .model, .value, .status] | @tsv' \
  .open-arena/math-compare/result.json

items.title: What each metric means
items.text: Every number is per cell: one model over all the rows of one dataset.

items.title: reward
items.text:
The mean of the dataset's reward over its rows. Most rewards score a row from 0 to 1, so the mean reads as a share: 0.85 is 85% of the rows, or 85% of the credit when the reward gives partial credit. A row the model answered nothing for scores 0 and still counts.

Its direction is the reward's own direction. A min reward (a toxicity, a hallucination score) is better low; leaderboards account for it.

items.title: Extra metrics
items.text:
A dataset's or the evaluation's metrics: adds columns (Datasets). A catalog reward used as a metric is averaged over the rows like reward. Cost, tokens and latency are metrics too, counted on the model calls of the program under test. A column is in result.json only when it is listed:

evaluations:
  math-compare:
    # ...
    metrics:
      - cost                    # min: lower is better, from the name
      - output_tokens           # min
      - avg_latency             # min
      - {class: answer_accuracy, alias: accuracy}   # max
