name unit what it counts cost USD the cell's total spend on the model under test, priced by litellm input_tokens, output_tokens, total_tokens tokens the cell's totals avg_input_tokens_per_call, avg_output_tokens_per_call, avg_total_tokens_per_call tokens per model call avg_reasoning_tokens_per_call, avg_cached_tokens_per_call tokens per model call avg_cost_per_call USD per model call avg_latency seconds mean duration of one model call, however many ran at once throughput, tokens_per_second tokens/s output tokens, or all tokens, over the cell's wall-clock time; these depend on batch_size program_calls, program_elapsed_time count, seconds calls to the program under test, and the wall-clock time spent in them reward_cost USD what the reward's model calls spent: the judge, apart from the model under test embedding_cost USD the embedding model's spend, for retrieval datasets

Cost, tokens and latency rank lower first

Without direction:, a metric measuring what the calls spend (a name ending in tokens, cost, latency, time_to_..., elapsed_time, error_rate, failed_calls, ... with an optional _per_call) is min; every other metric, avg_cached_tokens_per_call, throughput and tokens_per_second included, is max. An explicit direction: wins. Running evaluations has the full rule.

When cost reads 0

A local model (ollama/..., vllm/...) costs 0 by design. A hosted model at 0 usually means no price source knows its id: check its price before you compare costs.

items.title: Harbor cells
items.text: The agent calls the model itself, inside the sandbox, so a Harbor cell's usage is what the agent reported per trial: its tokens and its cost. avg_latency is the agent's run time divided by its model calls, so the commands it ran between calls are included. That is the wait a task costs, not the model's speed.

items.title: The Pareto frontier
items.text:
With one axis there is no trade-off: the best model is the top of the reward column, frontier_by_ds is empty and every on_frontier is false. Mark a metric objective: true to make it an axis:

datasets:
  gsm8k-20:
    # ...
    metrics:
      - {class: cost, objective: true}

A model is then on the frontier when no other model is at least as good on every axis and better on one. A model with a missing value on any axis is left out. Use it when "best" depends on a budget: the frontier is the short list, and a leaderboard then weighs the axes.

items.title: When a cell failed or scored 0
items.text:
The failed: line is the last line of the error. The whole traceback is in the cell's trial, under the dataset's folder:

grep -lE '"status": "(FAILED|INVALID)"' .open-arena/math-compare/*/trial_*/trial.json
python -c "import json,sys; t=json.load(open(sys.argv[1])); print(t['hyperparameters']['values'], t['status']); print(t['message'])" \
  .open-arena/math-compare/gsm8k-20/trial_1/trial.json

hyperparameters.values.language_model names the model, status the outcome, message the traceback.

symptom likely cause fix no row got an answer: all N row(s) failed; the first error: <error> no row of the cell got an answer; the error after the first error: says why, as in the rows below fix it and run again: the failed cell runs, no --no-cache needed an authentication error the provider's key is not set set it in .env, run again (it resumes) connection refused no Ollama running, or HOSTED_VLLM_API_BASE unset start the model server model not found a wrong id in models.yaml fix model: could not load the MCP tools of [...] an agent's MCP server is down, its command is not on the PATH, or it exposes no tools start the server or fix its entry; only that agent's cells failed an error reading the dataset a wrong path, name or split, or a template naming a missing column look at a real row, fix config reward 0 everywhere, answers look right the answer's form differs from the expected one ("42" and "42.0", "B" and "B) ...") tighten the output_schema or the template, or use answer_accuracy or a judge a judge reward fails the judge model's key is not set set its provider's key none of the N Harbor task(s) got an answer the sandbox: no Docker or E2B key, a failed image build, no tmux read harbor/trials.jsonl

Every cell runs

A failed cell never stops the run, however many fail in a row: every cell runs, result.json is written with every failure in it, and the command exits 1. The trial state stays, so the next run resumes and runs only the failed cells.

items.title: Model or infrastructure
items.text:
A low number has three possible owners: the model, the scoring, or the plumbing between them. Rule out the last two before blaming the first.

signal points to status is FAILED or INVALID infrastructure or config: the cell never produced a score every model scores 0 on a dataset the scoring or the data: a template, a schema, an expected answer, a Harbor task whose solution fails its own tests one model at 0, the others fine that model's setup first (key, id, server), then the model a low reward with output_tokens near 0 the model answered nothing: the provider failed on the rows a Harbor line with "status": "failed" the sandbox did not run that row; it scored 0 a Harbor line answered with an error the agent ran but stopped short (a timeout, nothing in the answer file); the score is the model's scores move when only batch_size changes rate limits, or a struggling local server

A provider error on some rows does not fail the cell

When a call fails on one row, or an A2A agent does not answer it, that row gets no answer and scores 0, with a warning, and the cell still completes. A rate limit therefore shows as a lower reward, not as an error, and the cell is kept on a rerun. Only a cell where no row got an answer fails. Add output_tokens to the metrics: a model that scored low because it never answered spent no output tokens.

items.title: From a number to the rows
items.text: The aggregate tells you which cell to look at; the rows tell you why.

items.title: Harbor runs
items.text:
Each row's trial writes one line to harbor/trials.jsonl:

key meaning trial, dir the trial's name, and where its logs are dataset, model, agent the cell, and the Harbor agent that ran task, question the task folder (task datasets), the instruction asked status answered, or failed when the trial left no trajectory answer, steps what the agent answered, and how many steps it took rewards what the verifier, or the task's rewards.yaml, scored error why it failed, or why an answered trial stopped short seconds, input_tokens, output_tokens, cost_usd that row's time and usage 
jq -c 'select(.model == "qwen38") | {task, status, rewards, error}' \
  .open-arena/swe-smoke/harbor/trials.jsonl

Then open the trial's dir: Harbor keeps the agent's session under agent/, the verifier's output under verifier/, and its own trial.log. The trials sit in the run's harbor/trials/ unless ARENA_HARBOR_WORKDIR moves them, or a snap Docker cannot read a hidden folder (then ~/arena-harbor/); dir always says where.

items.title: Other datasets
items.text:
The CLI keeps only the aggregates. To read the answers, run the sweep from Python with on_sample: it receives the first samples_per_cell rows of each cell.

import asyncio, json
from pathlib import Path
from openarena.cli.main import load_env
from openarena.evaluate import run_sweep

load_env(Path("."))  # the workspace's .env, as the CLI reads it
with open("samples.jsonl", "w") as out:
    asyncio.run(run_sweep(
        ".open-arena/math-compare/config.yaml",   # the config the CLI gathered
        state_dir=Path(".open-arena/math-compare-samples"),
        on_sample=lambda row: out.write(json.dumps(row) + "\n"),
        samples_per_cell=20,
    ))

Each line is {dataset, model, index, input, target, output, reward}. index is the row's place in the dataset, the same row for every model, so two models' answers can be put side by side. output: null is a row the model answered nothing for. reward is the dataset's reward for that row; extra metrics are not recorded per row.

Use a fresh state_dir

Only cells that run are recorded. A cell cached in the state dir is read back, not run, so pointed at the evaluation's own folder the call records nothing for the cells already done.

The arena app does this for its runs and shows the answers beside the scores.

items.title: What to look for
items.text:
• The answer is right, the score is 0. The form differs from the target. Fix the template or schema, or switch to a reward that tolerates form (Rewards).
  • The answer is empty or null. The call failed, or the model ran out of tokens or iterations. Check max_tokens and the agent's limits.
  • The answer is wrong. That is the model. Compare it with another model's answer on the same index.

items.title: Checking a judge
items.text:
A judge reward is a model: it can be wrong, lenient, or partial to its own family. Before trusting a ranking built on one, check it.

  • Put a second scorer beside it. Add a deterministic metric where the data allows it, or a second judge on another provider, under its own alias. The columns land side by side in result.json.

    datasets:
  support-qa:
    # ...
    reward: judge-gpt
    metrics:
      - answer_accuracy
      - {class: lm_as_judge, alias: judge_b, language_model: claude-haiku}

  • Compare orders, not values. Two judges rarely agree on the number; they should agree on which model is better. When the orders differ, read the rows of the cells that swapped.

  • Read the rows it scored. With on_sample, read the answers it gave 1 and those it gave 0. A judge that gives 1 to an empty answer is broken.
  • Use a panel when one judge is not enough. multi_judge_panel asks several models and reconciles them (Rewards).
  • Mind the cost. Each judge is a model call per row. List reward_cost to see what the judging spent.

items.title: Tracing in MLflow
items.text:
Tracing records each model call of a run, with its inputs, outputs, tokens and cost, in an MLflow server. Use it when a number needs the full story of a row: every step of an agent, every tool call, what each call cost.

The CLI does not trace

openarena evaluations run never turns tracing on, whatever MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI says. The arena app traces its runs; from Python, turn it on yourself.

Turn it on before the sweep builds anything, and name the experiment:

import asyncio
from openarena.evaluate import run_sweep
from openarena.programs.observability import enable_observability, run_experiment_name, tracking_uri

experiment = run_experiment_name("math-compare/1")
if enable_observability(experiment_name=experiment):
    print("tracing into", experiment)
asyncio.run(run_sweep(
    ".open-arena/math-compare/config.yaml",
    mlflow_experiment=experiment,
    mlflow_tracking_uri=tracking_uri(),
    mlflow_tags={"note": "baseline"},
))
variable effect MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI the server; unset, tracing is off ARENA_MLFLOW_TRACING on by default; 0, false, no or off turns it off while keeping the URI MLFLOW_EXPERIMENT_NAME the base of every experiment name MLFLOW_HTTP_REQUEST_TIMEOUT, MLFLOW_HTTP_REQUEST_MAX_RETRIES the client's budget per request; 10 s and 2 retries unless you set them

What lands in the server:

  • One experiment per run: <base>/eval-<run>, with an optional scope between them, so two launches of one evaluation never mix.
  • One MLflow run per cell, named <dataset> · <model> and tagged dataset and language_model, plus your mlflow_tags, holding the cell's metrics.
  • One span per module call, the model call's span carrying its cost.

Tracing never decides whether a cell runs:

  • A server that does not answer GET /health leaves tracing off, with a warning. A sqlite:/// or file store needs no server and is not checked.
  • A cell whose MLflow run cannot be opened runs untraced, with a warning.

items.title: Comparing runs over time
items.text:
A run's scores depend on everything in its config.yaml: model ids and params, the dataset's rows and templates, the reward and its judge. Compare two runs only when you know what changed between them: diff their config.yaml first.

you want do the same evaluation after a fix run it again; finished cells are kept, failed ones run again fresh numbers after changing a dataset, a model's params or a reward run with --no-cache, or old cells are reused as they are to keep each run --json results/2026-10-15-math-compare.json, or a new evaluation name two setups side by side two evaluations with different names: each has its own folder less noise between runs seed: on the evaluation, and temperature: 0 on the models; the provider's sampling can still vary

Leaderboards read the newest cell

leaderboards run reads every <state-dir>/*/result.json and, for each model and dataset, takes the cell from the newest file that scored it. An old evaluation folder still counts for the cells no newer run has. Move or delete a folder to drop its numbers.

To compare two saved results cell by cell:

python - old.json new.json <<'EOF'
import json, sys
def load(p):
    return {(r["dataset"], r["model"], r["metric"]): r["value"] for r in json.load(open(p))["rows"]}
old, new = load(sys.argv[1]), load(sys.argv[2])
for key in sorted(old.keys() | new.keys()):
    a, b = old.get(key), new.get(key)
    if a != b:
        print(*key, a, "->", b)
EOF

items.title: Exporting
items.text:
what how the scores, anywhere openarena evaluations run NAME --json FILE writes the same content as result.json a ranking openarena leaderboards run NAME --json FILE (CLI) a spreadsheet result.json is long form: one row per cell and metric, ready for a pivot Harbor rows harbor/trials.jsonl, one JSON object per line 
jq -r '["model","dataset","metric","value","status","direction"],
       (.rows[] | [.model, .dataset, .metric, .value, .status, .direction]) | @csv' \
  .open-arena/math-compare/result.json > math-compare.csv

items.title: Rewards
items.text:
A reward scores one answer, from 0 to 1. It is the number a run is about: the reward column of every cell, and the first thing a leaderboard ranks on. Pick the wrong reward and every number after it measures the wrong thing, so this page takes its time.

configs/rewards.yaml gives each reward a name. Behind the name sit a catalog reward (type), its settings (config) and which way is better (direction). A dataset names the reward that scores it with reward:, and a dataset cannot run without one.

flowchart LR
    row[dataset row] --> prog[model under test]
    row -->|output_template| ref[expected answer]
    prog --> pred[answer]
    ref --> R{reward}
    pred --> R
    R -->|0 to 1, per row| cell[cell mean: the reward column]
    cell --> lb[leaderboard, read with direction]

items.title: The entry
items.text:
rewards:
  exact-match:                       # the name a dataset's `reward:` uses
    type: exact_match                # required: a catalog reward, see below
    direction: max                   # max (higher is better, the default) or min
    description: One when the answer is exactly the reference, zero otherwise.
    tags: [strict]
  judge:
    type: lm_as_judge
    description: A grader model scores correctness against the reference.
    tags: [judge]
    config:                          # the type's settings, and only those
      language_model: gpt-4o-mini    # a models.yaml name, never a litellm id
      instructions: |
        Score 1.0 when the answer is correct and complete, 0.0 when it is wrong.
field values default effect type a catalog reward, below required what computes the score direction max, min max which way is better on leaderboards and the Pareto frontier config the type's settings {} handed to the reward; models are resolved by name first description text none shown by openarena rewards list tags a list of labels [] for browsing; lower-cased and de-duplicated

config takes the type's settings and nothing else. name and direction may not appear in it: type: and direction: sit beside config:. Every model setting (language_model, smart_language_model, sub_language_model, panel_language_models, embedding_model) is a key of models.yaml, and of the right type: an llm model for a judge, an embedding model for embedding_model.

The same entry can score many datasets. Give a reward a name that says what it measures (math-exact, support-judge), not which dataset uses it.

items.title: Deterministic or judged
items.text:
There are two families, and the choice between them matters more than any setting.

Deterministic rewards compare the answer with the expected answer by a rule: equality, token overlap, embedding distance, set recall. Judged rewards ask a language model to read the answer and grade it.

deterministic judged expected answer required optional; used as a reference when present cost per row nothing (embeddings: two embedding calls) one model call or more, counted as reward_cost same answer, same score always only as stable as the judge model what it can grade short, checkable answers free text, style, reasoning, faithfulness bias none beyond the rule the judge's own preferences: length, wording, its own family's style failure mode marks a right answer wrong for its form marks a wrong answer right because it sounds sure

Use a deterministic reward whenever the answer can be checked by rule. A number, the letter of a multiple choice, a label, a list of retrieved passages, a function call: compare them. It is free, instant, reproducible, and nobody can argue with it. The work is in the dataset: make the output_template render a short, normalized expected answer, and ask the model for the same shape (Templates).

Use a judge when no rule can tell right from wrong: a summary, an explanation, an email, an answer that is right in many wordings. Then spend time on the judge: its model, its instructions, and a check that its scores agree with yours (Choosing and calibrating a judge).

Read the answers before you pick

Run the dataset with limit: 5 and any reward, then read the answers in the result. If a correct answer would fail exact_match only because of its form, fix the templates first. Reach for a judge when the form cannot be fixed.

items.title: What a reward compares
items.text:
The model's answer is a JSON object, and so is the expected answer the dataset's output_template renders. Before scoring, the engine picks the fields each reward sees:

  • A deterministic reward sees only the top-level fields the output_template renders, and compares each one's value whole: a field that holds an object or a list of objects (a nested answer, a list of tool calls) is compared with everything inside it. Whatever else the program returns (the question, when the program returns its inputs; a chain of thought's thinking; an agent's messages) is left out, so it never costs a point.
  • A judge sees every field the program returns, since judging them is its job. Two exceptions: on an MCP agent dataset the agent's messages transcript is left out, and on a Harbor dataset only the agent's answer is read.

Setting any mask yourself (below) turns this automatic choice off: the reward then sees what your mask keeps, applied as written.

A judge reads the expected answer beside the answer, with the expected answer's fields prefixed gold_. It does not read the question unless the program returns it: set return_inputs: true in the dataset's generator: block when the judge needs the question to grade (relevancy, instruction following).

datasets:
  support-replies:
    # ...
    generator:
      return_inputs: true            # the answer carries the question, so the judge reads it
    reward: support-judge

items.title: Masks
items.text:
Every type takes four optional settings that choose the fields by hand. The automatic choice above fits most datasets; reach for a mask when a field the output_template renders should not count, or when a judge should not see a field.

field values default effect in_mask a list of field names none keep only these fields out_mask a list of field names none drop these fields in_mask_pattern a regex none keep the fields whose name matches; combined with in_mask, either keeps a field out_mask_pattern a regex none drop the fields whose name matches

Masks apply to both sides, the answer and the expected answer, and at every level of nesting: in_mask: [answer] on {"answer": {"value": 1}} keeps {"answer": {}}.

Masks and nested values

Because masks reach into nested objects, keeping a field whose value is an object or a list of objects empties it, and every answer then scores the same. The automatic choice does not have this problem: it keeps whole values. To leave a field out, prefer out_mask over an in_mask naming the others.

items.title: Deterministic rewards
items.text:
All of them need the expected answer, so the dataset needs an output_template. None calls a language model.

type settings scores fits exact_match masks 1 when the answer equals the expected answer, else 0 numbers, letters, labels answer_accuracy masks each field compared by its type, averaged, with partial credit structured answers, several fields cosine_similarity embedding_model, masks embedding similarity, 0 to 1 short free text with a reference retrieval_recall masks the share of gold passages retrieved retrieval datasets tool_calls_accuracy masks the right functions with the right arguments tool-call datasets harbor_verifier key, masks what a Harbor task's own tests wrote Harbor tasks

items.title: exact_match
items.text:
One when the answer's fields equal the expected answer's, zero otherwise. It is plain equality of the JSON values: "42" and 42 differ, "Paris" and "paris" differ, a trailing space differs.

rewards:
  exact-match:
    type: exact_match
    description: One when the answer is exactly the reference.

When: the answer is one value with one correct spelling: a multiple-choice letter, a final number, a class label, true or false. Make the template and the instructions agree on the form ("B", not "B) Paris").

Not when: the answer has several fields and you want partial credit (use answer_accuracy), or it is a sentence (use a judge, or cosine_similarity).

items.title: answer_accuracy
items.text:
Scores each field of the expected answer on its own, with the comparison its value calls for, then averages the fields:

expected value comparison partial credit true / false binary accuracy no a number equality no text, a list, an object token overlap: shared tokens over all tokens yes

A one-word text scores like an exact match; a longer text or a list of labels scores the share of tokens in common. A correct negative (false expected, false given) scores 1. A field missing from the answer scores 0.

rewards:
  graded:
    type: answer_accuracy
    description: Each field compared by its type, averaged.

The comparison is chosen from the expected value, not from the dataset's schema. A number rendered as text ({{ answer | string | tojson }}) is compared as text, by tokens. Render it as a number ({{ answer | tojson }}) when it should be compared as one.

When: an answer with several fields (a verdict and a label, an extraction with five slots), where four right out of five should beat none. It also makes a good extra column beside exact_match: the gap between the two shows how many answers were nearly right.

items.title: cosine_similarity
items.text:
Embeds each field of the answer and of the expected answer, and scores how close they are. Several fields are averaged.

rewards:
  similar:
    type: cosine_similarity
    description: Embedding similarity to the reference answer.
    config:
      embedding_model: minilm        # a models.yaml key of `type: embedding`
field values default effect embedding_model a type: embedding model name the evaluation's default_embedding_model the model that embeds both sides

The score is the cosine rescaled to 0 to 1, (cos + 1) / 2. Two unrelated texts land near 0.5, not near 0, and answers on the same topic crowd together near the top. Read it as a ranking between models, not as a share correct.

When: short free-text answers with a reference, where the wording varies and a judge's cost or variance is not worth it (definitions, short factual sentences). Not when: correctness hinges on a detail. "The meeting is on Monday" and "The meeting is not on Monday" embed close together.

Note

Every row embeds both sides; the cost is counted as embedding_cost. Another embedding model gives other scores, so keep it fixed across the runs you compare.

items.title: retrieval_recall
items.text:
The reward of a retrieval dataset: of the gold passages, the share the embedding model ranked in its top k. Passages are compared as text, trimmed. Every list field of the expected answer is scored this way and the fields averaged; with one chunks list, that is recall at k.

rewards:
  recall:
    type: retrieval_recall
    description: Share of the gold passages among the top k retrieved.

The score depends on the dataset's k as much as on the model: with k as large as the number of chunks, every model scores 1. Compare embedding models at the same k, and pick a k close to what your application hands a model.

items.title: tool_calls_accuracy
items.text:
The reward of a tool-call dataset. Each gold call is matched with one call of the answer that has the same function name and the same arguments (as JSON, key order aside). The score is the matched calls over the longer of the two lists, so a missed call, an extra call and a wrong argument all cost. Both lists empty scores 1: the model rightly called nothing.

rewards:
  tool-calls:
    type: tool_calls_accuracy
    description: The right functions called with the right arguments.

Arguments must match exactly: {"city": "Paris"} and {"city": "paris"} differ, and so do {"limit": 10} and {"limit": "10"}. Write the gold calls in the form the function declaration asks for.

It needs no mask: the automatic field choice keeps the tool_calls field whole, and a call's id, which differs from run to run, is never compared.

items.title: harbor_verifier
items.text:
The reward of a Harbor task folder dataset. After the agent works, Harbor runs the task's own tests/, which write /logs/verifier/reward.txt (one number) or reward.json (named numbers). This reward reads that score; it needs no expected answer.

rewards:
  harbor-tests:
    type: harbor_verifier
    description: The score the task's own tests gave.
field values default effect key a name in reward.json reward which number to read; reward.txt is read as reward

A trial whose tests wrote nothing scores 0. A value that is not a number scores 0, and one outside 0 to 1 is clamped into it; both log a warning asking you to fix the task's tests/test.sh. Set key when the tests write several numbers ({"reward": 0.5, "tests_passed": 0.8}) and you want one other than reward.

items.title: Judged rewards
items.text:
A judge is a language model that reads the answer, and the expected answer when the dataset has one, then writes a critique and a grade. The grade is normalized to 0 to 1.

type judge grade calls per row lm_as_judge one model one score, 0 to 1 in steps of 0.05 1 rubrics_as_judge one model one score per criterion, 1 to 20, weighted mean 1 ready-made rubrics as rubrics_as_judge, criteria built in as rubrics_as_judge 1 multi_judge_panel several models, a stronger one on disagreement the panel's or the arbiter's one per panelist, plus 1 on disagreement rlm_as_judge a model writing and running Python any value from 1 to 20 up to max_iterations turns, plus sub-model calls deep_agent_as_judge a coding agent with files and a shell 1 to 20 up to max_iterations turns

Every judge's model needs its provider key, like any model (Providers and keys). Its calls are counted apart from the model under test's, as reward_cost.

Every judge takes, besides the masks:

field values default effect language_model an llm model name the evaluation's default_language_model the judge (multi_judge_panel names its models otherwise) instructions text the type's own what the judge is asked to do; replaces the default reduction mean, sum, min, max, none mean how several values from one call combine; a judge returns one, so leave it

Always name the judge

Without language_model, a judge uses the evaluation's default_language_model, so the same reward means something else in another evaluation. Name the judge in the reward.

The scale and the prompt layout belong to the engine: a config cannot change them. You control the judge model and the instructions.

items.title: lm_as_judge
items.text:
One call per row. The judge critiques the answer, then picks a score from 0.0 to 1.0 in steps of 0.05.

rewards:
  support-judge:
    type: lm_as_judge
    description: Correct, complete and polite, against the reference reply.
    tags: [judge]
    config:
      language_model: judge-4o       # the judge's own models.yaml entry
      instructions: |
        You grade a support reply against a reference reply (the gold_ fields).
        Score 1.0 when it solves the customer's problem as the reference does
        and is polite. Score 0.5 when it is correct but misses a step.
        Score 0.0 when it is wrong, invents a policy, or refuses.
        Length and tone beyond politeness do not count.

Writing instructions. Without them the judge grades on its own idea of quality. Say what full marks, half marks and zero look like, with the concrete faults that cost points. Say what does not count (length, format): judges otherwise favour long, confident answers. Mention the gold_ fields when there is a reference, so the judge grades against it rather than against its own knowledge.

When: free text with one notion of good: correctness against a reference, helpfulness, a style rule. To know which aspect failed, use rubrics.

items.title: rubrics_as_judge
items.text:
The judge scores each criterion on its own, from 1 to 20, and the reward is the weighted mean of the criteria, normalized to 0 to 1. One call per row, however many criteria.

rewards:
  math-rubrics:
    type: rubrics_as_judge
    description: Correct result, shown work, stated unit.
    config:
      language_model: judge-4o
      rubrics:
        - The final answer is correct              # a bare string: the name is derived from it
        - name: shows_steps
          description: Each step of the computation is written out.
        - name: units
          description: The answer states its unit.
          weight: 0.5                              # counts half as much as the others
field values default effect rubrics a list of criteria, or a preset name required what is graded rubrics[].name text, turned into snake_case derived from the description the criterion's name; unique rubrics[].description text required what the judge checks rubrics[].weight a number above 0 1.0 the criterion's share of the mean instructions text grade each criterion independently, then critique the judge's task

A criterion is a bare string (its name derived from it) or a mapping with name, description and weight. rubrics can also name a preset from the next section (rubrics: faithfulness).

When: the answer has several qualities you care about, and one number would hide which one a model lacks. Write each criterion as one checkable statement; "is good" grades nothing. Two to five criteria work better than fifteen: each one dilutes the others in the mean.

Note

The reward is still one number. To see a criterion apart in the results, give it its own reward as an extra metric.

items.title: Ready-made rubric judges
items.text:
Rubric judges with their criteria built in, for common checks. Each takes language_model, instructions, reduction and the masks; none takes rubrics.

rewards:
  faithful:
    type: faithfulness
    description: The answer does not contradict the retrieved context.
    config:
      language_model: judge-4o
task types answers and RAG answer_relevancy, faithfulness, hallucination, citation_faithfulness, contextual_precision, contextual_recall, contextual_relevancy, summarization agents and tools task_completion, goal_accuracy, plan_quality, plan_adherence, step_efficiency, tool_correctness, tool_use, tool_permission, argument_correctness, agent_loop_detection conversations topic_adherence, role_adherence, role_violation, prompt_alignment, knowledge_retention, conversation_completeness, turn_faithfulness, turn_relevancy safety bias, toxicity, pii_leakage, misuse, non_advice

They grade what the judge can see. faithfulness needs the context in the answer or in the reference. Agent checks such as step_efficiency need the agent's steps, which an MCP agent dataset hides from rewards by default: set a mask that keeps them (out_mask: [thinking] turns the default off and leaves messages in).

Check which way a preset scores

Each preset is one criterion written as a task ("indicate whether each opinion is toxic"). Whether a high score means clean or toxic is left to the judge's reading. Run five rows whose answer you know, read the scores, then set direction. When in doubt, use rubrics_as_judge with a criterion that says which way is good ("The answer contains no insult").

items.title: multi_judge_panel
items.text:
Several judges grade each row in parallel, with the same instructions. When their scores lie within agreement_threshold of each other, the panelist closest to the panel's mean gives the score. When they disagree, a stronger model judges the row alone, and its score is the reward.

rewards:
  panel:
    type: multi_judge_panel
    description: Two small judges, a large one on disagreement.
    config:
      panel_language_models: [qwen38, gpt-4o-mini]   # from different families
      smart_language_model: gpt-4o                   # required
      agreement_threshold: 0.2
      instructions: |
        Score 1.0 when the answer matches the reference (the gold_ fields), 0.0 when not.
field values default effect panel_language_models a non-empty list of llm model names required the panelists smart_language_model an llm model name required the arbiter on disagreement, and the fallback when every panelist fails agreement_threshold a number, 0 to 1 0.2 the widest spread (highest score minus lowest) still read as agreement instructions text the judge's own given to every panelist and to the arbiter

Panelists grade 0 to 1 in steps of 0.05. A panelist that returns no score is dropped.

When: you want a strong judge's quality at a fraction of its cost, and most rows are easy. Easy rows cost the small panel; hard ones add one call of the arbiter. A lower agreement_threshold sends more rows to the arbiter (dearer, closer to the strong judge alone); a higher one trusts the panel more (cheaper, noisier). Panelists from different families also dilute any one family's bias.

Both are required. openarena check reports a panel left empty (multi_judge_panel needs `panel_language_models`: at least one judge) and a missing arbiter (multi_judge_panel needs `smart_language_model`: the judge that settles a split panel).

items.title: rlm_as_judge and deep_agent_as_judge
items.text:
Judges that work before they grade, for answers whose correctness cannot be read off the text: code to run, a long output to diff, a figure to recompute.

  • rlm_as_judge writes and runs Python in a sandbox, with the answer and the reference bound as data. It can compute its grade (a pass rate, a field-by-field ratio), so any value on its scale is allowed, and it can hand pieces of a long answer to a sub-model.
  • deep_agent_as_judge is a coding agent in a sandbox, with file tools and a shell. The answer and the reference are written to a file there, so it can run a generated script before grading. Each row starts from a clean sandbox.
rewards:
  code-judge:
    type: rlm_as_judge
    description: Runs the generated code and compares its output with the reference.
    config:
      language_model: judge-4o
      max_iterations: 10
      timeout: 60
      instructions: |
        Run the code in the answer. Score 1.0 when its output equals the
        reference output (the gold_ fields), 0.0 when it fails or differs.
field rlm_as_judge default deep_agent_as_judge default effect language_model the evaluation's default the evaluation's default the judge sub_language_model language_model language_model the model for sub-queries (rlm) or sub-agents (deep) max_iterations 20 10 turns before the judge must grade timeout 60 30.0 seconds per code turn (rlm) or per shell command (deep) use_chain_of_thought false false think step by step before each turn instructions the type's own the type's own the judging task

Both grade on 1 to 20, normalized. They are the slowest and dearest rewards: each row is a small agent run. Lower max_iterations to bound the cost, and keep them for rows a single read cannot decide.

agent_as_judge is in the catalog too, but it needs tools to call, and a config entry cannot give it any. openarena check refuses it (agent_as_judge cannot be built from an entry: it needs `tools`, which an entry cannot give) and points to the alternatives: rlm_as_judge or deep_agent_as_judge, which need no tools, or a judge such as lm_as_judge over the agent's messages.

items.title: The judge model
items.text:
A judge should be at least as capable as the models it grades, on the task it grades. A small judge grading a large model's math marks right answers wrong. Give the judge its own entry in models.yaml, so it is never confused with a model under test:

models:
  judge-4o:
    model: openai/gpt-4o
    params:
      temperature: 0                 # the same answer gets the same grade, as far as the provider allows
    description: The judge. Never under test.
    tags: [judge]

Give the judge entry temperature: 0. A judge's params (temperature, max_tokens, reasoning_effort) are sent with each of its calls, as a model under test's are (Where the params apply). At 0 it grades steadily from row to row and from run to run; a sampling judge adds its own noise to every score. Even at 0, hosted providers do not promise identical answers, so expect a small spread between reruns.

Keep the judge fixed across every run you compare: scores from two judges are not on the same scale. The evaluation's seed does not make a judge reproducible; it seeds local randomness, not the provider's sampling. temperature: 0 is what steadies the judge.

items.title: Self-preference
items.text:
A model judging its own answers, or answers from its own family, tends to score them higher. Nothing stops you from naming the same model as judge and as candidate, so guard against it yourself:

  • Never put the judge in the evaluation's language_models.
  • Prefer a judge from another provider than the candidates. When the candidates span several providers, a multi_judge_panel mixing families spreads the bias instead of favouring one side.
  • When your own model family is under test, do not let that family judge.

items.title: Calibrating
items.text:
A judge is an instrument: check it before trusting its readings.

  1. Take 20 to 30 rows and grade the answers yourself.
  2. Run the judge on the same answers.
  3. Compare. Where you disagree, read the judge's critique and tighten the instructions: name the fault it missed, or say what should not count.
  4. Repeat until it agrees with you on nearly every row, then freeze the model and the instructions.

Then run the judge twice on the same answers: the spread between the two runs is the smallest gap between models you can believe.

items.title: Combining rewards
items.text:
A dataset has one reward: it fills the reward column, and leaderboards rank on it first. Any other reward can score the same rows as an extra column, under a dataset's or an evaluation's metrics: (Extra metrics). There, a catalog reward is named with class:, its settings written inline, an alias naming the column, and its own direction. A metric written without direction: is read as max, except a cost, tokens or latency measurement, read as min; write direction: to say otherwise, as toxicity does below.

datasets:
  gsm8k-20:
    # ...
    reward: exact-match                              # the primary score
    metrics:
      - answer_accuracy                              # partial credit beside it
      - {class: lm_as_judge, alias: reasoning, language_model: judge-4o, instructions: "Score 1.0 when every step is correct."}
      - {class: toxicity, alias: toxicity, language_model: judge-4o, direction: min}

A leaderboard then weighs the columns with shares: ({reward: 60, reasoning: 30, cost: 10}) and can leave a model out with budgets:.

goal primary reward extra metrics a strict score, and how close the misses were exact_match answer_accuracy correctness with a safety gate a judge or exact_match toxicity, pii_leakage, used as budgets several criteria reported apart rubrics_as_judge for the whole one judge per criterion a cheap rule, checked by a judge exact_match lm_as_judge, to spot where the rule is too strict

Make the primary reward the one you would defend alone. The extra metrics explain it; they should not be needed to read it.

items.title: Direction
items.text: direction: min is for a reward where lower is better: a score read as "how much" of something bad. The run records the direction, and leaderboards and the Pareto frontier read it: you never invert a score yourself. Every reward above scores "how good" by design; only the safety and hallucination presets may read the other way (see their warning).

items.text: dataset or task reward why multiple choice (MMLU style) exact_match on the letter one correct token math with a final number (GSM8K style) exact_match on the number, answer_accuracy beside it the number decides classification, extraction into fields answer_accuracy partial credit per field short factual answer, varied wording lm_as_judge with the reference; cosine_similarity if cost matters a rule cannot see synonyms summaries, emails, open answers rubrics_as_judge several qualities in one score RAG answers faithfulness, answer_relevancy, or your own rubrics grounding is not in the reference retrieval with embedding models retrieval_recall the gold passages are known function calling, nothing executed tool_calls_accuracy calls can be checked MCP agents exact_match or a judge on the final answer; agent presets as extra metrics the answer and the path are scored apart A2A agents as for the task the agent answers the reward reads the answer, whoever gave it Harbor task folders harbor_verifier the task's tests decide code that must run rlm_as_judge, deep_agent_as_judge, or a Harbor task the text alone cannot tell

items.title: Common mistakes
items.text:
openarena check reads the files, without calling anything, and reports:

mistake what it says a misspelt type unknown reward 'exact_matsh', with the closest name as the fix a setting the type does not take lm_as_judge does not take `language_modl`, with the rename name or direction inside config config cannot set direction: use `type` and `direction` a litellm id instead of a model name 'openai/gpt-4o-mini' is not in `models`; the fix names the entry that calls it an embedding model as a judge, or the reverse 'minilm' is an embedding model; this setting needs a language model a dataset naming a reward that does not exist the dataset's reward is not in rewards, with the closest name rubrics_as_judge without rubrics rubrics_as_judge needs `rubrics`: the criteria it grades, with an example list as the fix multi_judge_panel without its panel or its arbiter multi_judge_panel needs `panel_language_models`: at least one judge, multi_judge_panel needs `smart_language_model`: the judge that settles a split panel reduction on a deterministic reward exact_match does not take `reduction`; only judges take it a judge's setting beside type: instead of under config: (reduction: mean) not a field of a `rewards` entry, with the fix move it under `config:` agent_as_judge agent_as_judge cannot be built from an entry: it needs `tools`, which an entry cannot give, with the alternatives

What only the run finds:

  • a dataset with no reward: the run refuses it.
  • a judge whose provider key is missing: the cell fails (Reading results).
  • every row scoring 0 with exact_match: compare an answer with its expected answer in the result. The form differs: a string against a number, extra words, another case.

items.text:
openarena rewards list --configs configs       # each reward, its type and direction
openarena check configs/rewards.yaml           # validate, references checked against the folder
